Which is still - A fashion that the cats keep op, And, doubtless, always will. OF TIIE Have they told yea I tem going p• To the land of rest? I am very patient. knigin , All is for the best Yet the summer light is clearest •• . Ere the soul departs, Nature seems to draw the nearest Under dying hearts: Have they told you I am leaving Earthly things behind ? Love, perhaps, was but deceiving., Friendship proved unkind Yet the sunshine, slowly stealing Down the soft green slope. Brings back all the trustful 'feeling, All the dreams of hope, - Have they told you I am hasting - To a fairer home ? Yes; but here are roses wasting, Blossoms white as foam ; Here are sun-gilt vine-leaves wreathilfg Round our cottsge door; Here are solemn fir-trees breathing Fragrance evermore. Have they told you I tun setting All my thoughts on high? Yes; but can I learn forgetting While old haunts are nigh? When the bracken plumes are swaying On our pine-orewn'd hill, I can almost hear you saying That you love me still. Hush! I hear a footstep falling * On the garden plot, And a voice spasks, softly calling, Yet I answer not- Till I feel your arras around me, On my face your breath. Love and faith have sought and found me; This is life—not death. —SsaAn DOIIDM, in G•od Words.

A RUSSIAN STUDENT DEVOURED BY WOLVES—The Gales publishes the following :—" On the 12th inst. Alex- ander Vassilwitch Elisaieff, a Mediae.' student, the author of many articles that have hone time to time- appeared in Russian journals, and an indefatigable student of the aranolog and anthropology of the ancient ptovinee of Nov-11 Worod, arrived on the 11th inst., on the estate of a Mr.' Vassilief, in Old Russia, in, order to hunt wolves. He was desired to stay the night at the house, and not to face the dangers of the chase alone. To this he agreed, bat when , Mr. Vassilief, who had been obliged to absent himself during the day, returned in the evening, he learnt that his guest had left the house about four o'clock in the afternoon. His ; return was looked for from hour to hour, but the whole of the night pissed without his arrival. On the following day,! towards eventt peasant.brought the intelligence pat the , young man had been torn to pieces and devoured by wolves, I When a search was made the snow was found to be covered with blood stains, and scattered around were pieces of clothes and hunting appurtenances. Not far from the place were found several large bones, and the stock of the student's gun, with the barrel broken off in the life and death struggle which he had eeidently maintained with his numerous foes. The many wolf-tracks and blood stains all around showed that a severe struggle had taken place, and that several of the animals had been killed and devoured by their fellows." AGRARIAN OFFENCHS IN IRELAND.—It appears from return published on Monday—the first of a series of fort- nightly returns—that the total number of agrarian offences specially reported to the Irish Constabulary between the Ist And 14th instant, both days inclusive, was 287. The offences are thus classified :—Firing at persona 2, aggravated assault 5, assault endangering life 1, assault on bailiffs and process- servers 1, incendiary, fire, and arson 11, burglary and rob- bery 3, taking and holding forcible possession 5, killitg, cutting, or maiming cattle 1, demand or robbery of arms 15, riots and frays 1, administering unlawful oaths 7, intimida- tion by threatening letters and notices 150, otherwise 23, 'eattacking houses 4, resistance to legal process 1, injury to property 118, firing into dwellings 12, assault on police I, making the total named. The Largest number of offences, 119, were reported from Connaught, while Munster is re- sponsible for 100, Leinster for 39, and Ulster for 29. The largest number reported for any one county was in Mayo, where 50 took place. In the West Riding of Galway there 33, in the West Riding of Cork 32, and in the East Riding of the same county 24. In three counties there were no outrages reported; these were Fermanagh, Dublin, and Meath. The only basis of comparison at present available is the return for December. From this it appears that during the thirty-one days of December, 1580, 867 eases were re- ported against the 287 reported during the first fourteen days of January, showing a marked diminution. PHOTOGRAPHS or NEBUL2E.—At the last meeting of the Royal Astronomical Society, Mr. 0. Ranyard, described the first photograph of nebulte ever taken. It was made by Dr. Draper, of New York, son of the Dr. Draper 'who first used the daguerreotype process in 1840 for taking a human photograph. The nebulas are those in Orion. The photo- graph shows plainly the "Fish's head.' Hand drawings of nebulas have been made from telescopic observation by Bond, Herschel, Liaponnov,•Lassell, Sechi, and Lord Rosse, but they differ much. A bet was recently made by two French gourmands, one of whom asserted that he could detect the component parts of any dish put before him, the other betting at great odds that he would not be able to tell the material wherewith his cook would prepare a "savoury dish" for them. The bet was taken, the one confident in his quick natural sense, the other in the skill of hi cook. The cook a Frenchman, of course—exerted all his talents, and surpassed all praise. The dish was placed before the knowing epicure. He tastes smacks his lips, tastes again, smells it, tastes again. Alas! it is redolent of all rich odours ;such sauces, so marvellously blended ; such gravy, such solids--so soft so tender! What can it be? A wondrous prepared tripe? No! Calves' head in a new shape? No, no, no l—a thousand "Noes." Our epicure gives it up. "It is old white kid gloves !" is the cool explanation, when the bet is resigned as lost. THE SOUNDS OF BELLS IN CONTACT WITH LIQUIDS..-- Every one knows that a glass gives a graver sound on being struck when containing water than when empty. The rela- tions of this class of phenomena have been studied by M. Montigny, who got eleven bells belonging to the chime of an old clockand compared their tones when merely filled with liquideuor when immersed in iquids, with those they gave in the 'air. He tried different liquids—viz., water, alcohol, ether, and sulphide of carbon, He found that, however the liquid was applied, the sound given in contact with it was always graver than the natural; that the lower- ing of tone was more marked the denser the liquid (thus it was less with ether than with sulphide of carbon) ; also more sett rked , whatever the liquid, when the bell was completely Immersed than when it was merely filled; and that, with either mode of application, the lowering was greater for grave than for acute notes. The additional fact that the lowering of tone when aa, bell is merely filled with a liquid and that which occurs when, being empty, it is immersed in the liquid up to its lip are exactly the same, shows that ;the alteration:blue. tO the influence which that part of the liquid in contact with the metal has on the vibrations of the latter (not to • the metal and liquid 'forming a vibrating whole). Further, the compressibility of the liquid is a sac- „tor in the result.. Water is both less compressible and more -dense than alcohol and ether, and it lowers the tone more. The result is also affected by the form of the bell and. he elasticity and density of its substance. It Mobviettselastiv, that a chime which presents a perfect gamut in air no longer does so when in contact with liquid.

VARIATIONS /N THE QUALITY OF MILK. At most farmhouses where milk is not sold, but made Into cheese, the greater number of cows calve in the early spring. Most cheesernakerwknow that the milk in the early part of the season is not nearly so rich as it is towards the end of the season; but perhaps few know the actual yield of cheese from a given quantity of milk in each month. It perhaps may be interesting to some if I state the quantity of cheese made from a given quantity of milk during each month of the cheesemaking season in one of the Derbyshire factories in the years 1876 to 1880. I may say the cheese which was made each day was weighed the following morn- ing. Ido not know how , to account for this unusual increase In November, 1879. I state the simple facts. Your readers can then draw their own conclusions. The cows were not giving half the quan- tity of milk they were giving in November, 1878. Whether that would have anything to do with it I do not know. Again, from this table we may gather that, taking the figures for IflBo for our guide in April it would take 26,8911b5. of milk to make a ton of cheese (reckoning the Cwt. at 1201b5.), whereas that number of pounds of milk would in November make 1 ton 7cwts. aqrs. 23Ibs. I am by no means satisfied in my own mind that the richness of the milk in November is entirely due to the cows being " old milched," but I have had no opportunity of proving this. If any one of the readers of the Agricul- tural Gazette could tell us how much cheese I,ooolbs. of milk from newly-calved cows would make in November, it would tend to show whiether milk is naturally richer in No- vember, or whether the variation between April and Novem- ber is entirely owing to the cows being newly-calved in April, and to their being" old milehed "in November. The variations in the degrees of cream are no less striking than the variations in the weight of cheese, and they are much more difficult to account for. The data at my com- mand for these are much more imperfect than those for the weight of cheese, but I will give them for one dairy as often as they were taken by means of the cream gauges in the year 179. It is rare (so far as I have ' observed) to see 'the healthy bloom, the fresh, clear complexion so common to no deposit banks, no societies for clothing the Hottentots. English girls and young women, and I am assured that As I said before, it was the good old days. The zodiac was both the teeth and the hair are prematurely. lost in this in perfect order. Not a Christian man had heard of the colony. I will not May to 'inquire why or how this is, but vagaries of the Gulf Stream. May Day brought its flowem it would seem probable that one Cause is the absence of and its festivals to the moment by the record of strictest winter, or of sufficient cold to brace and give tone to the sundial. At Easter there were gammons of bacon all over system. Without this bracing frost neither English oaks, the land, and Easter huts even in the Warren of Staines nor fruits, nor young folk thrive as in the "old country," and Forest. The red man roamed at will in the undreamed-of to this same cause may probably in a great measure be at- forests of the New World. Tee dusky Indian bad no master tributed the dyspepsia, liver and heart affections which lam but his untamed will. The wild boar and the wolf challenged told prevail here. Hence too, a certain loss of working illlei hunter's power in English woods. The eagle sat in , praergy, the necessity of a Change during the summer, the solemn state eft tile white cliffs of Dover. There were omens. The owl shrieked, the night crow crowed, the raven clapped ftequency and popularity of holidays, the shortness of work-e ing hours, and the indisposition to take long walks. -.Many his wings, death-bells were beard at sea; your grandfather, persons have resided in Auckland for years without ascend- clad in armour as he lived, walked out of his ancient picture- ing either of the "mounts" I have referred to, although frame; and once is a way some weird and witched tree the most distant, "Mount Albert," is but five miles off, and ;would spout fire from its shrunken boughs. Night was night, , setting off with a few sandwiches you may spend the day and day VMS day. You rose with the lark, you rested when amid scenery far surpassing Whitewell or Longridge. the sun went down on lands not yet weighed„and mapped, Riding is here almost as common as walking, and I should and colonised. Knives and forks were unknown'iniplements ; say more frequent than it was 30 years ago in the remote and when Prinee struck his wife he struck her with his, rural districts of England. 1 With so much sunehise and with a prolific soil, it is dis- mailed hand, and none could say him nay.—Joseph Hatton. appointing to find so little fruit grown in and around Auck- I label, and that it is far dearer than in England. Apples are now 6d. and 81 a pound; rhubarb is poorer in quality and , six times as dear as in the "old country ; ' oranges cost lls. ler 12s. a case containing 120, so that, if all sound, they are , a little over Id. each; peaches have of late been under a blight in this neighbourhood, but some years ago a peck could be bought for a few pence; gooseberries are Bd. a pound (not (part). Mosethings, I may say, are dearer here than in England. Rents are higher, because investors re- quire a higher per centage of interest than usually obtains "at home.' Here, for instannis, is what in England would be called a very very small house, with four rooms (none of them large) and a small kitchen cn the first floor, and four attic rooms on the second. The rent is £7B a year, and the tenant pays all the rates; these, including the cost of night soil, are within a fraction equal to what I paid " at home." .Ironmongery, crockery, drugs, machinery, groceries (with one or two exceptions), glass, books and stationery, and English-made furniture, are from 20 per cent. to 50 per cent. dearer than in Englartd, some articles much more than that. The fact is that " Protection " (of which New Zealand lecturers say so little) means high prices, and when to the , 1 duty of, say, 16 per cent., you add cost of packing and I freight, of course the Colonial consumer is heavily mulcted, , But a few articles are cheaper than at home—butcher's meat; , 1 for instance, and potatoes, but the best meat (such as bbeSC steak) is Bd. a pound, and mutton sd. (this may be had as low as 3d., and a suspicious-looking article for 2d. and 2ed.); bacon is 9d. per lb., and likely to be dearer. Fish is cer- tainly cheaper, but, except the mullet, it is coarse and tough in fibre and miserably destitute of flavour. Flour, bread, ' and tea are about the same as in England; eggsare 12 (very small) for ls. 3d., and likely to be dearer. Boots and shoes are lower in price, but by no means cheaper tban in Eng- land, for Colonial leather is at present notably inferior to imported. Furniture, if really good, is also very expensive. Many people (wisely enough) buy low-priced Kauri furni- ture and American cane-seated chairs ; if you require better wood (for Kauri, except the "mottled," is soft and feeble), say cedar, you must pay for it. A dining-room suite in cedar, covered with horse-hair and stuffed with flax, con- sisting of six chairs, two arm chairs, and a couch, may be had for £25. If finished off, as is usual in England, this would be reasonable, but the brand of Colonial work, so tar as my experience yet goes, is want of finish, and, what is more, the workers know and excuse it. If you point out this or that defect, you are assured that what you desire is quite unnecessary. "I am told," said a lady critic writing from this very city, "that they are satisfied with shams." This said suite, for example, will be sent out only half polished, in some parts not polished at all, and with indenta- tionswhich would lead an Englishman to swear it was second- hand. It is perhaps unavoidable that this feature (want of finish) should be truly Colonial. What ought we to expect from half a century? Auck- land has not yet seen its jubilee, yet we have a large and spreading city of 30,000 inhabitants, with beautiful suburbs, numerous banks, churches, and schools, newspapers (two daily) gas, telegraphs, &c. All this (considering the short- ness of the time and the scant population) is simply mar- vellous, t and presents a splendid monument o English in- dustry and public spirit, remarkable for its magnitude rather than for its solidity and finish. Crudeness, immaturity, and roughness are visible enough to the "microscopic eye,' but will disappear with increasing prosperity, educaeion, and re- finement. A colony so infantile has scarcely emerged Pont its first conflict—the struggle to live—or, at most, has Only just entered upon its second and long conflict—the struggle to progress and improve. What this city will be dothatot yet appear, but if so much has been accomplished- in '4O years' who can estimate or conceive the achievements of the next 400?

div.p: 11% the whole, furnishing and living in any approach to conlEirt and tespectability are decidedly more costly in the colony than "at home ;' for, besides the higher scale of 'Most necessaries, labour is vastly dearer. A joiner works eight -hours a day and gets from Bs. to 125.; a gas-fitter, from Bs. to lls. per day.; bricklayers and coachbuilders, 10s.. to 12s. a. day, dm— A charwoman charges 4s. to ss. a day, all found. In some branches trade is at present very bad: many persons, I am told, cannot get situations; even domestic servants are not in great demand, and in some cases are returning "home." Professional fees, however, except legal, which are extravagantly high, are in this city less than in England. Two more impressions I will name, because they are un- avoidable. The luxuriance of Nature impresses every_ observer. Foliage, plants, grasses, and flowers super-abound. This whole neighbourhood might be made one vast garden. Roses, lilies, and other flowers, which in many an English home would be welcome gifts, grow wild and in profusion ;and as to garlien roses, though not endowed with the fragrance of those at home," they are superb in colour, purity, and propertion. Animal life is equally prolific. Horses, cows, sheep, dogs, rabbits, rats, and mice multiply and enjoy life famously; and as to insects, they are like the plagues of Egypt; this region seems the paradise of flies, mosquitoes (known more Or less all over Anckand and vicinity), snails, moths, centipedes, Sm. This abounding life could only ob- tain in• a healthful and semi-tropical climate. , First, last, and deepest of all is the iMpression how very English New, Zealand is—how all that is English has been transplanted and reproduced, or, shall we say, has saturated the atmoSphere of colonial life socially, politically, and reli; " HQW eo you like Auckland ?" I ask a colonist who some ten yedrs Ago reaclecl, in Preston. "I like the' Climate and the scenery," he replied, ",but not the people." • I have met several who expressed a similar feeling; such people are to be found in connection with Over' town. Aucklanders they say are cold, distant, suspicioua, as 'cut as Yankees and care for nothing but what they can get out of you. Tlk, some extedt these charges may be true, and naturally so. Most communities would grow suspicious If flooded every, year with new arrivals, some of whom might truly say—

True pate( ots we, who left our country For our country's good. and who have sionsly. transferred their evil habits from an old to a new social condition, blessing neither. As to cute- ness, it is undoubtedly true as a rule that those who go to the colonies go to make money, honestly if possible—but to make it. As to cordiality, so far as my experience goes, to anyone coming here with fair credentials as to character and ability an old English welcome and a right hearty shake.of the hand are invariably given. Had I been known person- ally before my arrival, I could hardly have received greater kindness. 'Ministers, too, are always ready to hail acces- sions; the spirit of competition (or whatever else it may be called) invades the churches, which in the main are faC- similes of those at horse and of which more anon. Amuse- ments are English. Minicipal cusitorns and laws and getne- ral legislation as far as posslble follow English precedent. The early scenes in the history of nearly every person we meet were. laid in Old England, and no tOpic of conversa- tion is more fruitful or Congenial than the "bygones" awl memeri4and associations of English life; What, then, is "the Conclusion of the whole matter?'? Why, that again' and again we new corners unconsciously-forget distance, and dream we'are still in the dear "old country," it is in, many- ways so like; but alas! as we pass down the:streets and look"expectingly for familiar forms andlacee—they are gone,: and the smiles of life-long friendships h4ve vanished. This Is not our own, our nativeiland I—Yours faithfully,
EDWIN Cox.

THE GREAT STNTKE OF MINERS.
PRECAUTIONS AGAINST DISTURBANCES.

, On Sunday morning another body of county police left North Lancashire for Skelmersdale. During Saturday night the police observed some colliers skulking round the house of Mr. Hewitt, colliery proprietor, Standish, add their inten- tions being susp2cted they were driven off. The residence is proteeted. •• There were about a thousand constables, out of a total force of thirteen Mildred, stationed within a safe distance ready to quell any outbreak. - There were cavalry at Hindley and infantry arSt. Helens. , Arrangements had been coriapleted for the immediate despatch, if necessary, of cavalry and-infantry from Preston, Salford, Warrington, and Ashton-under-Lyne. ARRIVAL OF THE MILI Y AT WIGAN.

In-accordsince with the requisition of the Wigan County Magistrates, a troop of the 11th Hussars, 30 in number, under the command of Captain Parker "arrived at Wigan on Saturday morning from Preston. On the caYalry leaving the station they were greeted with groan& They marched through the town to Hindley, and the men were quartered in the Public Hall. About 50 County Constabulary also occupied the premises. A mass meeting of miners was intended to be held about noon on 6aturday on Amberswood Common, a large open apace between Ince and Hindley. The men attended in' great numbers from the Leigh, Tyldesley, and Hindley dis- trict, and it was estimated that nearly 6,000 persons were present. The promoters of qie meeting, said to be from the Leigh division, did not consider that the Wigan men were sufficiently represented, owing probably to the feet that the meeting bad not been made known in that part, and they therefore decided to adjourn to the borough of Wigan. The crowd then marched in procession to Wigan, but instead of increasing the men gradually stopped behind or went in other directions, so that on reaching the Market Square, Wigan, the number was not half that it was on the Corn- mon. The speakers mounted the frozen drinking fountain surrounding the market lamp, and Mr. J. Bradshaw, of Atherton, was called upon to preside. He was supportedby delegates from Leigh, Bedford, Tyldeeley, Atherton, Hind- ley, Ice, and St. Helens. The following resolution was carried :--" That each and every man at this meeting shall play, and not resume work no matter what cond'tions the masters offer until all go in and they give us what we are asking for—an advance of wages equal to the last reduction and weekly pays."

During -the tlene the above meeting was taking place the Wigan delezates and representatives from each pit set of men contributing to the Check-weighman's Fund were hold- ing a meeting in the Miners' Hall. This fund is contributed to at the collieries for the special purpose of meeting the expenses in connection with the providing of check-weigh- men. The subscribers are not necessarily connected with the Miners' Union, but nearly all those in the Union are also members of this fund. 'there is now in hand a sum of £l,OOO, and it was decided that with the exception of £2OO, which should be retained in hand to carry on the fund, the amount should be divided amongst the members. These number about 4,000, so 'that the distribution will be at the rate of 4s. each. The meeting also resolved that a deputa- tion should wait upon Mr. Peace, the secretary of the West Lancashire Coal Association, in order to ascertain whether the masters have any fresh proposals to make tl the men, and further to see if the masters were having another meet- ing, and whether they would be prepared to give an inter- view to Mr. W. Pickard (Vegan) and Mr. Wood (Ashton-in- Makerfield), as a deputation from the men, to talk the whole matter over.

Most of the men have been idle since January 1. The only relief received from-the Union has been one week's pay to about 1,000 men (the whole number of Union men in the Wigan district is some 1,600 or 1,700) and the above distri- tion from the Check-weighman's Fund. ADVANCE IN THH PRICI3 OF DURHAM COAL.—OWITIg to the great demand brought about by the cold weather and increased by the Lancashire strike--coal having been taken to the west coast district in consemsence—the Durham coalovvners decided on Saturday to at orlon advance their prices Is. per ton. On Monday, the miners held a meeting in the Temper- ance Hall, Tyldesley, the room being packed. The chair- man said hebelieved they were beaten, and, amid interrup- tion, he declared that public opinion was against them. A speaker declared that if the employers won they would use the cat-o'-nine-tails to them. There were several disor- derly scenes, and it was resolved to continue the strike. Over a hundred men went to work :on Monday morning at the Rash Colliery. Another meeting was held at Leigh at noon on Monday. The speakers throughout were in favour of remaining out until what was asked for was conceded. One of the speakers condemned the lethargy of the shareholders of the collieries in not looking after their own interests as the reason the men did not get what they deserved. The men agreed to remain firm and not resume work. The strike in Bolton and Farnwortb virtually concluded on Monday, the colliers resuming well( under the Em- ployers' Liability Act, and in some instances at an ad- vance in wages. At the pits owned by the leading Manchester firms the th miners remain at work, and at e principal pi now very nearly the full complement of men down. Any i pressure arising from actual scarcity of coal s now to a great extent removed. ENCOUNTER BETWEEN POLICE AND COLLIERS AT TYLDESLEY. ONE MAN KILLED. On Tuesday, at noon, after the meeting in Tyldesley- square, an immense body of colliers, several thousand strong, hurried off, but not in processional order, in the direction of the Wharton Hall Coal Company's Colliery. The mob took the field way, the distance from the place of meeting being some two miles. On their way they passed the Combermere pit of the Tyldesley Coal Company, on to the brow of which some hundreds clambered. The cry, however, was "No- body's down," so the crowd passed on, as numbers of them had done previously, taking various paths, some by the lane, others across the field, and an equal number by the footpath. On reaching the Wharton Hall Company's Pits, known to the men by the name of Wash Pits, but properly named Black and White and Rams Pits, the great throng, despite the body of police present, swept on to the pit banks, where they clamoured for the men below to be brought out. For some minutes there was good order in the sense of no damage being done to property. Mr. Beswick, the manager, was told if lie would bring out his colliers and their drawers he ghould have no damage done, but if not it would be worse for him. The mouths of both pits were surround ed by the mob. The police, some score in number, were in charge of Inspector Charnley. It seemed evid t ent that he polie- were outnumbered. Assistance ex- pected from Little Hutton and 'Farnworth. For 9. time l- ives, however, twas evident the constabulary were waiting their oppor- tunity. tunity. Mr. Charnley everZwent so far as to appease. The la mob by saying the men would come t mob, which covered the pit banks, became momentarily more impatient, and declared they would never budge until the knobsticks" were brought out. The state of affairs grew more and more exciting ;. frightful were the execrations of the enraged colliers; they seemed

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY,

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsac:, shortly iwfore five o'clock. RIVERS CONSERVANCY BILL —The Duke of Ilicifluomn and GORDO', in reply to Earl Spencer, said it would be con- venient to the Opposition if the second reading of the Rivers Conservancy Bill we taken on Monday next. BURNETT'S LITERARY FUND—The Earl of ROSEBERY presented a petition from a number of professors of the Uni- versity of Aberdeen praying that their Lordships' House would be pleased to allow the Commissioners' order with regard to " Burnett's Literary Fund" to be carried into effect. —The Duke of RICHMOND rose to call attention to the pro- visional order made by the Secretary of State relating to the fund in question, and to move "That this House disap- proves of the said Provisional Order." The noble Duke presented petitions in favour of his motion—one from the city clergy of Aberdeen and the other from the Principal of the University, Dr. Pins. He explained that Butnett's Fund was a fund vested in trustees for the purpose of award- ing prizes every forty years in connection with the Aber- deen University in proof of the existence of the Deity. The fund of late years had been augmented, and it was proposed by the Provisional Order made by the Secretary of State to divert the fund and endow two lectureships, and under that scheme it was possible for Theism to be taught instead ef Christian evidences, which the testator desired to support.— The Earl of ROSERERY said the testator had bequeathed five- eights of £l,OOO, to be divided between the two successful essayists every 40 years, and the fund had now se grown that £6,000 would be divided amongst the next two successful essayists. Very few of the prize essays were ever circulated, and he believed that the wishes of the testator would be carried out if the Provisional Order were allowed to become law.—The motion was, however, agreed to. IRISH AORICULTURE.—On the motion of Lord Cum- CURRY, returns were agreed to of the total area of grass lands, including meadows and pastures, and the total area of tillage land, including all kinds of crops and fellows, in Ireland for the years 1850, 1855, 1860, 1865, 1870, 1875, and 1880. • Their Lordships adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. A CROWDED HOUSH.—The House was crowded in antici- pation of Mr. Forster's statement on introducing the first of the Coercion Bills which deals with the protection of person and property in Ireland. When the Mouse of Lords had completed its brief sitting, there was a rush of Peers for the limited accommodation provided in the gallery over the clock. One of the first to arrive and secure a favourable seat was the Earl of Derby. Lord Sydney and Lord Aber- dare also obtained places; but Lord 'Sherbrooke, coming a little late, was obliged to stand during the earlier portion of Mr. Forster's speech. Neither Mr. Parnell nor Mr. Shaw was present, but the tale of Irish representatives was other- wise full. The two front benches were even inconveniently crowded. The Premier was in his place, and all the Cabinet Ministers, including Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamber- lain.

QuEsnoNs.—There were thirty-nine questions on the paper, of which twenty-seven related to Irish affairs. As it is apparently necessary to set forth Irish questions at greater length than any other, and as many of the Irish members insist upon reciting :their compositions at full length, even these figures do not afford a precisely accurate view of the proportion of time occupied. TICE IRISH LAND BILL.—In reply to a question from Mr. Smythe, Mr. GrAnsvoNE regretted that it was not in his power to state when he would be in a position to give the House some indication of the provisions of the intended Irish Land Bill. The House had been in session some time, but actually they occupied a position similar to what in ordinary times would be reckoned as the third day of the session. Possibly, when the state of business was a little mOre developed the question might be more conveniently dealt with. . .

STREET CLELNSING.—In reply to a question on the sub- ject of cleansing the streets from snow, Sir JAMES Hon° Incidentally mentioned that a six inch fall of snow on the Victoria Embankment alone, which was the only road under the jurisdiction of the Metropolitan Board of Works, repre- sented a weight of eight and three-quarter millions of tons, "which," he observed, "was not to be disposed of in a few days." NEW WRIT FOR NEW Ross.—On the motion of Mr. R. Powxn, a new writ was ordered to be issued for New Ross. PROTECTION OF PERSON AND PROPERTY (IRELAND) BILL—At half-past five Mr. FORSTER rose, amid cheers, to l'ask leave to bring in a Bill for the better protection of per- sons and property in Ireland. At the outset he cited statistics to show that the condition of Ireland is more alarming than some people were aware of. During last year there had been 1,253 cases of agrarian outrage, exclu- awe of threatening letters, against 050 in 1845, the worst year previously known. The greatest increase had been in the last three months of the year, in which two-thirds of the whole had been perpetrated, and there had been more crime in December than in October and November put together. Moreover, whilst when Parliament separated, anxiety had existed with respect only to one county, crime was now ex- tending north, south, and centre. The chief object of the outrages was intimidation with a view to securing obedience to the mandates of the Land League. Mr.Forster'sreferences to the Land League were defiantly taken up by Mr. Healy and one or two other hon, gentlemen who combine member- ship of the Land League with that of the House of Com- mons. These indications of approval were not refrained from when the Chief Secretary described the procedure of the Land League courts and their sentences passed upon men for the crime of paying their rent. Having thus made the ground sure in advance Mr. Forster abandoned the nar- rative tone in which he had hitherto spoken, and dropped into plain language with respect to the Land League and its officers. Those who break the law are safe, and those who keep it, the honest men, go in fear. What were the Go- vernment, placed in such circumstances, to do ? "Take , away the power and punish the criminalrMr. Forster said, answering his own question, " and that's what we mean to do. They create a state of terror, and we must strike terror ' into them." This frank announcement was greeted with prolonged cheers, the loudest burst coming from below the gangway on the Ministerial side. Amid renewed cheers Mr. Forster described some active agents of the Land League as "those village tyrants, men known to the police as matteeris sujets, the dissolute blackguards of!the place." "What shall we do with them ?" Mr. Forster asked; and again quickly answering, amid prolonged cheers, " Keep them in prison, so that they shall, not tyran- nise over their neighbours." This, as it turned out, was a short but fair summary of the objects of the Bill which he had to introduce. It may be stated in further detail that the Bill proposes to take power to enable the Lord Lieutenant by his warrant to arrest any person whom he reasonably suspects of having, either before or after the passage of the Bill, been guilty, as prin- cipal or accessory, of high treason, treasen-felony, treason- able practices, or of crimes punishable by law, and tending to hitterfere with or disturb the maintenance of law and order. Persons so arrested may be detained in pursuance of the warrant as accused of crime, and not as a convicted prisoner. The Bill is to extend to the 30th of September, 1882. As far as treasonable offences are concerned, the Lord Lieutenant's warrant will run all over Ireland; in res- pect of agrarian outrages it will have currency only in proclaimed districts. Incidentally the Chief Secretary ex- , plained that his second Bill would provide thatno unlicensed I person might possess arms. Amid loud cheers Mr. Forster resumed his seat at ten minutes past seven, having occupied an hour and forty mirutes in the delivery of a speech of great power, and delivered with more than usual animation. —Dr. LYONS, rising to propose an amendment, censuring the Government for not first introducing the Land Bill, the crowded House melted away as if by magic, and for some hours remained in an almost empty state.—The amendment was seconded by Mr. GIYAN, Mr. DILLow following with an undaunted speech, in which he challenged the accuracy of the Chief Secretary's arguments, and prophesied evil things as the result of passing the Bill.—Mr. BRADLAUGH opposed coercion, unless it were accompanied or preceded by remedial measures; whilst Mr. JUSTIN MCCARTHY, speaking in the absence of Mr. Parnell as the leader of the Irish party, de- clared his uncompromising hostility to the measure, and his determination to oppose it by every means in his power.— Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE said that Mr. Forster had rather understated than overstated the condition of affairs in Ire- land, and without going hack into the question whether the measure should have been brought in earlier, he desired to say that the Opposition would glare Her Majesty's Govern- ment the fullest measure of support in passing the Bill into law.—On the motion of Mr. LABOCCHERE the debate was adjourned. The remaining orders were disposed of, and the House adjourned.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. THE PROPOSED ABANDONMENT OF CANDAHAR.—Lord INctinrirr asked if the ministers were in possession of any memorandum containing the views of Lord Napier of Magdala in reference to the retention of Candahar, and, if so, would they lay it on the table of the House.—Lord Estrum) said he believed the Secretary for India had received friam a hip official of the Horse Guards e memorandum of Lord Napier of Magdala on the subject. The Marquis of Har- tington, Lord Enfield added, did not intend to publish this document for the same reason that he had refrained from consulting Lord Napier of Magdala on the question of the retention of Candahar, namely, that that distinguished officer had not, for some time past, been officially con- nected either with the military or political affairs of the East. Their Lordships adjourned after having sat for twenty five minutes.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TDESDAY. ATTACK 17PON A MAIL CAR IN IRELAND.—Mr. FAWCETT said there had been one attack on a mail car in Ireland, and that in another case a district post-office had been closed in consequence of threats of intimidation. THE DRAWBACK ON MALT.—Mr. GLADSTONE stated, in reply to Mr. Watney, that the total amount paid as the drawback on malt up to November last was £1,318,000. The amount could not be included in the revenue accounts, as those accounts were founded upon distinct payments, and the drawback was paid out of Excise receipts arrested on its way to the Exchequer. THE WITHDRAWAL FROM CANDAHAR--The Marquis Of ITARTINGTON declined to be led into a discussion on the question of the retention or abandonment of Candahar. Mr. Grant Duff said the Government were ready to take steps to alleviate the sufferings caused by the famine which had broken out in Zululand. AUDIT OF JOINT•STOCK 13.0nts.—Mr. GLADSTONE in- formed Mr. Macliver that it was not the Government who had suppressed the publication in the newspapers of the lists of shareholders in joint-stock banking companies, but

it had been brought about by a clause in the Banking Act. The late Chancellor of the Exchequer, he thought wisely, made it clearly understood that he repudiated any Govern- ment interference in the audit of joint-stock banks, consider- ing that when provision had been made by law for an audit the duty of the Government terminated.. The pre.stllt Government had considered the matter, and they entirely agreed with the view of the late Government, and had no intention of disturbing the existing arrangements. FAMINE IN ZULULAND.—Mr. GRANT Dcrr, answering Sir Wilfrid Lawson, stated that the Governor of Natal had re- ported a serious scarcity in Zululand, and that he had given instructions for th• adoptim of measures which might safely be taken without interfering with ordinary trade. The home Government did not communicate with Zululand except through the Governer of Natal. LETTERS ADDRESSED TO INIEMIII4:RS OF PARLIAMENT.—Mr, FAWCETT, in reply to Mr. Carbutt, stated that he was in error in his previous 'answer that letters addressed to mem- bers of Parliament at the House were forwarded free to their country addresses. Members of Parliament were now placed , by statute under the same conditions as the general public, and letters were forwarded free to another address in the same town, but not to the country. He had no power to make any alteration.
THE COERCION BILL.
OBSTRUCTIVE TACTICS OF THE IRISH MEMBERS.
SUSPENSION OF AIR. BIGGAR. A TWENTY TWO HOURS' SITTING.

The House was impatient for Mr. Gladstone to rise and curious as to what would happen when he submitted his motion for giving precedence to the Coercion Bills. He had scarcely left his seat before Mr. GREY sprang up in the midst of the Home Rule camp and raised his ob- jection on a point of order. To the general relief it proved to be of a technical character which was easily disposed of by the Speaker, and afforded no encouragement for a wrangle. Less than five minutes sufficed to get rid of this preliminary obstacle, and then Mr.-GLansvoNE, who was re- ceived with cordial cheers, proposed and enforced his resolu- tion with such strength, freshness, and vigour as proved how unjustified were the constant insinuations as to his want of health made by professed friends of the Premier. In twenty minutes the right hon. gentle- man had put his case so as to convince every mem- ber of the House, except the gentlemen from Ireland, of the absolute necessity for his extiaordinary motion. He showed that the Government would be justly censurable if, having come to the conclusion that coercion was necessary, they allowed any waste of time which it was their power to pre- vent. He declared that coercion was necessary to restore " peace and order and freedom to Ireland." He protested that it would not be decent in the circumstances to allow the debate to drag on interminably, generating a fresh crop of speeches at each stage. After that the Irishmen took the matter into their own hands, and carried on a desultory dis- cussion, relieved only by numerous calls to order and two brief admonitory speeches from English members, until they wasted four hours and a half. During the long interval, in , which the Speaker was busily engaged in restraining the irrelevant discourse of one Hibernian orator after another, the Chamber was almost deserted, and the number of Irish members remaining in their places fell to so low a point as to strengthen the growing suspicion that arrangements were being made for a system of relays to carry on an "all night" sitting. Exasperated by the cool obstinacy of Mr. Finigan in pursuing a line of argument frequently con- demned by the Speaker, Mr. Millbank had proposed that the hon. member should be no more heard, but it was not thought advisable to take action in that form at the time, and the dreary and wearisome loquacity of the Irishmen pro- ceeded amidst an ominous quietude, highly suggestive of the lull before the storm, for some time longer. While ilie Speaker was temporary absent Mr. Sexton received a tele- gram annouacing the discharge without agreement of the , Dublin jury, ten of whom hl been against conviction, and the non, member's compati iuts, who had almost entire possession of the House, offered him their cordial congratu- lations in the form of straggling chi. es—Directly the de- bate had been resumed, and Mr. BIGGAR had insisted as 'usual on a count to obtain an audience, Mr. M'Come, im- pulsively interrupting Mr. Barry's speech, demanded to know whether the Solicitor-General for Ireland had any confirmation of a private telegram which had arrived from Ireland.—He was promptly suppressed, and Mr. Barry having finished his remarks gave place to Mr. BIGGAR. The Imember for Cavan had surrounded himself with a large pile of documents, and, aided by constant references to selec- tions from this collection, he contrived to pursue with great deliberation a strange discourse which the SPEAKER eight times interrupted to point out that It was not relevant to the question before the House. Still Mr. Biggar was not to be diverted from his purpose, and totally uninfluenced by so many reproofs he calmly picked up from the heap beside aim two strings of extracts taken from blue-books and fasrened together so as to form a couple of paper ropes each several yards hing. Mr. Biggar was apparently about to read them to the House when the Speaker once more intervened, and amidst exulting cheers from all parts of the House solemnly " named " Mr. Biggar in the form pre- scribed by Sir Stafford Northcote's famous standing order for disregarding the authority of the chair.—Mr. FORSTER was prepared with the requisite motion, and it was promptly proposed and put from the chair.—Mr. BIGGAR wished to discuss it, but no debate could be allowed upon it, and the division was at once called. Members poured in in large numbers, and within three minutes the chamber was crowded again.—The motion, which Sir H. D. WOLFF had seconded on behalf of the Opposition, was put, and after shrieks of "No, no," from the Home Rulers, members made their way into the division lobbies.—Mr. BIGGAR, having carefully gathered up his papers and rolled them in a blue-book, folios' ed to vote with the minority in his own defence. The declaration of the numbers proved that 160 as against 30 were resolved to punish Mr. Biggar by suspending him from the service of the House during the rest of the sitting how- ever long it might last, but Mr. Biggar remained in his place till the Speaker commanded him to withdraw. Then he slowly arose, took leave of his friends, and, dejectedly walking to the bar, passed through the throng assembled there, and vanished through the doors. A cheer from some rash Radical was met with an outburst of cries of " Shame " and " Order " from the Irishmen, and Mr. IlmaLv, standing on the floor in a defiant attitude with his hands in his pockets, angrily moved the adjournment of the debate, and involved himself in a contest with the chair. Eventually he was put down, but the eeraged representatives of Erin were deter- mined to make the most of their new excuse for preventing the progress of business, and they dilated in a full House on the urgent necessity for adjournment, while Mr. Biggar looked benignly down upon them from the highest bench of the Strangers' topmost gallery, to which he had earned his beloved blue-book. A series of violent scenes, tempered by occasional divisions which proved that the malcontent minority numbered ;bout 35 members, led up to a crisis at half-past twelve, when Mr. GLansroxx, in a dispassionate but very resolute manner, advised the House to refuse all motions for adjournment.—The Liberal party broke out into a demonstration of applause.—Sir S. NORTHCOTH an- nounced that the Opposition would assist the Government, and Messrs. Dillon and Sexton having avowed that they would resist to the last, the long-looked for battle was fully joined. Mr. GRAYS motion for the adjournment of the debate was defeated.—Mr. BYRNE moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. HEALY, the new member from whom so much had been expected, supported the motion, and distinguished himself only by displaying a stolid antipathy and unaffected want of respect for the powers that be, and failed to enliven the proceedings except by resort to the old and simple de- vice of getting himself frequently called to order.—Mr. O'DONNELL, who suffered very much from a castigation administered to him by the Premier before midnightssbut re- covering somewhat in the small hours, assailed the Ministers who then remained in the House for their stately silence, and observing Mr. Mundella reclining upon the Treasury Bench, referred to the right hon. gentleman's red stockings as being "symptomatic of the seas ef gore "through which the Government meant to wade in Ireland. This ebullition of Hibernian humour was greatly applauded by Mr. O'Don- nell's friends, but it drew upon him a rebuke from the Chair, and he then excused himself on the plea that he was physically exhausted.—By two o'clock Mr. Gladstone and the greater number of members had gone borne for an inter- val of rest, and tke thin attendance which remained passed several wearisome hours in painful endurance. The minority, whose arrangements for the conflict were less com- plete and systematic than might have been expected, were encouraged by signs of sympathy from one of two of the "Irish Whigs, ' of Mr. Given's stamp, and they were stimu- lated by the desire of keeping the contest open until Mr. Parnell, who was coming by the Irish mail, should have reached St. Stephen's. For some time there remained on the Treasury bench Mr. Forster, Sir W. Harcourt, the Solicitor General for Ireland, and Mr. Mundeila, while the front Opposition bench was occupied by Sir R. Cross, Sir M. H. Beach, Lord Sandon, Mr. Gibson, Lord E. Cecil, and Mr. Beresford Hope. During the next two or three hours several of these gentlemen withdrew, and their places were taken by Sir H. S. Ibbetson, Mr. R. Winn, Sir W. Hart Dyke, Lord H. F. Thynne, and Colonel Taylor on the one side, and Mr. Childers, Mr. Dodson, Mr. Courtney, and Mr. E. Ashley on the other. About three o'clock in the morning Mr. DAWEON endeavoured to defend his party from the accusation of " clumsiness " brought against them by Mr. M. Henry, and to convince the House by reiteration of of the phrase that the opposition the Home Rulers were offering to the Government was of an "impromptu charac- ter." A wily suggestion presented by Mr. MOORE in the form of a possible compromise failed altogether to catch the Government, and the Irish members, annoyed at the failure of a specious device, continued their obstruction in a au lien I spirit. It was at five o'clock that one of them, in support- ing a fresh motion for adjournment, expressed his faith in "stern pi essure, scientifically applied, to resist the unwar- rantable tyranny of the majority." Sir W. HARCOURT, after preserving silence for nearly six hours, made some comments upon what he regarded as a threat, but his re- marks were brief, and no Ministers interposed again until the forenoon was far advanced. None of the gentlemen from Ireland had forgiven the Home Secretary's concise defiance of them uttered at half-past twelve, and Mr. M'CoaN, throwing himself into the discussion after the right hon. gentleman's second manifesto, declared that Sir William's "imperious manner" had "set his back up.", Meeting with the inevitable check from the Chair, Mr. M'Coan revenged himself by announcing that he did not care for the laughter of Professor Rogers. The learned pro- fessor instantly disclaimed any disposition to hilarity, say- ing that he was grieved at the "disgraceful exhibition " he had witnessed. Of course, Mr. Callan, who is at times a great stickler for propriety, took exception to the expres- sion and an incidental controversy ensued, in which Mr. L. STANLEY took an unobstrusive part.—Mr. M'Coirr candidly Confessed that he was talking against time and that his "conception" of the rules of the House was " very crude."

The dispute was in full course at a quarter past seven, when Lord BAR- TINGTON succeeded to the leadership of the House, and set Mr. Forster free to seek repose.—Mr. HEALY, remarking that the Liberal majority was in bed, affected to be over- joyed at seeing the noble Marquis, and continued to talk in a strain which brought Up Lord E. Fitzmaurice, Mr. M. Guest—Sir R. Cross officiating as Opposition leader,—Mr. Alexander Brown, and Mr. W. Cartwright. Adopting a plan he had carried out with success en the previous evening, Mr. HEALY abruptly sat down just as the Deputy Speaker was en the point of pronouncing a severe judgment upon him. Presently Mr. Chamberlain joined Lord Hartington, the two Law Officers of the Crown, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, and Mr. Grant Duff upon the Treasury Beach, and like the other new arrivals now rapidly coming in was heartily welcomed. As the Ministerial forces increased the minority fell off, and the Irish members anxiously appealed to Ministers to be good enough to give way and help them out of their difficulty. The Rev. ISAAC 'NELSON es- sayed, as he put it, to "throw oil on the troubled waters," and gravely admitted that he was expected to waste time, but he could not do so, though he could take his turn at verbiage as readily as any man. Being called to order he said he would " submit like a lanib," yet ere subsiding he supplicated, implored, entreated, beseeched—which ever word the noble Marquis liked best—to relieve them from this dilemma. One qualification for the leader of a great party MS imperturbability of look, and he wished he could catch the slightest shade of feeling on the countenance ef the noble Marquis. No response could be elicited from Lord HARTINOTON, and the struggle went on. Having re- gard to the smallness of their force, the Irish members had refrained from proposing many motions lest their rights in that respect should expire, but at nine o'clock they con- sented to a division en the motion for adjoernment which had been made at five. From the result it appeared that their numbers had been reduced by about ten. Still the hoped-for chief did not come, and Mr. SEXTON brought for- ward another motion for adjournment. An hour and a half plaAteßrN, D ELL, who, thiteLugohN %w,oarsnonolciet mmitohrefatoingueh, ishaldeghsUrrTerd. down from Euston, entered the House, and was hailed with acclamation by his faithful followers. Mr. BIGGAR, having already returned to Westminster after a good night's sleep at Islington, obseived this demonstration with interest from the Strangers' Gallery, to which he had a second time gained admission in virtue of a member's order written and signed by himself. Singularly enough Mr. GLAD- STONE also arrived at this juncture, looking much refreshed arid ready for a renewal of strife. Sir Stafford Northeote and Colonel Stanley had long been in their _places. Towards 11 o'clock, when the gas had been extinguikhedt and such day- light as could- penetrate through a white fog revealed a dis- ordered Chamber occupied by jaded and disgusted legisla- tors, Dr. Playfair went out to take a late breakfast or an early lunch. Hostilities were revived after a short truce, and the Speaker's chaplain presenting himself in full canonicals for the purpose of reading prayers to open the ordinary Wednesday's sitting, was amazed to find that in a Parliamentary sense Tuesday night continued. The rev. gentleman therefore hastily withdrew, and at noon the final obitructive motien was negatived without a division. Mr. Biggar still sat up aloft keeping watch over his compatriots and holding himself ready to resume his interrupted speech at the first available opportunity. Many other spectators bad reached the galleries, and a bevy of ladies cast sympa- thetic glances upon the worn-out assembly from their gilded cage. So far Mr. Parnell had been mute, but he found that his band could bold out no longer, and consequently as soon as an amendment to the main question, proposed by Mr. A. O'Comfon about nine o'clock on the previous evening, had been formally negatived, the hassle CHIEF arose and sought to win from the Government a promise to put off their bills to Thursday. Ministers were obdurate, and Mr GLADSTONE refused to enter into any terms, in spite of the fact that, as he said, no matter whether the divison was taken immediately or not, they had now arrived at such a period of time that after the division the Tuesday sitting would have stretched into Wednesday, and Wednesday would ipso facto have disappeared. He supposed it was not necessary for him to repeat his former declaration,„made at one o'clock in the morning. The great majority of speeches it was admitted had been made in view of what had taken place ha reference to the member for Cavan. Anything more fatal to the general procedure of this House he held could not happen than that its authority should have been called in question, and that attempts should have been made to prolong the matter. Government would decline to enter into any arrangement to allow the sitting to be broken for the purpose of allowing the debate to be continued on a future day, and he added, amidst approving cheers, Ministers fully accepted the responsibility of their motion. Not satisfied with so bold and uncom- promising a tone, Sir S. Northcote, feeling that he ought to cut a figure in the proceedings, tried to extort from the Government a pledge that they would not allow the sitting, to be commenced on Thursday, to terminate until the Coercion Bill had been introduced. His ill-timed interposi- tion caused much irritation and excitement, which was in- tensified by an indignant harrangne :from Mr. COWEN, defending the Irish patriots fighting for their countries liberty and bitterly attacking the Government. Mr. A. Moons reproached Ministers for their obstinancy in refusing the compromise he had recommended 11 hours and 40 minutes ago, and two or three English Radicals joined in the closing discussion. At two o'clock in the afternoon the resolution proposed by Mr. Gladstone 21 hours before was carried on a division by 251 against 33 Without explana- tion Mr. GLADSTONE then took the judicious step of patting an end to the sitting. Thus, while the Government had gained their point in securing precedence for the Coercion Bills, the Irish members had eneured the loss of another sitting, and Wednesday was wholly abandoned by the House of Commons. THE POSITION OF MAJOR NOLAN.--11l reply to the Duke of Montrose, the Earl of MORLEY said that Major Nolan had in 1879 done 134 days' duty with his batiery and 86 days' in 1850, making altogether 220 days' duty in the two years. Major Nolan bad drawn his usual pay as major of the Royal Artillery—that was to say, 16s. a day, which made for the whole period about £584. The gallant officer had drawn no allowances, in consequence probably of his being in quarters. Their Lordships rose at a quarter past five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIICASDAY.

. THE Hasa PROTECTION BILL. The debate on Mr. Forster's motion for leave to bring in his "Protection" Bill was resumed by Mr. LABOUCHERE, who strongly opposed any resort to coercive measures in Ireland. The hon. mem- ber expressed the opinion that the Home Rulers were justi- fied in using and even abusing all the forms of the House in order to obstruct the measures in question. He then pro- ceeded to quote at length from statistics with a view to showing that the disturbed state of Ireland had been greatly exaggerated. He opposed the bill, and was followed by Mr. SIMON, who supported the Government.—After speeches from The O'Dobroonun and other Irish members, during which two or three attempta were made to count the House, Mr. Join; BRIGHT rose at a quarter to eleven, amidst cheers. The right hon. gentleman expressed his sorrow that though he had been a member of that House for thirty- seven years he had never lived to see the time when coer- cive measures for Ireland should have become absolutely necessary. Many such measures had been introduced in his own day, none of which ha had approved, several of which he had opposed, but their introduction had never been accompanied by an admission of grievances, and there had been no promise of attempted remedy. He quoted the testimony of the late John Martin that he had never uttered a word that was insulting to Ireland. but had always been willing to do justice to her. Nor would he have been sitting on that Treasury bench now if the proposal to introduce fresh measures of coercion were not accompanied by an attempt to re medy the grievances of Ireland. He justified the statement and statistics of Mr. Forster on the ground that they were exact and unexaggerated. During the last six months bp had received more letters from Ireland than he before re- ceived in the whole course of his political life, from land- lords and shopkeepers farmers and labourers, and one and all told the same deplorable story as to the condition of the country. They were of such a nature as to convince him that during the last months the condition of the country had been drifting from bad to worse. For years England had been a home for refugees from Russia, France, and other Continental nations, but now it had become a home for another class of refugees who came from Ireland. Not only were the facts borna out by public and private letters, but they were fully corroborated by the admission of the Land League. The leaders of that Association claimed that their unwritten Law was supreme, and that if this bill passed from that moment the payment of rent in Ireland would be put an end to. He 'had always condemned the state of the land tenure in Ire- I land, and be felt it was impoSsible to do anything for the the country until that question was fairly grasped by the Imperial Parliament.—On the motion of Mr. R. POWER, the debate was adjourned. THE Bunter. awn REGISTRATION Acrs (Doubts Re- moval) Bill and the Judicial Committee Bill passed through committee.

THE DIETA.Ry TABLE. Mr. MEADOWS said there was a very important matter in abeyance, and he should like to have some information on it, as waste was going on in the Workhouse at the present time. A little over two years ago the matter was gone into, several Unions were written to in reference to their dietary scale, and it was found that that Board was in excess in a great many articles. The late Master and the Medical Officer spent several weeks in prepairng a dietary table, and he would like to know what had become of it. The CLERK said he forwarded it to the Local Government Board and since that time the Local Government Board had communicated with every Union in the country, and he be- lieved himself that they were trying to frame a uniform dietary table for the whole of the countly. If the Board liked he Would write to the Local Government Beard on the subject. The Board directed the Clerk to write to the Local Govern- ment Board in reference to the matter. WIDNES CHEMICAL LABOURERS APPLYING FOR RELIEF. About 40 chemical labourers from Widnes attended the Relief Committee and made application for relief, but it was decided to bring their cases before the whole Board. The Cutux: The Widnes section of the Relief Committee have had before them this morning a great number of able- bodied men who are out of work in consequence of the severe weather and I suppose the coal miners' strike. It is for the Guardians to say what kind of relief they will afford these able bodied applicants. If the Guardians give relief to an able-bodied male person outside the Workhouse that person must be set to work.

After some discussion, it was decided to employ the men at wheeling stone from a neighbouring quarry to the Workhouse on the same terms as granted two years ago. At that time the following resolution was passed : " Resolved that able-bodied men be in the workhouse as under to entitlethem to the following scale of relief :—Prescot 7to 4, Widues 9 to 4, St. Helens Bto 4. Single men Is. per day, married men with two children Is. Bd. per day, married men with above two children 2s. per day, and dinner daily at the workhouse. One half, at least, of the relief to be in kind." This was all the business.

ST. HELENS,COUNTY COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, Judge. A CASE OF A WIFE OBTAINING GOODS ON CREDIT.— Joseph Platt, provision dealers Croppers-bill, St. Helens, saught to recover £l3 Ps. lid., the amount for goods sup- plied to John Hankey, stoker at the Ravenkead Glass Works, and residing in Eldon-street, Croppers-hill.—Mr. Riley, for Mr. Massey who was absent, appeared on behalf of the plaintiff; and Mr. Swift appeared for the defendant.—Mr. Riley said it would be a question for His Honour to decide whether, the %bole of the goods having been delivered to 'the wife, and payments paid by the wife, the defendant was in such a station of life in which it was customary the wife should have the husband's authority to deal in the manner she had done, and lie contended that he was in that position, and therefore liable for the debt.—Evidence was then given by plaintiff and his wife showing that the defendant's wife had been in the habit for a number of years of dealing with them, and the amount sued for represented a period of three years. Haakey lived near them. 103. of the amount claimed was lent to the defendant's wife, and was booked as provisions.—Mr. Swift having addressed his Honour, and read from weekly notes to the effect that a man wko sup- plied his wife with a certain amount of money a year to provide herself and her children with clothing was not held liable by the judge for his wife's debts on account of cloth- ing, he called defendant, who said he gave his wife 245. a week with which to provide household necessaries, and he forbade kis wife soon after their marriage, and he had since repeated it, to obtain goods on credit, either at a shop or from a Scotchman. On one occasion plaintiff came to his door and his wife answered, and, bearing they were quar- relling, he suspected there was something, and on going to the door his wife said that Mr. Platt had only come to see the canaries, but he did not believe that tale, and grew very angry, mid said he would "cry a notchell," meaning that would insert an advertisement in the paper that he would not be responsible for his wife's debts.—His Honour asking what the phrase meant, Mr. Riley gave it as his opinion that it was a corruption of" shall not."—Mr. Swift said the lower orders at St. Helens had a greater opinion of the efficacy of that sort of proceduis than either they (the court) or the Lord Chief Justice. (Laughter.) —His Honour said there was one point upon which he must find for the defendant. He was sorry there was no case which was vet decided clearly bow far a man was liable for goods which be intended to buy for ready money, but which were procured by his agent on credit. Supposing he employed a man in the street to go to a saddler and say, " Here's £5; go and get a new saddle for me ;" and the man went and told the saddler that his master would pay him nest week, and then keep the money, and that he resisted the claim on the ground that he had furnished his agent with money to buy the saddle with— could the claimant receive the money P That had never been decided, so far as he knew, when applied to goods such as groceries. EDINBURGH ELECTION.—The polling at Edinburgh resulted in the election of the Lord Advocate (Mr. J. M‘Laren), who polled 11,390 votes, against 3,940 recorded for Mr. Edward Jenkins. At the Manchester Assizes, on Thursday, John Hilton and Mark Tuer were indicted for conspiracy to defraud certain tradesmen by means of fictitious cheques. They were found guilty, and Mr. Justice Field sentenced them to ten years' penal servitude. REVIVAL OF THE EVSI'OE-SQUARE MYSTERY.— 11l the Court of Queen's Benet, on Thursday, the libel case Bastendorff v. Purkess came on. The alleged libel was published in a pamphlet entitled " The Euston-sqaare Mystery," which is purported to be a confession of Hannah Dobbs. In it Mr. Bastenilorff was charged with committing no less than three murders, and also with adultery with Hannah Dobbs. Ultimately an arrangement was arrived at between the two lifigants, and a verdict was entered for £5OO and costs for the plaintiff, together with a withdrawal of all imputations. div.head: IMBECILE WARDS.
div.p: THE IMBECILE WARDS.
The MASTER reported that the house and hospital were both crowded.
The CLERK read the following letter:—

Dear Sir,—The alterations at Ile workhouse schools to vert them into imbecile wards are so far completed that, with the exception of £2O, the amount of the contract may be paid to the contractors. The small balance is to be retained in hand until spring, when the new walls may be pointed without fear of injury from frost.—Yoursjruly, Joan TWIST. Mr. MEADOWS: The mailer has reported that the hospital is overcrowded, and I should like to know whether the im- becile wards are ready for the imbeciles. They have been a long time in hand now. The CLERK: I have just read a letter from Mr. Twist showing that they are almost completed. That letter ought to go before the Building Committee. The Caeraltax: He says they are very nearly completed. ' Mr. TYREE: He simply intimates that they want pointing outside. It seemed to him the Board had been providing in- creased accommodation and they were overcrowding again. The Camamew : Certainly. The MASTER was called in and he said the ward was not I completed. The frost had interfered with the work, and She men were now away. Mr. Maa.nows asked was there any time stipulated for the completion of the work? The CLERK thought there was in May neat. Mr. LEATIIERBARROW : Would it not be advisable to see the building and see if some of the rooms could not be occupied? The MASTER stated that he was using the building for the old men. Mr. MEADOWS : That shows they we ready for occupation. The CLEaa : I think it is a matter for the Building Com- mittee.
On the motion of Mr. LONGTON, seconded by Mr. MEADOWS, the matter was referred to the Building Com- mittee.

WOMEN WITHOUT WORE. The MenEn reported There are more women in the house than are necessary for the washing, nursing, and other work, as there is nothing for some of them to do, will the Board consider the ad- visability of fitting and using the room near the laundry as a work room, and employing them there at oakum picking, as is done in most large workhouses ? The CHAIRMAN said he had had a conversation with the Master of the workhouse on the subject that morning. There was nothing for the women to do, and the Master thought it was advisable to put them all to oakum picking, which would do them no harm. They were all in a warm room, and he thought that the best suggestion the Masbnr could make. Let the women be engaged at picking oakum. There was very little made by it, but it was better than let- ting them wander about talking to one another. The Board had no right to put the women to manual labour. Mr. LONGTON : Are they able-bodied? The MASTER: Most of them. _

Mr. Jecasos said oakum picking was unprofitable. Thc CHAIRMAN asked if the Board could find anything better. Mr. TYREII: If you keep them here daing nothing 'you will have any number of them. The Cmunm.or : I put it this way. If you allow a lot of women to congregate together day after day they are always concocting something, and that not for the benefit of 4 the Union. _ _ _

Mr. llinknows : It is very necessary to find them employ- ment at something, and I don't believe there is a loss on oakum picking. lie moved that the master's suggestion be adopted. The CHAIRMAN: Certainly; and that the governor take the matter into his own hands. The motion was seconded and carried. MUSIC AT DIVINE SERVICE, .

The CHAPLAIIZIWIis report, stated :—I beg to call the attention of the Board to the fact that since the resignation of Mr. Smith, the schoolmaster, there has been no one to I play the harmonium at divine service, and that conse- quently, to the undoubted disappointment of the ,inniates, all music and singin, has had to be omitted. I may add that, with the consent and approval of the Board, Mr. Geo. R. Eyre, of Rainhill, is prepared to play the harmonium until the appointment of a schoolmaster' at the same salary —£lo—as was allowed to Mr. Smith for performing the duty. The Board gave the necessary approval en the motion of Mr. Paris, seconded by the Rev. T. Chambers.

div.head: DISHONEST RELIEVING OFFICER.
div.p: THE DISHONEST RELIEVING OFFICER.

The CLERK read the following letter from the Guarantee Society :—" Re Prescott—Dear Sir,—Referring to the correspondence in this case, will you be kind enougiit to inform me by return of post, if possible, whether you call upon the society to pay anything on itccount of Prescott, , Stating the amount as near as you may be able."k The CLERE.! T have replied to that. The CHAIRMAN: Well, how much is the amount; although the books have mt, been examined, and cannot be before the auditor comes, have 7ou given them an estima- tion ? The CLERK I have; I will read you the ief ten "25th Jamiary.—Re Prescott.—Dear Sir,—l am in receipt of your letter. The Guardians will certainly claim from you the deficiencies which will be certified by the auditor. So far as I can see the amount will be £35.'

The CHAIRMAN : Canyou say. as near as possible, when yon anticipate or expect the auditor will be over? The CLERK replied that he could not say. He also stated that it was only on the certificate of the auditor that the Society would be required to pay anything at all.

div.head: LEASING PARISI( PROPERTY:
div.p: LEASING PARISI( PROPERTY:

_ The CLERK: I wish to have the authority of the Guar- dians to take the necessary proceedings towards having the lease executed for the parish property of Woolton. The Board granted the requisite authority.
THE- CALLS.
The CLERK read the amount of calls paid by the overseers since the last meeting. Mr. MEADOWS asked what had been paid by the Widnes overseers. _ . - •

The CLERK: Nothing; but I have a letter from them as follows:—" Assistant Overseer's:Office, Farnworth, Widnes, Jan. 26th, 1881.—Dear Sir,—ln reply to your letter of the 24th inst., I am sorry to inform you that the overseers of Widnes are not prepared at present to meet their overdue calls. I am just completing a new rate which will be passed next Wednesday), and I have no hesitation in saying that before the expiration of the present half year they will be able to pay the whole of the amount due. The present overseers think it rather hard that they should be blamed, and have to suffer for the neglect of their predecessors in not making a rate sufficiently large • to, meet their calls, taking into consideration the fact that there had been no rate laid for the year 1877. With regard to the townships of Ditton and Crouton, I believe the overseers will be able to comply with your request.—Believe me, etc., JOHN S. RIGBY."
Mr. MEADOWS: What is the amount in arrear ? The CLEux : £5,001.

The Cumulus was going to suggest that the Clerk write to the overseers of Widnes to ask them to make a payment immediately even of one-half, and then give them the re- mainder of the time to the 25th March, or otherwise the Board would get into a dilemma. The overseers now said in 1877 there was no rate laid for the township of Widnes. Here came the very difficulty again, and if the Board let the present overseers got out of office on the 25th March the Board would be in a worse dilemma than they were now. Mr. MEADOWS: This is a very serious amount, over £5,000, and as a matter of fact we cannot pay the trades- men's accounts now at all. I therefo-e move that unless they pay the amount or half of it in seven days they be prosecuted. Mr. JACKSON: Make it 14 days. Mr. MEanows: Well, you are keeping the tradesmen without their cheques, which I think is very wrong. Mr. TYRER : If you allow them 14 days you have a cer- tain time to wait to bring them before the magistrates. Per- haps the magistrates will give them another 14 days, and where will you be then ? Mr. Maar:Howl included Eccleston in his motion, this town- ship being £1,63.5 in arrears. Rev. T. CHAMBERS said it seemed to him veryperemptory to call upon the overseers to find £.2,500 in 7 days. He suggested that the overseers be allowed 10 days. Mr. LowYrotr seconded. After some discussion it was decided to allow the overseers ten days longer.
