div.head: MINERS' STRIKE.
div.p: THE MINERS' STRIKE.

ST. HELENS. The miners in this district, who came out on strike on Dared ly week, have net yet resumed work. Accounts of miewanduct on the part of St. Helens miners in entering 11 II known buti n repudiate tt hh ee that goodsehahavet tther eobenentheanthargeeepxsaccounter, have been , I provision and other shops and demanding goods, and in some i freelycl cases sa iutda_jisig circulated,lnywaet pgpugrleeorfuaeartereddisaatrindgacittnhit I _.„.„,..tra ,,"strikes or lock-outs, there is an influx into tha In"'ellg bonAtta. of.amrtnnimeibpaerteofinvaagnayboenngdsageamndenrtouogf has mwie.he are ever eager' Se Begging to a groat sixtenctonitieihcilasionndeberofenmoennea. arcringlappent cbievous nature, azia. t? men of this character some of the looting. perpetrated 10 the district is put down. and on Friday night A Hill, refused the demanded a SM. attack was triode upon the confectionery on the counter, and it is said that one of the men had the impxlence, in a polite manner,to bid Mrs. Grice '-good night," other shops injlie town were treated in a similar manner. A number of—Ma entered the fish shop of Mrs. Ashton, Ormskirls-street, and carried away one or two articles. In Higher Parr-street a number of men solicited alms at the shop kept by Mr. Robin- son who said they could take three loaves out of the window and they diet so. One of Mr. E. Johnson's shops at Parr was entered and, the demands of the men not being ncceded to some biscnits and bacon were carried away. On the whole, however, St. Helens has been comparativel3 quite, and the men have conducted themselves in a peaceable manner. Great inconvenience and discomfort has been caused to ruan3 families from the difficulty of obtaining coals which have risen to an enormous price, in some eases to Is. 6d a , met, and even 15..104.1n the beginning of the week a few small veins of coal were discovered in Hardshaw fells, and some relief, though but small, has been afforded by the supply of an inferior coal from this sourse. One or two other like discoveries has been made. On Saturday morning upwards of 100 soldiers, under the command of Captain Skills, from Fulwood barracks, near Preston, arrived in the town, and attracted considerable notice. Since then they haveleen quartered at the Volunteer Hall, but have not yet been called into action. The colliers presented themselves at the different pits in the district on Saturday, and contrary to the rumours which had been circulated, they received the wages they had earned, and which were due to them, and no disturbance whatever took place. The shopkeepers are beginning to feel the effects of the strike, and are wishing the men "will get what they want and go in." On Sunday a number of soldiers marched to the Parish Church, where they attended divine service, and others visited some of the other places of worship in the town. Many of the inhabitants turned out to view them. On Monday a few thousand miners assembled on the Fair Ground, 'and were addressed by " Captain " Cross, their leader. Mr. Peter McKinley presided, and said he fully sympathised with their cause, and their good beha- viour certainly did them credit, though it appeared someone had degraded the town by bringing in the military: with the object of dragooning them and frightening them into doing something wrong. He believed that if the men would keep Lo one another they would gain their cause in a week or so. Mr. Cross referred to the action of Mr. France, Manager of the St. Helens Colliery Company, Limited, in sending for a deputation of men to meet him. Having gone as requested, Mr."Frauce said he did not know anything about sending for them, but he was willing to hold a conference with them on the matter. Mr. Cross was of opinion that Mr. France wished to get hold of some of the leaders of the men and persuade them to go to work, but Mr. Glover, of Messrs. Evans's, acting on different principles, said "if you will go to work we will consider giving you an edvance." There were, however, some clever men among-the deputation, who gave a few hard blows to Mr. Glover. Mr. Cross condemned the action of one of the masters in bringing one or two hundred people into the town, and said that if it were not for the policemen the men would have been at their work that day. The men were only asking for what was fair, and if they acted on fair principles they could not fail to have the support of the public. Mr. Cross referred to an ancestor of Mr. Evan's of Haydock, who came as a cotton weaver into the town about 70 years ago with about MOO and now the firm was with over £3,000,000. That was done by grinding down the men and taking money off them for such matters as sharpening picks. Speaking about the sliding scale he (Mr. Cross) would not give his consent to one which did not give the men ss. a day, and then wagts ought to be at least 275. ed. instead of an average of Ifis. A resolutien that all the men should hold, out until they got the advance was carried unanimously. On Tuesday eight or nine policemen went by train to Skelmersdale, a telegram baying been received that a riot was inevitable. On Wed- I netelay morning a few thousand colliers marched from St. Helens to a meeting at Wigan headed by Mr. Cross and a band of music. Mr. Cross cautioned them at the starting point—George Inn—to conduct themselves properly. ST. HELENS, Friday. Strangers who have heard the exaggerated accounts of misconduct on the part of the miners would, no doubt, be surprised on visiting the town to-day to find the streets comparatively quiet, without the least sign of ilisturbanee anywhere; yet such is the case. There are now about 4,000 miners out in this district, and there is a widespread feeling that the miners are underpaid for the enormous risks they run; but it is scarcely to be expected that the employers , will at once concede all that the men demand. Mr. Cross, the i district miners' agent, and other delegates yesterday (Thurs- day) attended a delegate meeting at Wigan convened by the Wigan Miners' Union, and at which there were about 70 delegates present altogether, from Wigan, St. Helens, Hind- ley, and Skelmersdale. Mr. ‘Vm. Pickard, who presided, announced the receipt of a letter from Mr. Peace, secretary of the West Lancashire Coal Association, in reply to a com- munication from the previous delegate meeting, stating that the conditions offered by the masters at the Liverpool meet- ing were still open to the men if they chose to accept them, these being the formation of a sliding scale te regulate the wages for the present and future, and considera- tion by that committee of weekly payment of wages. A discussion ensued, which lasted upwards of four hours, in the course of which it was repotted by several delegates that the employers were willing to concede the advance asked for provided the men will consent t > resume work at the oldrate of wages for a fortnight, and, eventually, these resolutions wets adopted :—" That we resum work if the employers will bind themselves to give an advance equal to the last reduction, and weekly payments in fourteen days from the commencement of working, that agreement to be made before we commence work; that it goes before the i surrounding districts to consider as to the basis for a sliding scale, and to choose a fit and proper person to be the repre- sentative on that committe as to the sliding scale after the same has been agreed upon and formed." It is now stated that the whole of the colliery proprietors in the Skelmersdale and Rainford districts have agreed to give the advance of wages, and will consider the question of weekly payments in a fortnight, with the exception of two viz: Messrs. D. Brownlow and Co. and the White MOM Colliery Company, and a mass meeting of miners is con- Vened at Rainford to-day (Friday) to take into considera- tion the propriety of accepting this offer. We learn that no organisation has been made for the purpose of affording relief to those on strike, it being alleged that if no settlemea is come to, the men are in a position to hold out for some time yet.

A good deal of interest is being felt in the legal proceed- ing will take place at Prescot Petty Sessions, on It Tuesday ne't appears that the Wigan aad Whiston :. colliery company have Leen Aupined by the miners for stopping the check-waighman, without, t 7 alleg justifiable cause and cross summonses have been issued ,641 r the company against e miners for leaving their work with- out proper notice. Both eases will be heard on .Tnesday,

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

On Thursday a large body of colliers from Standish visited Elms Colliery, belonging to Messrs. Smethurst Hoyle, and Grime, where work had been carried on, and threatened what they would do... Police and military arrived from Wigan by special train, but the mob had then dispersed. It was ascertained that the crowd, as they returned home, robbed several shopkeepers, several gentle- men were roughly pelted with melted snowballs, and some windows were smashed. There are now 100 infantry in Wigan. At Hindley there is one troop of Hussars, and in each district the police force has been considerably strengthened. The men parade the town and neighbonthood in parties, begging from pedes- trians, and several bread carts in the country districts have been stopped and emptied of their contents. SKELMERSDALE. Since the riot which took place at Skelmersdale, on Tues- day, matters have been very quiet. With the exception of a few men working at one of the Earl:of Lathom's pits, the whole of the men in Skeltnersdale were stopped on Thurs- day.

div.head: WEST HOUGHTON.
div.p: WEST HOUGHTON.

Disturbances by c.o.fliers were expected at Wt Houghton, near Bolton, yesterday afternoon, and about 100 police were assembled; but the colliers, supposed to be coming from the Wigan district, made no appearance. BURNLEY. The executors of Colonel Hargreaves on Thursday granted 5 per cent, advance to their colliers, numbering about 1,500.

AccatErrAT PRESCOT.—An accident occurred on Tues- day to a little boy named Stockley, living at Honghton-st. Whilst warming his hands by the fire, and venturing too near, his clothes suddenly caught fire. The boy's screams soon brought assistance, and he was found to be badly burnt about the body. He is now progressing favourably.

The child had suffered from a mouth dise.44, but I.al not been 'attended by a doctor.

SANKEY Bins.—On Monday night a supper was given by the masters of the New Chemical Workes, Sankey Bridges, at the Black Horse Inn. The sapper was provided by the host and hostess of the above place, and they deserve every praise for the manner in which it was provided. Over 30 sat down to supper, and each appeared to do ample justice to the repast. After supper the cloth was removed, and the chair was occcupied by the oldest workman in the firm. The chairman proposed the health of "The masters," which was respended to amid great applause. A very pleasant evening was spent in singing, reading, and recitations by the workmen.

Mrs NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF MASTEN BUILDERS OF GREAT BRITAIN held their sixth half-yearly meeting at the Palatine Hotel, Manchester, on Wednesday, the 26th of January, 1881, when the following towns were represented: —London, Liverpoel, Manchester and Salford, Lancaster, Wolverhampton, Bradfurd, Northampton, Lincoln, Leeds, Warrington, Wigan, Birmingham, Sheffield, Huddersfield, Portsmouth, Doneaster, Edinburgh, Dundee, Rochdale, Crewe, Macclesfield, Bolton, Kidderminster, Stalybridge, St. Helens, Hull, Oldham and Meltham, when the report of the council, and accounts for the last half-year, were adopted and directed to be circulated. The following gentlemen were elected as officers for the ensuing year :—Mr. Stanley G. Bird, London, president; Mr. W. H. Cowlin, Bristol, and Mr. Robert Neill,jun . , treasurer. It was decided to increase the number of gentlemen forming the council from 21 to 25, and representatives from Edinburgh, Bolton, Hull, Sheffield, and Portsmouth were duly elected members. It was also decided to hold the next half-yearly meeting in London, and an increase of local associations was recommended. Several schemes of insurance in respect of the Employers' Liability Act were submitted by the sub-committee, and it was decided to ask them to bring forward a matured plan at the earliest possible date. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY 'JANUARY 29, 1881

men on strike and the police, in which the former have in all instances fared the worst. At Tyldesley, this week, as we report in another column, several thousands of colliers visited a pit, and demanded that the men at work in the mine should be drawn up the pit shaft. 4 strong body of police put in an appearance Ad a desperate fight ensued, in which the police behaved in a most courageous manner. Though the constables were vigorously assailed by the mob, they succeeded in dispersing it after repeated charges. The result of the conflict was that one of the rioters was killed, numerous colliers' heads and limbs were broken and fractured, and several police officers were badly injured. Equally serious riots have taken place at Skelmersdale and elsewhere, and just now the police and military are scattered about the coal mining districts of Lancashire in very strong force, ready at a moment's notice to quell any further outrages that the folly of the colliers may lead them to engage in. The miners have succeeded in establishing a reign of terror, and if the lawlessness which they have been recently practising is perpetuated, it is not unlikely that a cry will be raised for a Coercion' Bill for the protection of life and property in Lancashire as well as in Ireland. The continuance of the strike has been productive of untold misery throughout the country, by causing fuel in the meet inclement of weather to advance to rices which are pro- hibitive to the poor; but the hardships resulting from the contest have been no more keenly felt by any class of people than by the colliers themselves and their families.
VDEsToN Mums", IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—Mr. james Ball, jun., read an essay before the members of this class, at their last meeting. The subject was, "The human soul."

HOLY nun= Yousto Mures CHTLISTILI ASSOCIATION. —On Monday evening, an essay was read by Mr. H. A. Hankinson, in connection with the members of this class, on "The Prayer Book ; its beauties and blemishes."

RUNCORN WESLEYAN METHODIST TEMPERANCE SOCIETY —The annual meeting of this society will be held on Wed- nesday evening, in St. Paul's Chapel. The chair will be occupied by Mr. John Simpson, and the meeting will be addressed by the Revs. John Colwell and Thomas Hardy (both of Manchester), and the circuit ministers and friends.

Vourumzu BALL AT Runccuor.—The F and G Companies of the 2nd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers held a ball on Tuesday evening at the Public 1411, Runcorn, under the patronage of the non-commissionedltficers. A stretcher had been laid, and the arrangements for dancing were good, but the attendance was not large; and perhaps this may be accounted for owing to the indifferent manner in which the affair had been advertised. The band was a very fair one, and under the leadership of Mr. Powell. Dancing com- menced at nine o'clock and was continued until the early hours of the morning.

WIDNES PARISH CHURCH ENTERTAINMENTS.—The ninth of the series given in the schoolroom, Waterloo-road, on Monday evening, was well attended. The Vicar (the Rev. J. Wright Williams) occupied the chair. The entertain- ment, with the exception of a reading by Mr. Balmer was entirely musical. Songs were given by Mr. F. Scott, Miss Davies, Mrs. White, and Mr. E. Lnison. Mr. R. Pierpoint gave two cornet solos. .The Misses Lord gave a pianoforte duet. A glee was also rendered by Misses Parr' Fairley, and Broad, and Messrs. Ireland, Wilkinson and Imison. The entertainment was a thorough success, the whole of the vocalists and instrumentalists being encored. RE THOMAS KIRKHAM AND Co.—A meeting of the creditors of Mr. Thomas Kirkham, of Church-street, Run- corn (trading under the name of Thomas Kirkham and Co.), chemical plumber and contractor, was held at the offices of Messrs. Da and Lake, Runcorn, yesterday afternoon. We anderata hat the liabilities of the debtor amount to about .f 4 £BOO of which is owing to Mr. Timmins and lit £4OO to the Widnes Foundry Co. Mr. Kirkham has lately been carrying out a contract of about £lB,OOO for the Widnes Alkali Co. The assets were stated at ,C5OO. Mr. Knight, accountant (Runcorn), and Mr. Butcher (Manches- ter), were appointed trustees; and Messrs. Day and Lake, solicitors, a committee of inspection.

GOOD TEMPLARISII AT WIDNES.— On Wednesday, a public tea meeting was held in the Lacey-street Wesleyan schoolroom„ in connection with the Star of Widnes and Haste to the Rescue Lodge of Good Templars. The fol- lowing ladies presided over the tables :—Mesdatnes Stanley, Clarke, and Hughes, and the Misses Weant, Hudson, Bold, and Thompson. After tea an entertainment took place, Bro. Scrymageour, of St. Helens, occupying the chair. The fol- lowing ladies and gentlemen took part :—Bros. Rodgers, Johnson, Pickergill, Brocklebank, Pownall, and Sisters Mellor, Marshall, and Toft. The band of the order was present, and contributed much to the pleasure of the meeting. The proceedings terminated with the passing'of several votes of thanks.

A Marc KILLED AT RUNCORN YESTEEDAY.--. Yesterday morning, about half-past seven, a fatal accident occurred at the quarry, belonging to the Bridgewater Trustees, in Heath- street, Runcorn. John Dawson, aged 47, a labourer, of Ring-street, was assisting his brother, Samuel Dawson, and a man named Charles Woods to move a stone weighing about two tons, which was upon a wagon. The stone slipped and the wagon, which is without sides, turned over, and deceased was crushed between the stone and the tram- way which leads down to the canal. He was taken home in a light cart, and Dr. Mouritz sent for, but before his arrival Dawson died, after uttering the words "My back is broken."

FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT, AT FARNWORTIL A labourer, named Thomas. Craig, was killed at the goods station of the Cheshire Lines Railway, early on Thursday morning. The deceased was in the employ of Mr. Riddel, a quarry proprietor, of Appleton, and went to the yard with some stone. Whilst he was pushing an empty wagon towards the crane, a train of fifteen trucks came in contact with it, and he was caught between the buffers and terribly hurt internally. Dr. Booth was sent for, but the deceased only lived a few minutes after saying "I am done." The body was removed to his own home, Derbyshire-road, Farn- worth. We are informed that deceased's mother is a widow, with several young children, and much in need of pecuniary help.

Mass AMY DOT AT WEDNEB. Captain Austin under whose manaaement Miss Amy Dot, the sister of Tom Thumb, is exhibiting, has visited Widnes during the last week. The entertainment, which is of a very interesting character, was held in the Volunteer Hall, and, considering the severe character of the weather, proved exceptionally successful in these dull times. Miss Dot is stated to be a native of New York, her age is 15, and she is only 26 inches in height. Her figure is remarkably well proportioned, and her conversational powers are very good, some of her say- ings being of a rather amusing description. The captain himself goes through an entertainment of some length, consisting of conjuring and ventriloquism. In the latter he is what a Yankee would call "a mighty smart man," and wins the hearty applause of the audience. Miss Annie Wynne, another of the company, is a first-class ballad singer; and the pianist's manipulation is remarkably clever. In addition to the above attractions we may state the a number of presents are distributed, and the competition'fre- qnently attracts large crowds. Tlar,rox MUTUAL hallovszErr SociEn.—At the general meeting, on Monday evening, Mr. W. Collier read a paper on the Ashantee Expedition. The essayist has been 21 years a soldier, and was actively engaged in the Ashen- tee war. He is now pensioned by the Government. Mr. Collier minutely described the voyage to the Gold Coast. Every station the expedition touched at they met with a hearty reception. At Sierra Leone they took on board some natives, called crew-boys, to fill the place of the stokers,who could not stand the heat of the engine fires combined With that of the climate. The expedition landed on the Gold Coast January Ist, 1874. The march to Eoomassie was very difficult and wearying. The mode of fighting on the march was like skirmishing, the files being two or three paces apart. Every company was divided into sections, with an officer or non-commissioned officer at their head. Each section had orders not to get mixed with any other. The fighting in the bush was like fighting by twilight; the dense 'bushes and trees prevented the full amount of daylight reaching the earth. Every shot must be deliberately aimed ' and fired low. The Ashantees fired from the hip, with guns about six feet long, and generally took no aim. They fired with slugs, or small, smooth pebleles. Slug wounds were larger and more dangerous than those made by bullets. No village or camp was to be set on fire or plundered, exceptby order of the commanding officer. The essayist mentioned the difficulty they had with their native attendants, who wcKoeinroinaie egrsesst, thlyaefraid of the Ashantees. When they reached capital of Ashantee, they found it deserted. King Koffee's son, however, on behalf of his father, made withef cSai nr Gatma nsr inee wlnVao al eet nyn, fitrhee, and E n g tl hi sehn coo me ma aalnddi eerr termsn-chi marched back to Coast Castle, and from thence to England. Here they met with an enthusiastic reception. The paper gave great satisfaction. The following members of the society made a few remarks: Messrs. G. Pennington, R. Hughes, and J. Looker. The Rev. J. Bateman presided.— COM. J

LzvEnroor. WINTER Assmus.---The commission for I holding these assizes will be opened on Thursday, the 3rd of February. The Court will sit on Friday, the 4th FebraarY, at eleven a.m., and on every other day during the assizes at ten am., unless otherwise directed. The calender contains the names of 31 persons. THE SHAREHOLDERS OP THE SOL"TIIPORT AND WEST LANCASHIRE BANE met, on Wednesday, to receive a report from the directors and the committee of investigation, and unanimously resolved to recommend reconstruction. The chairman of the company (Mr. Walter Smith) denied that the directors had been selling their shares, or that they had used the money of the Bank to pro- mote their own interests in other companies. A resoln:ion to wind up voluntarily was passed, and a c9mmittee was appointed to draw up a scheme of reconstruction.

RUNCORN PARIIAMENTART DEBATING SOCIETT.—The weekly sitting of this house took place on Tuesday evening. The weather interfered with the attendance, which was small. The Ballot Bill was brought up in committee and clause 3, with a few amendments was passed. The hours of polling were fixed—For county elections, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m; borough elections from 12 noon to 8 p.m. An amend- ment proposed by the member for Walsall was accepted by the Government, which provides for the closing of public- houses on the day of election and stands part of the bill. The Leader of the (*position gave notice to ask the Chief Secretary for Ireland " Whecliar he can inform the House in how many districts in Ireland the amounts advanced by the last Administration last Spring to provide seed, have been repaid, and in how many districts the collection has been susdended 2" The House then rose. AN OXD WOMAN BOWED TO DELTIC, AT WIDNES. —Mr. Barker,' the deputy coroner fur the county, held an inquest on Tuesday, at the Derby Arras, Widnes, on the body of Hannah Hesketh, 64 years of age, of Chatham- street, that town, who died on Sunday morning from injuries received on the previous Friday evening through falling on the fire.. Deceased was the wife of a man named William Hesketh, and on the night of the 21st instant, he went out I to purchase some tobacco, leaving her sitting in a chair Lear I the fire place. He returned in about twenty minutes, and found that in his absence the poor woman had fallen upon the fire, whilst attempting to get up from her chair, and re- ceived serious injuries to her left side. Mr Brown, assistant to Dr. McDonnell, was called in, and attended deceased up to the time of her death. She had been in a weak state of health for some time.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

A. Max Pam= TO DRAM AT WIDNES. —On Tues- day an inquest was held at the Main Top Hotel, Mersey- road, Widnes, on the_body of Jervais Merricks, aged 58, labourer, formerly living on the Marsh, who was found frozen to death in the lobby of his house early on Saturday morning. Margery Howard deposed that she 44 known deceased for about 30 years. He was a fireman in .connee- tion with the steam crane at the Widnes dock. She iden- tified the body, and added that deceased's wife had lost her speech through a paralytic stroke, no that she could not give evidence„—Peter Leadbetter said he had known Mer- ricks for more than 26 years, and he had always found him steady in his habits. He last saw him alive at half-past eight on Friday night. He (witness) had been over to the locks, and was going home again, when he overtook de- ceased and walked with him from the crane to his own door. Deceased had had drink, but be was not incapable of taking care of himself, andhad never known him to suffer any sick- ness. Merricks had not had nny trouble or threatened to do anything to himself.—Henry Drapery stated he had known deceased between six and seven years, and he was a bteady man. He last saw him alive at half-past six o'clock on Friday morning, when he was going towards the dock. He worked with deceased, who had com- plained to him of rheumatic pains. About ball-past eight at night a neighbour came into his house and told him Mer- ricks was dead, behind his own front door, as if in a sleep- ing position. He went for Dr. McDonnell, who pronounced deceased to have beei . dead some hours, and added that be had been frozen to death. He saw the body laid out, and there were no marks of violence upon it.—After the Coroner had summed up, the jury returned an open verdict.

SONS or TEMPERANCE ANNUAL MEETING, AT WEB. Tom.—The first anniversary of the Sons of Temperance, at Weston, took place in the schoolroom of St. John the Evan- gelist, on the night of the 21st instant. Tea of a substantial character was provided, to which a good number sat down. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mesdames Aaron, Ford, J. W. Kirkham, Daniels, Poole, Ellis, Somer- ville, Parker, Price, Holford, Moores, and Andrews. After tea the chair was taken by Mr. Thomas Norman, of Run- corn, and there was a large audience, among whom were Mrs. Aaron, jun. Mrs. T. Ford, Mrs. J. W. Kirkham, Mr. and Mrs. Daniels, dr. and MneAndrews, Mr. and Mrs. Moores, Mr. and Mrs. J. Holford, the Misses Ford, and Messrs. Merriles, Cooke, Heesom, and T. Faulkner. The Chairman, in open- ing the proceedings, said that speaking as a member of the Board of Guardians, he felt he was not exaggerating when he said that nine-tenths of the cases which came before them resulted from drink. The cases of distress which he had had to deal with were sometimes heartrending. The Brunswick glee party, with Miss Norman as accompanist, gave the glees' "0, who will o'er the downs," "Hail smiling morn," and "Now pray we for our country." Mr. F. Nick-, son sang Arthur Lloyd's "Unfortunate man" it( a style which caused much laughter. He and Miss Horton sang a duet "Lc,ve and pride,' and a trio entitled "Come sail in my light canoe. with Mr. Morris (tenor.) Mr. John Pownall sang with taste "The death of Nelson," and took part in the duet "Larboard watch," with Mr. Morris. Mr. Morris gave "The tar's farewell." The elocutionary part of the programme was in the hands of Messrs. Craig (head master of the Collegiate School), Falkner, John Saunders, and Thomas Saunders, a little by, who recited Laycock's "Quality row," a Lancashire piece, in a capital manner for one so young. Mr. Craig convulsed the audience by read- ing Lover's story of Paddy Grogan, giving the brogue with all the naturalness of a son of the Emerald Isle. Mr. John Saunders was successful in the piece "How to please the wind;" and Mr. Faulkner pleased the audience with his fine rendering of William Tell. During the evening, Mr. F. Faulkner, one of the officers of the order of Sons of Temper- ance. explained the principles and aims of the order in a clear and vigorous speech. In answer to the Chairman's question as to the difference between teetotalism and the Some of Temperance, he said the members were teetotallers, but something more. He showed that while they could be teetotallers without becoming Sons of Temperance they could not be members of the order without becoming teeto- tallers. He dwelt on the provident character of their aims, and urged all who had not joined to take advantage of the special advantages offered for one month, viz., a nominal entrance fee of Is. up to 35 years of age, and 2s. 6d. up to 45.

CATTLE DISEASE IN CAESHIItE.-At a meeting of the local authority, held at Chester on Saturday, it was decided net to grant any licenses for the sale of stock, on account of cattle disease having been reported in the county. There are at present four cases of the disease in Cheshire. ACCIDENT IN THE CREWE Woßßs.—On Saturday a sad accident befel a young man named Heary Rogers, engaged in the Crewe works. He was assisting to lift the tyre of an engine wheel upon a trolly in the steel works, when the conveyance overturned and 'knocked him ,down, and the tyre fell upon his body, crushing him's° severely that but little hope is entertained "of his recovery. The metal was hot at the time, and his legs were much burned.

WILD SWANS ON THE Mzu.sEY.—As one of the many interesting results of the severe weather, may be mentioned the fact that on Saturday, about midday, three exceedingly fine specimens of the wild swan were seen on the river lay a number of passengers on one of the New Brighton ferry boats. They were full grown, being of the size of the tame swan usually found en English lakes, but each had several spots on various parts of the boly. Numerous wild ducks have also been seen in the same neighbourhood. A WAREINGTONIAN DISTINGUISHING HIMSELF AT BOLD.—At the St. Helens police conrt on Monday, Joseph Bibby, a young man from Warrington, was charged with being drunk at the Tipping Arms, Bold. A policeman stated that a great disturbance was taking place in the public- house, and he went into see what was the matter when the prisoner caught hold of the policemah by the legs and tried Ito throw him over his head. He also kicked the officer's lamp and broke it. A portion of the lamp was produced, the other portion being missing. An elderly man named Samuel Whitfield, a market gardener, living at Bold, corro- borated the statement, and prisoner, who had his left eye damaged, and who is said to be a Warringtonian, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly, and 103. and costs for the assault, 2s. 6d. being allowed for the witness Whitfield. The charge of damaging the lamp was with- drawn.

NORTHERN COI7NTIES' ATHLETIC AMOCIATION.—A meeting of the Northern Counties' Athletic Association was held at the Fountain Hotel, Meal-street, Manchester, on Saturday afternoon, when representatives attended from Crewe, Widnes, Sutton (near Liverpool), Great Crosby, East Lancashire, Manchester, and Southport. Mr. T. M. Abraham (Crewe) took the chair, and Mr. George Duxfield, one of the honorary secretaries, reported a balance in the bank of LID 13s. 4d. in favour of the Association. It was arranged that the next championship meeting of the Amciation should be held in Widnes on the 18th June, and the Widnes Athletic Club was requested to make the necessary arrange- ments for the event. Messrs. Dusfield and Fairbrother having resigned their positions as honorary secretaries, Mr. Walter Platt, Manchester, was appointed secretary to the Association. It was resolved that a representation should be made to the Amateur Athletic Association to alter rule 5 to the effect that nine members selected by the respective associations should represent thenorth, south, and midlands, and also as to the desirability of giving the Northern Coun- ties' Athletic Association an increased representation on the committee. The dates of several athletic meetings were arranged.

DISTRESS Its Ruitormis AND WIDNES. - During the first four days of the week the distress in Runcorn and Widnes was very severe, but the Runcorn Committee, established on the previous Friday, did much for its alleviation. The "sum at its disposal was about £7O, and weekly subscrip- tions to the fund were promised by the leading gentlemen in the town. The committee dispensed relief to about 12,000 persons from Saturday to Thursday; and Mt. Bowyer, the school attendance officer, with the means placed at his disposal, has given dinners to about 1,350 children. But other agencies have been at work, the masters and mis- tresses in charge of the various schools having provided nearly 2,006 meals, whilst Mr. Shaw, the president of the Mersey Mission to Seamen at Runcorn, gave a breakfast to 166 children at the mission rooms, on Sunday, afterwards presenting each with a soup ticket. It has come to our knowledge that several people have succeeded in exchanging relief cheques for tobacco and snuff at a certain grocery shop in the town. The thaw which set in on Thursday was everywhere hailed with great satisfaction, and the town presented a very animated appearance, large crowds assembling on Waterloo Bridge to witness the attempts which were being made to break up the ice. The past week has been a terrible one indeed for the poor of Whines, and it will be long remembered by the thousands of workingmen who have been thrown out of em- ployment owing to the stoppage of the principal works, as recorded in our last issue. The retail price of coal has averaged one shilling and five pence per hundred-weight, and we need hardly say that many of the poorer families in our midst have been utterly unable to purchase any but the smallest quantities under such a state of affairs. Much dis- tress has existed on all hands, but no special organisation has been established to meet it. The colliers' strike in Lan- cashire has seriously affected the staple industry of Widnes, but many of the manufacturers ordered coal in Yorkshire and Staffordshire at the beginning of the week, and on Wed- nesday between 2,000 and 3,000 tons arriVed in the town, and it was expected that the works which were standing would commence operations. It is gratifying to be able to record the fact that Mr. R. U. Davies (of the firm of Golding and Davies) presented all the men out of employment through the stoppage of their works with a half a sovereign, and a few who had been kept at the works cleaning the boilers received 55.

Iturroonx Birasswicx MIITCrAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —The weekly meeting of this society took place in the large Chas room, Brunswick school, on Wednesday evening. Mr. Simister occupied the chair, and considering the severe weather, there was a good attendance of members The Rev. H. Valentine delivered a lecture on "True Greatness," which was replete with sound advice, and met with a hearty recep- tion. .011uding to the false views of greatness that were held by many, the lecturer said the saying that "the shoe- maker should stick to his last" was the maxim of a fool. If that gigantic blunder had been made by Ben Jonsen he would have remained a bricklayer, Franklin a printer, Elihn Burritt a blacksmith, and the immortal dreamer, John Bunyan, a tinker. There were scores of great and good men who wisely did not "stick to the last." The question what was true greatness' was an important °tie. It did not con- sist in physical power, nor wealth and grandeur. It did not consist in military daring and achievements—war had its uses and BO had-treifimills and mustard-plasters. Brilliant gifts and splendid endowments did not constitute true greatness. He believed the idolatry of talent and unianctified genius was as bad as the idolatry of wealth. He instanced Shelley, Dr. Dodd, Roger Bacon, Burns, and Sheridan as men of superior talent and gifts, who were turfortunately lacking in moral qullities. Men were truly great in the proportion to which the sensual was subordinated to the moral nature. No man was truly great who was not truly good. True greatness included fidelity to God and principle in circumstances of trial and difficulty. The sacrificing of self for the good of others was another element in true greatnes4. If he were asked who was the greatest man, he would answer the best. The rev, lecturer concluded his able and interesting lecture by saying the gist then of all that had been itaid was this: it you would be great be good; if you would be happy be generous; if you would be powerful be patient; if you would be noble be Christ-like.—Mr. S. Coventry proposed a vote of thanks to the lectatrer, which was seconded by Mr. C. Nickson, and carried unanimously.

DARESSURY PETTY SESSIONS. At these sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. E. Greenall (chairman) and J. Maroon, temporary authority was granted to William Turner Cewap to sell at the Bowling Green, Little Leigh, in lieu of his mother, recently deceased.—James Jones was summoned for having, on the 11th inst., been found asleep in his lurry on the highway at Higher Whitley. The defendant ad- mitted the offence, but said he had "been on the road" for 90 years, and that was the first time he had been summoned. Defendant was ordered to pay the costs, Bs.—.-John Grounds, charged with having, on the 4th inst., at Walton Inferior, assaulted William Wilson, was fined 10s. and costs.--William Tipping was summoned for having, on the 20th January, at tippleton, committed a trespass in search of game in the day time, on land in the occupation of Mr. George War- burton. Mr. Moore appeared for the defendant. A game- .keeper named Peter Lockett, in the employ of Sir Gilbert Greenall, stated that he saw the defendant on the land on the afternoon of the 20th January. Defendant had two dogs with him, and when asked what he was doing upon the land stated he did not know he was trespassing, and that he was on his way home. The dogs " put up" a hare and ran after it. Witness stated, in answer to Mr. Moore, that the defendant, wher, he saw the doge running after the hare, called them back, but they took no notice of him. Mr. Moore, in defence, said the defendant was on his way home, and certainly never intended either to commit a trespass or go in search of game. The magistrates ordered the defen- dant to pay the costs.

EXTRACEDINAIIY SCENE IN 6 CHTTECNYAILD.-0 Sun- day evening a Mrs. Price, a widow. of Buckley, near Chester, died under peculiar circumstances. Since the death of her husband she had lived by herself, and her mind seamed attunes to be somewhat affected. On Friday night she was seen aboet the house, but on Saturday at midnight obpo aenrnothingsedw be having at tvwhi nei with bheeern s brother, bre:tnh eorf tohe hr edru hr i?nugs et .h eTdhaeyw, it nh onwe iwg ha s. and he, hearing hi s sister breathing, retired, thinking all was right. On Sunday, however, as she did not appear to have come downstairs or to be moving about, the door of Mrs. Price's house was burst open. She was then found in bed senseless, and the same evening died. Some amount of curiosity was expressed in the neighbourhood at the fact that there was to be no inquest on the body of the deceased. It is assumed that a local doctor must have given a certificate of the cause of death, as the burial was arranged for Thurday. At the last moment doubts were freely expressed as to whether the woman was really dead. The relatives of the deceased then determined, after tLe coffin had bees taken into the churchyard, that it should not be interred. Dr. M'Millan was sent for, and both he add his son attended. The coffin was unscrewed,•the lid was taken off, and an examination of the corpse made by the medical men. They expressed a decided opinion that the woman was dead, and the burial was then nroceeded with. The event caused somewhat of a sensation in the neighbourhood.

THE HUSSARS AT WARRINGTON.—On Tuesday at noon the town was visited by a troop of the 18th Hussars. The men and officers, numbering about 40, were en route from Manchester to Liverpool. During Tuesday night the men were billeted at the different public-houses, and proceeded on their journey early on Wednesday morning. PENKETH WORKMAN'S CLIIII. —On Thursday evening last, the members of the above club, who have just formed a mutual improvement clav, held their first general meeting in one of the rooms of the club. A very interesting paper was read by Mr. Colin Cooke, subject: "Free trade." The paper was well received. The following gentlemen took part in the discussion which followed :—Messrs. Hobson, D. Garnett, W.ll. Hughes, and A. White (chairman.) Amongst those present were Messrs J. W. Holden, J. Plumpton, J. Baxter, E. Hankinson, J. Mainley, P. Johnson (secretary), J. Walton, and H. Holding. The debate was adjourned for a week.

PENICETH CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION.-011 Thursday the above association held their first tea party and ball, in the clubroom, Stocks lane. Tea was provided for 150, and about 130 were present. Amongst those who rendered good service in effecting the arrangements, were Messrs. P. Davies (president), G. Segar, Jonas Forster, R. Boardman, P. Naylor, etc. Dancing was kept up with con • siderable spirit, and all present seemed to enjoy themselves. The music was supplied by Mr. J. Healy, Warrington, and his band. The room was nicely decorated for the occasion by Mr. P. Naylor, arsisted by the other members of the associa- tion.

DEATH FROM SUFFOCATION AT WARRINGTON.—An in- ' quest was held in the parade room of the Police Office, on Thesday afternoon, before Mr. T. W. Barker, deputy coroner, to inquire into the cause of the death of Edward Donnelly, aged 8 weeks, son of Peter Donnelly, labourer, Dolan's-yard, Warrington. The parents, a girl two years of age, and the deceased, all slept in one bed, and on Monday morning, at half-past four, the child was found to be dead, the little girl having been laid across its face. This was the statement made by the parents to Sergeant Spinks at the time. When called, however, the mother stated that the child was in good health when she took it to bed at 10-45 on Sunday night. When she awoke at 4-30 the following morning, the child was in her aims, quite dead, and the girl was laid across the bolster, and not upon the child. One side of the face was black and the hands were clenched. Deceased had not been subject to fits. The husband confirmed this statement. Sergt. Spinks said he went to see the deceased on Monday morning. One side of the face was black and appeared to have been laid upon, the cheek being much pressed,and one eye was completely closed, whilst the other was wide open. There was a little foam coming from the mouth. The neck also was dis- coloured, and the child had all the appearances of haying been suffocated. The parents informed him that the girl had been laid across the face of the child, but they ap- peared much confused. The Coroner said it was a question for the jury to decide whether the child had died from suffocation or from natural causes by convulsions. The appearances in both cases were very much the same, but in this particular instance, the evidence pointed to suffocation by overlaying. The jury returned a verdict that death re- sulted from suffocation.

div.p: RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRIST [AN

- ASSOCIATION. ------ ANNUAL MEETING. The annual tea meeting of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association was held on Thursday evening. There was a good attendance. The ladies who presided at the trays were Miss Peacock, Miss Norman Miss E. Collier, and Miss Clarke. Previous to the rernsvaeof the cleth,a hearty vote of thanks was given to the ladies, on the motion of Mr. J. D. Jones, seconded by Mr. E. Rhodes. The annual meeting was held immediately afterwards. Mr. Robert Shaw (the President) occupied the chair. After devotional proceedings, The PRESIDENT said they must all be aware that for an association of this kind to be healthy, the expenditure and the income ought pretty nearly to balance. There should not be any large discrepancy between the two. (Hear, hear.) Having dwelt upon tile great advantages to be derived from such an organisation and the importance of trying to pro- vide attractions for ;he young amen of the district, he ex- pressed a hope that it would continue to grow in numbers and usefulness. They knew that in domestic arrangements, if a man was only getting 20s. per week, and he spent 225., it did not need any mathematician to tell him he was going the wrong way. That night it would be their duty to look at their financial position as an association. The Hon.. SECRETARY (Mr. J. H. Humphreys) then read the fifth annual report. The committee regretted to state that there had not been that progress which they hoped for at the commencement of the year; yet they rejoiced that the association had been enabled to hold on its way and render, as heretofore, some benefit to its members. ' There was a favourable increase to report in the number of members frequenting, the reading room. The library was very well patronized, and it was certain that ere long the catalogue of 507 volumes must be further increased, providing the I register continued to show an annual list of 84 gentlemen and six lady subscribers. The report next reviewed the various lectures delivered during the year. A profit of 10s. ld. was derived from the lecture in the Public Hall, on "Eastern customs." The Bible °Lisa under Mr. Charles Garnett had [moved fairly successful. The Saturday night mission had been placed in the bands of Mr. Wm. Shaw; and several very interesting meetings had been held at the rooms. The fruit banquet at Bethesda schoolroom, in Sep- tember, was attended by a large number of friends. The roll of membership showed the honorary subscribers as 30, 'which with 111 active or associate members gave a total for the year of 141. Seventeen of these were in arrears for the half year's subscription, and 18 had been lost through removal from the town. The treasurer's statement of ac- counts showed that the financial year had closed with a balance on the wrong side. The deficit amounted to £lO 19s. Id., and would have been still larger bad it not been for the munificent donation received from their esteemed president. (Loud applause) The committee saw DO possi- bility of placing theassociation upon a sound and satisfac- tory basis in respect of funds without increasing the mem- bers' subscriptions; and, after long and careful delibera- tion they had unanimously resolved to make the minimum subscription Bs. per annum, which, after all, was but a small sum for the many advantages offered to members. The committee tendered their thanks to the ladies and gentle- men through whose aid the fruit banquet was made so great a success, to those gentlemen who bed delivered lectures, and to the friends who bad rendered assistance in other wa s.

The financial statement wal also read by Mr. Garnett There had been two proposals before the committee in re- gard to the future of the association. It had been decided ,to revise the list of newspapers and periodicals. The yearly cost of the dailies would be £5 45., of weeklies £3. 183., and of monthlies £2 9s. This proposed expenditure would effect a very considerable saving. Last year's account (which included five quarters) showed that they paid £24 ss. 7d. for newspapers; whilst the revised list only showed an expen- diture of under £l2. The present ordinary subscription was ss. per annum ; and it was proposed to raise this to Bs. He supposed they had at least 100 members, and if they sub- scribed the extra amount during the year, it would raise £4O, whilst the amount of the ordinary subscriptions during the p.tst 12 months was £lB 7s. 81. The auxiliary sub- scriptions during this year would be about £l5, whereas last year they were only £l3. The re-sale of papers would, probably, raise between £5 and £O, and with the president's honorary subscription dl £lO 10s., they would have a total of £7l On the other side, they had the cost of the papers £ll. rent and taxes £4O, gas and coal £2O, and assistant secretary, £10; so that there was every prospect of their being able to raise £7l with which to meet £BO. This would only leave them with £lO to raise- and if they all did their part in the way of lectures, Jtc.,th'ey would manage to obtain that amount. Under these circumstances, their prospects for the coming year were very bright, fie had pleasure in moving that the terms of subscription, for the future, be Be. per annum, and that the report and statement I of accounts be adopted. Mr. J. W. Ctonow seconded the maim. The CHAIRMAN said that hitherto the rate of subscrip- tion had only been a little over osts' penny per week, so that he had every confidence the members would be glad to sup- port the committee in the advanced terms they proposed to charge. In reply to a question, the fact was elicited that the total amount subscribei by the friends of the Association in the town was not quite £l3. This statement gave rise to a lively and interesting discussion as to the difficulties ex- perienced in obtaining any reasonable amount of support from many gentlemen who made somewhat loud professions as to their deep interest in the evangelical young men of Runcorn. The general opinion was expressed that it was hopeless to expect much further help than the little at pre- sent given to the committee by outsiders, with the exception of a comparative few, and that the work of appealing for I subscriptions was altogether disheartening. Some surprise was expressed that a greater number of the leading men of the town were not liberal subscribers, and one of the speakers remarked that it appeared as if there were far more cry than wool on the part of some of the supposed leaders of religious thought in the neighbourhood, who professed such a deep interest in religious young men but could not be constrained to show any marked interest in an association comprising so many. - The CHAIRMAN said it ought not to be forgbtten that the Nonconformist bodies had to do a great deal in the way of supporting their own places of worship, and their ministers were frequently called upon to subscribe very considerably. I They could not expect so much to be done in Runcorn as in towns where the population did not consist to so large an ex- tent of the labouring class. The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. COVENTRY moved a very hearty vote of thanks to the President for his services during the year, and proposed his re-election, lie spoke of Mr. Shaw's kindness and generosity in eulogistic terms, and his remarks were received with loud applause. Mr. WILLIAM SHAW seconded the proposition, which was passed with acclamation. Mr. Charles Garnett was elected treasurer, on the motion of Mr. R. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. PeAnsoN. The vice-presidents were elected as follows, on the motion of Mr. Armstrong, seconded by Mr. C. Nickson :—Revs. J. Nowell, H. Valentine, E. Williams, J. D. Thomas, J. Jones, Billington, J. Morton, and Messrs. John Simpson, G. S. Hazlehurst, G. L. Davies, T.D. Jones, Philip Speakman, and W. B. Gibson.

Mr. J. D. JONES moved that a vote of thanks be presented to Mr. J. H. Humphreys, for his services as hon. sec. since the commencement of that Association, and that, as he wished to retire owing to his numerous engagements, Mr. B. Smith be elected in his place. There could be but one opinion as to the manner in which Mr. Humphreys bad dis- charged his duties.,, (Applause.) Mr. MILLING-vox seconded the proposal, and it was sup- ported by the CHAILMAN, and passed with enthusiasm. The Rev. EVAN WILLIAMS mada a few telling remarks upon self-help on the part of the members being essential to the prosperity of the Association. He was a thorough he- Bever in voluntaryism. He moved that the following gentlemen be elected on the committee :—Messrs. W. Shaw, S. Coventry, W. Armstrong, J. D. Jones, G. Bellamy, C. Nioknon, J. H. Humphreys, and G. Howard. Mr. F. NORMAN seconded the in tion, which was passed. Mr. Smaw and Mr. B. SMITH spoke upon the necessity of the members undertaking some evangelistic work. The CHAIRMAN read a letter from Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, apologising for his inability to attend the meeting, express- ing his full sympathy with the Association in its work, and stating he should be happy to subscribe his quota to assist the funds.
A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Johnson, the treasurer to the library; after which the proceedings terminated.

THE SECRETARY OF THE WARRINGTON INFIRMARY acknowledges with thanks £2O received from the employes of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., Limited. THE HOPE IRON, STEEL, AND WIRE COMPANY, LIMITED, WARRINGTON.—WO understand that this company has tern- porarily suspended operations pending alterations, with a view to the re-construction of the company.

INQUEST AT WARRINOTON.—Mr. T. W. Barker, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Ring O'Bells public-house, Church-street, Warrington, on Tuesday afternoon, touching the death of Sarah Ann Berry, infant daughter of William Berry, of 13, Roger-street. The deceased, who had been a delicate child since birth, was found to be expiring in bed, on Sunday morning, when the parents awoke. It died in about five minuts s. The deceased had all the appearance of having had convulsions; the legs were drawn up and slightly discoloured, and the hands clenched. There had been no doctor in attendance.—A verdict of "Death from natural causes" was returned.

SUDDEN DEL= AT TrxEmvirm.—An inquest was held at the Pickering Arms, Thelwall, on Tuesday, before Mr. T.J..Ridgway, coroner, en the body of William Dichfield, 70 years of age, residing with his nephew, Thomas Dich- fleld, at Town Pits Cottage, Thelwall. The deceased had always enjoyed good health up to a month ago, when he appeared to lose his reason, and Dr. Brabazon was called in. He, however, recovered in the course ef a few days, and nothing further was thought of the matter; but on Saturday, the 22nd inst., he was attacked in a similar manner.. The nephew managed to pacify him, and on Sunday mornin2 the deceased complained that his head was "mazy." At about a quarter-past six on that day, the nephew bearing a noise in the room the deceased occupied, went to look, and found him sat upon the floor in a helpless attitude. He was carried to bed, and the nephew called in a neighbour named Mrs. Berry, whilst he fetched a doctor, but on his return his uncle was dead. A verdict of "Death from natural causes" was returned.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED.

The annual ordinary general meeting of the above com- pany, was held yesterday, at the Bank, Winwick-street, Warrington, for the purpose of declaring a dividend, elect- ing directors and auditors, and conducting the ordinary business of the company. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Charlton Parr, and there were also present the following: Directors: COI. J. Fenton Greenall, Col. Gamble, Mr. Peter Stubs, Mr. Edward GreenaM Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr. Hy. Woodcock, Mr. John Pearson, Mr. Alfred Hewlett, Sir A. B. Walker, Mr. Cecil F. Parr, Col. McCorquodale, Mr. Thomas H. Dixon, Sir Thomas G. Frost, and Mr. John Thompson; shareholders: Messrs. R. Davies, _A. Mackie, Jas. Reynolds, Jno. White, Wm. Sharp, Hy. Bleckley Geo. j Blackhurst, Ed. Greens'', unr ~ Wm. Beamont, Dr. Beaman, Jas. Lythgoe, Dr. Argyle Robertson, David Garnett, W. Silcock, junr., Chas. Broadbent, Benja. Walker, Jas Marson, C. B. Johnson, Thumas Fairhurst, and John Dun (general manager.) The report of the directors, which has already appeared in these columns, was taken as read. The'Cuentaraw, in moving the adoption of the lima., said he was happy to feel that the figures th a directors had sub- mitted that day required no explanation, and certainly no apology. That was a matter for mutual congratulation and satisfaction. (Hear, hear.) All the leading banks had changed their constitution under the limited liability prin- ciple. That, as far. as they were concerned, must be an element of satisfaction, for it showed that the reformation which the bank was one of the first to initiate was now re- commended and universally approved. (Hear, hear.) lie ventured to think that in a few years to come a joint stock unlimited bank would be a thing of the past, and would be reckoned among other extinct institutions. There was another series of acts be ought to have enacted to, viz., the post office legislation, whereby that omnipotent and omnipresent institution had conyerted itself, in addition to its usual responsibility, into a universal banking, brokering, and he might say partial financial agency. How far this would answer remained to be seen, but there was one portion of this legislation, the postal notes system, which would give bankers a great deal of_ trouble, and which, if they had adopted the suggestion of the post office, might oleo have ineufted some little amount of risk. He spoke of the gua- rantee which they asked bankers to give that they should be answerable for every crossed postal note that came into their hands, is case any informality or disability should be discovered. Their bank, in connection with a good many other banks, had declined to give that guarantee; and no doubt the post office would discover means of protecting themselves other than by the very convenient means they had suggested of throwing the liability upon bankers. There was another point he might touch upon, as their name had been incidentally mentioned. He alluded to the negotiations that took place in regard to the Southport Bank. Those negotiations came to an end. Their directors would willingly have averted some of the annoyances which that suspension must necessarily have occasioned, and they still wished that every assistance and support should be given to those parties who were incon- venienced at the present moment, with due regard to pru- dence and without undue risk. Ile was happy to notice that they had given orders to their agents to that effect. In commencing a short analysis of the balance sheet, he said they might congratulate themselves upon the very satisfac- tory condition of business. There was no doubt ..I.Sat the progress was as good as it could be, that the number of accounts had increased very considerably in the whole area of the bank, and that each branch showed an increase. (Hear, hear.) They had not thought it requisite this time to place any specific sum to the reserve fund, because it already stood at a respectable figure; but they had devoted, £2,500 to the building account, which was partly in conse- quence of the state of their premises at •Northwicb, which, as a great many of them would have heard, had been considerably shaken by the late inunda- tions, and would necessitate a great amount of money being ;pent upon them. They would observe, on comparing the balance sheet with last year's, that the money lodged had increased satisfactorily. Their acceptances were still nominal, as they always hoped they would be, merely for the convenience of customers. On the other side of the account they would notice they had invested £90,000 in consols, which stood on their books at 90. Though their other inrestments showed a certain small increase it was counterbalanced by a decrease in cash in band and money at call, because under the present circumstances, whenl things were quieter, the directors felt it was not requisite to hold such a large amount of money in band. The bills of exchange had also increased. That was satisfactory, and showed to a certain extent a revival of business. They had no bills to discount. That was a proud position for that or any other bank to be in, he considered. The advances to customers had slightly increased, which was a natural con- sequence of the increase shown in the general business of the bank. He now CaM,3 to the current expenses, which, he was extremely happy to say, were the same as last year, and that their increased profits and increased business had been done at the same cost they worked upon last year. The interim dividend absorbed £36,000; and it was proposed to pay another dividend of the same amount, and also, be was happy to say, a bonus of 2i per cent, as usnal, because their position and the amount of their profits this year amply justified them in making:such a satisfactory dividend. He concluded by moving that the report be received and adopted. (Applause.) Colonel 3. F. Cinatmrsta. seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.

I Sir G. GREENALL proposed "That, as recommended by the directors, a dividend, for the half-year ending 31st December. at the rate of 15 per cent, per annum, and a bonus of 108. per share be now declared, both free of in- come tax; and that the same be made payable at Warring- ton, or at any of the branches of the bank, or at the house of Messrs. Glyn' Mills, Currie and Co., at London, on and after the 4th February, 1831." Mr. W. Bitanchwr, seconded the resolution, and said that in a very few years the bank would become a centenarian. It would have attained the age of 100 years. The resolution was passed.

Mr. H. BLECKLY proposed "That a vote of thanks be given to the directors for their services during the past year, and their remuneration for the year be £4,000 as formerly." Referring to a speech of the chairman of the directors of the Southport bank, he said he Loped the Government woold have examinations for gentlemen who sought situations as directors of banks. They had here a body of directors who brought 'forward: accounts which satisfied everybody and did so every year, and he was sure if they were called upon to pass an examination they would do so with great satisfac- tion.

Mr. C. BROADBENT seconded the resolution. The resolution was unanitnously carried. Mr. J. REYNOLDS moved that Mr. George McCorquodale, Mr. Thomas P. Parr, Mr. Edward Greenall, Lord Delamere, and Sir G. Greenall, whet retired by rotation, and were re- commended by the Board for re-election, be re-elected directors of the company. He did not think they quid possibly improve the position of the bank by changink the directors, and therefore he moved that they be re-elected. Mr. D. Ganngrr seconded the motion, which was ap- proved. On the proposition of Mr. JOHN WHITE, seconded by Mr. W. SHARP, Mr. T. C. Stead, accountant, Liverpool, was appointed auditor for the ensuing year at a salary of £350. Mr. J. Mensom, having remarked that they were fortunate in having possession of such a highly talented and respect- able body of directors, said they Nv ere very fortunate in having as well a staff of officers and clerks who carried out their directions ; and he proposed that a vote of thanks be given to the general manager, secretary, and other officers of the company for their services during the year. (Hear, hear.) Dr. ROBERTSON, in seconding the motion, bore testimony to the ability of Mr. Dun, and said be was sure the very flourishing and prosperous condition of the bank indicated that the management had been of a very high class. Mr. Dose acknowledged the vote of thanks on behalf of the officers of the bank and himself. It was always an encouragement to them in the discharge of their duty to know that they met with the approval sof the shareholders in whose service they laboured. (Applause.) Mr. A. MACKIE proposed, and Dr. Iliteareie seconded, a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was heartily carried. The CHAIRMAN, in reply, said he was sure the skill and ability of the directors were exercised on behalf of the bank, and be hoped they would be Bo as long as he had the honour of presiding over them. (Hear, hear.) The meeting then terminated.

DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON.—The unusual severity of the weather has occasioned great distress among the lower classes of the inhabitants, and their position has been aggra- vated by the fact that they have been unable to purchase coals, owing to the high price to which they have risen in consequence of the colliers' strike. The distress has been most prevalent on Cockhedge, and in the neighbourhood of School-brow, where some families have been reduced to a most pitiable condition. On Wednesday, the members of the Board of Guardians were engaged three and a half hours in hearing applications for relief, some of the applicants stating that they were entirely destitute of food and coal. The Board gave orders for the house in every case, but the applicants refund to acisept them, as they declined to break up their homes and dispose of their " bits o' sticks." For the purpose of affording relief to the distressed, the Rector, with commendable promptitude, opened a soup kitchen in a building at the Rectory, where large quantities of soup, bread, and coal have been distributed during the week. In aid of the destitute on Cockhedge contributions were male n at a meeting of the Wycliffe Congregational Church on Thursday evening, i response to an appeal by the Rev. John Yonge, and these will be disbursed by Mr. A. Smith, the missionary at Cockhedge Mission, who will doubtless be glad to receive further subscriptions from the charitable for alike purpose. It is to be hoped that with the change in the weather the privations which have been endured will now be alleviated, if not entirely removed. div.head: LATEST TELEGRAMS, &c.
div.p: LATEST TELEGRAMS, &c.

LOST IN um Foa. At Sedgeley a tradesman named Henry Gibbons during a dense fog on Tuesday, walked into a canal and was drowned. FENIAN Scanx.—A Shorncliffe correspondent telegraphs that extra precautions are now observed at the camp. Civilians must not enter the lines after sunset. No strangers are allowed in the camp during the day. RETREAT OF THE RGERE—DORBAN, FRIDAY, 12-15 p.m. —A telegram from Newcastle, of to-day's date, Announces that the artillery of Sir G. P. Colley's force opened The upon the Boers. The infantry afterwards advanced, whereupon the enemy retreated out of range. CAPTURE OF A Rom LAAGER.—TWENIT-SEVEN KILLED: MANE WODNDED.—A patrol from Pretoria has surprised and captured a Boer laager, after severe fighting, in which the Boers lost 27 killed and many wounded. The enemy fled, abandoning their stores. The British loss was four killed and five wounded. All is well in Pretoria. THE ALLEGED MURDER AT AOCRINGTON.—At Accring- ton, yesterday morning, James Leaver, weaver, was com- mitted to take his trial at the coming Liverpool 'Assizes on a charge of murdering his daughter, aged six years. The court was crowded, and great interest was manifested in the proceedings. The prisoner appeared quite unconcerned. The defence set up is that he is insane, and that he has already been an inmpte of a lunatic asylum in America. / THE STATE OF IRELAND. The Fethard branch of the Land League has passed a resolution calling upon Mr. Patrick J. Smyth, member for Tipperary, to resign on account of his secession from Mr. Paraell's party. At Clonmell a memorial has been signed by his constituents calling on Mr. A. Moore, the member for Clonmel, to join Mr. Parnell's party. At a meeting of the Cork branch of the Land League, on Thursday, it was resolved to call upon Messrs. Shaw and Colthurst to resign their seats for the county. The Roman Catholic prelates of Ireland, meeting tinder the presidency of the Archbishop of Dublin have passed resolutions asserting that the present state of 'the land code in Ireland is intrinsically dangerous to tke peace and hapipi- ness of their people, deprecating all faltering legislation on the subject, and expressing fears that "should order seem to reign by the power of coercion the branch of the Legislature which is regarded as unfavourable to popular rights may either totally reject or substantially nullify any measure of practical utility sabrnitted to its consideration "—a result they cannot contemplate without serious alarm. The scenes of last winter are said to be again visible in Mayo. On Tuesday alma 400 determined-looking country- men marched two deep to Swinford Workhouse and fiercely demanded either bread or work. They threatened to pall dtritn the boardroom if they were not at once relieved. The Guardians are doing their hest to allay the distress, but it is feared that if the present weather continues starvation nay lapse into famine.

div.head: REBELLION IN ARMENIA.
div.p: REBELLION IN ARMENIA.

ALLEGED RUSSIAN INTRIGUE. A Central News telegram from Constantinople yesterday says :—From intelligence received here a serious outbreak in Armenia is inticipated. It is reported that the rebellion is instigated by Russia, and that both money and men have been promised. The news has caused a great deal of alarm, and will possibly have some effect on the settlement of the Greek frontier question.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—L Num'. In the House of Lords, Earl KIMBERLEY read the same despatch as Mr. Childers did in the House of Commons re- lative to the advance of Sir G. Colley in the Transvaal.— Lord WAVENEY moved that Candahar and its dependant territory might be constituted an emporium of trade and commerce under British administration and rule.—Viscount ENFIELD said it would not pay to keep Candahar as an emporium of trade, and it would require 20,000 men to defend it.

HOUSE OF COMMONS--Lasi Num. THE ABOLITION OF JUDICAL OFFICES.--Sir H. JANES presented a petition from members of the Bar against the abolition of offices of the Chief Baron of Exchequer, and Chief Justice of Common Pleas. • Distranunott OF BIICILSHOT.—Mr. CHILDERS, replying to Mr. Biggar, said that buckshot had not been served out to the forces in ary part of the United Kingdom. THE LAND LEAGUE.— Mr. FORSTER, replying to Sir H. Taylor, said he was unable to give information as to the number of persons who have been compelled against their will to subscribe to the Land League. Tine OCCUPATION OF CANDAHAII.—Lord HARTINGTON said the information received respecting the Russian victory had not modified the intention of the Government to with- draw from Candahar. THE WAR IN TEE TRANSVAAL—Mr. CHILDEHS, in reply to Sir H. Havelock, said he had received a telegram from Sir G. P. Colley about an hour ago, dated Jan. 28, stating that an attack had been made on a pass and repulsed, and that the casualties were heavy, though not yet known. He held the camp three miles from the spot until the arrival of rein- forcements. He Wieved that the attack upon the Boers had been repulsed. The Lord Advocate took his seat for Edinburgh. THE PROTECTION OF PERSON AND P ROpll RTy (IRELAND) Grtansronn said it would be desirable for the adjourned debate to close that night. In that event he would proceed with the second reading on Monday; but the debate would be adjourned about ten o'clock, in order that the order in council, with regard to the abolition of the offices of Chief Justice of Common Pleas and the Chief Baron of Exchequer, sight be considered.—Mr. PARNELL did not think it was possible for the adjourned debate to close that night —The adjourned debate on Mr. Forster's motion for leave to introduce the Protection of Person and Property Bill was resumed by Mr. POWER.
