THE BATTLE OF THE SEXES (SECTS). Sir,— I have been much amused and edified by listening of 'ate to strong language employed by certain Chriatians of Rockenvag,e. This small rural hamlet was once the scene of wars, in the days of the Commonwealth; and it is said good 014 Oliver the Protector blew down the castle ivalls. Your correspondent is unable to vouch for the accuracy of this - historical report. However, since that stormy period the ruins.have witnessed terrible though bloodless battles, if not under the peaceful reign of the famous Earls of Rocksavage, by foes still more fearful. You will kindly pardon this digression. Now to the point. It appears that some few ,nontlis ago the village was invaded by a Christian Army, under the leadership of a Rencorn tradesman, of excellent repute as a Methodist local preacher. Certain other so-called Christians were waited upon, and asked if they would join in this laudable enter- /arise. These, bye-the-bye, are known by the villagers as tit e Prime. Oh! but holding up their hands in holy horror, they with one voice declared they could not be mixed up with sush a wild crew, for they were accustomed to worship God decently and in order. "Well," the leader said, "but there is no service of any kind held in the village pow, and we do not see why you should object to our coming to do good amongst the people." "Well, but do you see," sTal the leader of the Prints., "we first laid seige la the township, and you have no manner of right now to come. We shall some day go in to convert all the five hundred and seventy- one householders, and we have a school here now composed of two hundred and twenty-one good, honest souls. Get out of my sight; no one has any right to save these souls except the Holy Prims., a people founded by Hugh Bourne, just anterior to the flood." This terrible denunciation did not at all daunt the new glourch, now generally known as the Marshallite. They have gone along gloriously, and done much good in gathering crowds of the very worst character out of the lane every Sabbath. Now, however, comes the tug of war. If the Prime. cannot conquer one way they are determined to starve, out-and-out, the poor Marshallite follower. Going oyer there on Tuesday, I met a few poor women in earnest Conversation. At length I gleaned this much :—" Well, well," spoke aloud a very poorly-clad disciple of the Prima, "I am determined to stick close to the old ship; it landed all my fathers, and it shall land me." "On, never mind," said a strong-minded Marshallite, "we know what yon go to the meeting house for." " Oh, aye," said the Prim ,"I can have a bit of bread, for they'll never let me clem." " Loaf, or no loaf, glory be to God," screamed the Marshallite, "the Army for ever; if the Prims, do clem us out, we'll sing and shout salvation. We can keep ourselves warm withoutcoaLe these hard times, for we all sing till we are happy ; then it keeps out the cold." Now, I suppose, Mr. Editor, it is still a war with the sects. —Yours obediently, THOMAS.

KITCHEN BOILER EXPLOSIONS. Sir,—Having regard to the number of kitchen boiler explosions occurring at the present time, many of them attended with fatal consequences, it might perhaps be of service if you could find room for the following in your columns.—Yours faithfully, LAVTNGTON E. FLETCHER. INSTRUCTIONS FOR A PLACARD. On the recurrence of frost it might be well to have pla- cards printed in large clear type and posted in prominent positions in the public thoroughfares or other suitable • Places, explaining to the public the best means of prevent- ing kitchen and circulating boiler explosions. ' TEXT FOR PLACARD: Manchester Steam Users' Associa- tion on Kitchcn and Circulating Boiler Explosions.-Kitchen boiler explosions are due to an accumulation of pressure in the boiler in consequence of the outlets being stopped up while the fire is burning. These explosions occur during the frost through the choking up of the pipes with ice. Sometimes stop taps are placed to the circulating pipes, and should these taps be shut, or should the circulating pipes become choked with sediment or stopped up from any other cause, the pressure would then be bottled up and an explo- sion might result at any time, whether summer or winter. To prevent this every boiler should be fitted with a small • reliable safety valve, whether the boiler be of copper or of cast-iron, and whether it be fitted with a copper cylinder or not. A safety valve of dead weight construction is recom- mended as the most simple. In the event of the outlets becoming choked, it would relieve an undue pressure and prevent an accumulation, while at the earns time it would emit a slight hissing noise, which would tell those in the kitchen that something was wrong. In the meantime, until a safety valve can be fixed, open the hot water tap in the bath-room, and any other hot water taps coenected with the boiler. If the water cannot be drawn freely from these taps, do not light the fire, and if the fire be already lighted, put it out at once. If the water flows freely the fire may then be lighted, but this must be done with caution, and the taps just described frequently opened to see that the flow con- tinues and that the water gradually heats. If the flow does not continue, or if the water does not heat, the supply of water to the boiler must be running short or something must be wrong with the circulation and the fire must be drawn. Also the cold water cistern as well as the ball tap should be examined, and the cold water taps in the bath-room and elsewhere opened to see that the water supply is free, other- wise the boiler may run dry. When the fire is once lighted and the circulation proved to be free, the fire should be kept burning by night as well as by day as long as the frost lasts, otherwise the frost may get the mastery during the night, choke the pipes with ice; stop the circulation, bottle tip the pressure, and thus lead to the bursting of the boiler. But the only true safeguard is a reliable safety valve, and the sooner that is fixed to the boiler the better.—LAYING- TON E. FLETCHER, Chief Engineer. 9, Mount-st., Albert- square, Manchester, January, 1881.—P.S. The Manchester Steam Users' Association has nothing' whatever to do with the manufacture or sale of the dead weight safety valve recommended; but it may be of convenience to the public to state that one made in accordance with the association's drawings may be obtained for 103. 61. at Messrs. Isaac Storey and Sons, Cathedral-yard, Manchester.

KITCHEN BOILER EXPLOSIONS. Sir,—The usual list of killed and wounded from this cause has already far exceeded its average annual propor- tions Why such a cumbrous and costly mode of heating baths is persisted in is difficult to tell, but it is mm)able that until the plumber is made liable to be he.ught up for manslaughter there will be no change. The average Briton is far LOO conservative to give up an old system for a better. There is not the slightest reason why a kitchen or bath boiler should ever explode if properly fixed, by a plumber who has the smallest amount ef common sense. There are two simple ways by which an explosion can be totally pre- vented—one by fighlg a dead weight safety -valve which should be for cop,' en ience fixed when the apparatus is put up first. The oti-er is to cut a hole in the hot water return pipe, a little die.ance above the boiler, this hole being from inch 1, 1 inch in diameter, and to solder over this a piece of si.eet lead about 1-32nd inch thick, just sufficient to safely stand the general water pressure, making in fact a weak puce in the system of pipes which will be the first to give way. This hole must be cut in such A position that the pipe is certain to be warmed from the fire, and as near as possible to the boiler. It must also be where, in case of the sheet lead being blown out the water will note thrown into the room, but into the fire so as to extinguish it. Any plumber should do this for a shilling tar two, and although it is liable to make a mess it only does this when an explosion would occur in its absence. It is also easy to put an escape pipe tliough which the water could be led away to the out- side of the building in case of accident. This thin lead safety disc might be made so as to flx in a brass socket and be easily replaced if an accident did occur. The whole system of circulating boilers as at present fixed is radically wrong, as, with few exceptions, the bet water is rarely to be got when wanted in any quantity, and the cost in fuel expended is utterly out of proportion to the useful result obtained. There are many simpler, cheaper, and more satisfactory arrangements which can be fixed at less tban ' one-tenth the cost and of all these the best is a galvanized iron or copper cylinder of about eight gallons capacity, with a tap, and a good gas heating burner underneath it, the cylinder having a loose; lid and 7a water supply tap over it for filling as required. After some months' daily experience Nith this there is no doubt that it is far cheaper to use than fbe circulating boiler system, and far more usefel for general work. It as also the advantage of absolute safety under any possible condition. In case of a stoppage preventing the use of the kitchen fire, the use of gas for cooking prevents the slightest difficulty or inconvenience. This has now attained such a perfection that it is more than probable that a good gas cooking apparatus, even if g tas a make- shift, will qucickly find its proper place, and permanently supersede the fire for all work. It is generally considered that circulating boilers with a reserve cylinder are safe from explosion. This is a mistake, as a case where the cylinder burst and flooded a house has come under my notice within the last few days' and this is by no means the first accident of the kind whichl have known. THOS. FLETCHER R.C.S.
4, Museum-street, Warrington. I shall be glad to give any further information on this matter to those interested, but must desire that any letters Shall be as concise as possible.

div.head: WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.

The House assembled on Monday evening at the Co- operative Hall, Sankev-street, Dr. Huson-More (the speaker) in the chair. There was a good attendance of members, and the "stranger's gallery," contained a goodly number of visitors, including several ladies who appeared to take considerable interest in the proceedings. NOTICES. The member for WEST CUMBERLAND gave notice that he would next Monday ask the Secretary for Foreign Affairs, if the "more stringent temporary measure," mentioned in the Queen's speech is the same as propounded by him when In opposition, which was to place Ireland under the sea for a few hours ; and if he intends to be in Ireland at the time to see that the "more stringent temporary measure" is thoroughly carried out, or if he has prudently changed his views with his scat from the opposition to the Treasury Bench.—The member for DROGHEDA gave notice of the j following question: To ask the Secretary for Ireland if he I will be good enough to enumerate the various Coercion Acts I which have been passed from the data of the great Irish I potato famine up to the present time, stating the duration of each separate act, also giving the number of agrarian out- rages said to have occurred during the operation of such acts, and also stating the number of agrarian outrages which I have occurred during such times as Ireland has been Igoverned during the period above referred to without having recourse to coercion.—The thember for EVESHAM : to askthe Colonial Setretary whether the forced labour ordinance is in force in Cyprus, and, if such is the case, whether the ' Government will abolish the said ordinance.—The member for WoLvEnstaerrroer gave notice that he will ask the Prime Minister if the attention of the Government has been drawn to the painful scenes of clergymen in the Established Church being committed to prison under the provisions of Public Worship Regulation Act, for what they allege to be the dictates of, their conscience, and whether it is the in- tention of Her Majesty's Government to prevent a re- petition of such scenes by repealing the said act.— The ,nember for MID-LINCOLNSHIRE gave notice that he will ask the Prime Minister whether the attention of the Government has been drawn to the report which has been circulated through the press, that Mr. Parnell and other , members of the Irish Land League have appointed a com- mittee of Irish Land Leaguers to establish a Land League in England, and whether the Government intend to take any and what steps to discountenance such an institution here seeing the evils which are daily arising under a similar j society in Ireland.—The member for HALIFAX, to ask the Secretary of State for War if he could give any information with regard to the attempt to blow up Salford Barracks, and if any similar attempt had been made on any other barracks. —The member for ETESHA3f, to ask the Home Secretary whether the Government will bring in a measure dealing with the water question with regard to London. REPLIES. The PRIME MINISTER replying to the member for Mid- dlesex, said the Government would give the House full information in regard to crime in Ireland before bringing forward the measure which was needed of restoring law and order in that country. (Hear, hear.) ' In answer to the member for Carlisle, the HOME SECRE- I TARE said he was not aware that it was the intention of the Government to bring in a licensing bill this session. The CHANCELLOR of the DUCHY Of LANCASTER, replying to the member for West Cumberland, said colliery proprie- tors of Lancashire who were magistrates might have com- bined to protect themselves against what they considered an unjust Act, by trying to contract themselves outside the same, but the Government had not thought it of that im- portance either to mention their names or discharge them. (Hear, hear.) The DOME SECRETARY stated, in answer to the right hon. member for Kendal, that he believed the present intention of the Government was not to embody a measure respecting vivisection in the measures they intended to submit to the House ; but he believed the right hon. gentleman was him- self anxious to bring the matter before the House, and he would afford him every facility for doing so.—The right hon. member gave notice of his intention to introduce a bill dealing with vivisection. In reply to the member for Carlisle, the HOME SECRETARY said the Government measure for closing public-houses on , Sunday would contain provisions which would affect both England and Wales. (Hear, hear.) The PRIME MINISTER, in answer to the member for Wol- verhampton, said it was not possible to provide a return of the sales of livings in the Church of England, because there was no officer appointed for the purpose of procuring the returns of sales of any kind of property is England. Replying to the member for South Hampshire, the AT- TORNEY GENERAL said the Government did not intend to bring forward any measure the object or result of which would be to relieve from their matrimonial engage- ments those persons who had been so rash as to enter into them. (Loud laughter.) At the same time, they would be pleased to afford the member for Woodstock an opportunity of bringing in his measure on that subject, of which he had given notice. (Applause.) In answer to the member for Evesham, the WAR SECRE- TARY said be was afraid he could not hold out any hope that the Government would be able to bring in a bill to abolish flogging in the army, but there could not possibly be any objection to the bon. member introducing such a bill. The ATTORNEY GENERAL, in reply to the member for Dudley, said it was not the intention of the Government to introduce any measure in regard to the marriage of the deceased wife's sister. (Hear, hear.) In answer to the member for Chelsea, the PRIME Mims- TER said he presumed the hon. gentleman meant the scien- tific frontier mentioned by Lord Beaconsfield, and Lord Beaconsfield defined that scientific frontier as being the gates of India, the mountain passes of the north west frontier. ~.. The PRIME MINISTER, replying to the right hon. member for Northampton, said it was well known that the Irish constabulary were necessarily provided with arms, and as buck shot was less dangerous than ordinary shot he supposed, therefore, it was ordered. The PRIME MINISTER, in the absence of the Irish Secre- tary, stated, in answer to the member for Penrhyn and Fal- mouth, that the Government measure in regard to education in Ireland was not yet drafted, but the general opinion of the Government was that elementary education in Ireland as well as in all other parts of the country ought to be compulsory, and he thought it ought to be undenominational in. the same sense as elementary education in England was undenominational. The COLONIAL SECRETARY, replying to the member for Staleybridge, said when the supremacy of the Crown had been restored, and our position in regard to the TranaVaal settled on a satisfactory basis, the Government would be able to count the cost attending the annexation of the Transvaal and the Zulu war. The SPEAKER said it was necessary for the purpose of saving time that members who gave notice should either be present themselves at the time appointed to ask the ques- tions, or see that someone was entrusted with the duty they wished to be performed. (Hear, hear.) THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER resumed the debate on the Address to the Queen. Referring to Afghanistan, the right hon. gentlemen quoted a statement of Sir F. Roberts in favour of retaining Candahar, and said he could not add anything to that statement. He adverted to the remark of the member for Drogheda that there was a lying spirit abroad, and said the right hon. member was the only one ' under its benign influence. (‘ Oh.") The SPEAKER called upon the right lion, gentleman to withdraw the remark, and The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said if it was out of order he would do so. Speaking of Ireland, he hoped when the Government brought in a bill with respect to the land it would be of such a character as to commend itself to both sides of the House. (Hear, hear.) He expressed his opinion that in the land agitation there was :something hidden, and declared that it was tke repeal of the Union—(hear, hear) ; and concluded by condemning the action of Mr. Parnell and his colleagues. ' The member for the FLINT BOROUGHS complimented the 'douse upon the new ministry. In point of numbers they certainly did exceed their predecessors,—whether they would excel their strength remained to be seen. (Hear, hear.) He rejoiced to see a reference to the licensing laws in the Queen's speech, but taken as a whole with that speech Ihe was greatly disappointed. (Hear, hear.) Referring to 1 South Africa, he expressed his opinion that the annexation of the Transvaal was a huge blunder. (Hear, hear.) As to keeping possession of Candahar, the hon..member said j surely we had inflicted punishment enough upon that un- happy country, which had been thrown into a state!of an- archy for the sake of a non-essential scientific frontier. I (Hear, hear.) Speaking of; the European concert, the ! hon.ornember said he rejoiced at the results of the cession 'of Dulcigno. As to Ireland, it appeared to bins that the i Government knew very little about that country, or they Iwould not tell the House they were simply to consider i whether it was necessary to bring in a measure for im- proving the relations between landlords and tenants, and he quoted statistics which, he said, certainly showed that coer- cion would not prevent outrage in Ireland. Let them treat Ireland as a sister, and then they would make her one of the strongest links in our up ited empire. He commented on the statement in the Speech that "the estimates for the coming year would be carefully prepared," remarking that " carefully" was an unusual word in Conseivative speeches, and gave the estimated and actuat expenditure of the last few years, showing how necessary it was the Government should tell the House that for the future they were going to be careful. In conclusion he trusted that the well .known financial ability of certain members of the Government and the legal acumen of certain others, would prevent them committing an error like the piece of bungling which to satisfy Lord Beaconsfield's well-known craving for territory had thrown the tinancies of India into a state of confusion, saddled that country with increased taxation, and brought us little but disaster and dishonour. (Applause). The member for SorTn-WnesT Leercaswinn (the Under Secretary to the Treasury) afforded the House a little diver- sity to the serio'usnese which usually characterises it. He stated that he rose to support the address, adding that lie felt he would have a very difficult duty to perform, a re- mark which was greeted with hearty "bear, hears," by the Opposition. If hon. gentlemen would allow him he would tell them why. (Hear, hear.) Having told the House that it was in consequence of the able speeches of the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the member for the Flint Boroughs, he re- lated a story about some one giving half-a-crown for two and sixpence, and with a knowing nod he said no doubt hon. gentlemen opposite did net expect much more from them a statement that fairly convulsed the House. He had scarcely spoken on foreign affairs when he amused the House by stating that it was "quite enough for him." He expressed his surprise at the remark of the late Irish Secretary that the reference in the Speech to Ireland was a disgrace, as on

div.head: EXAMINER, _SATURDAY, JANUARY 29. ail.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, _SATURDAY, JANUARY 29. ail.

He asked the House to assist the Government to repress the anarchy in that country, and resumed his seat amid laughter and applause. The right hon. member for NORWICH criticised the speech cf the Chancellor of the Exchequer, who had made no reference to finance. The Speech, he said, seemed to be characteristic of the party, as it might mean anything they pleased. He deprecated the renewal of the Peace Preserva- tion Act, and said what was wanted was a more stringent measure for the landlords. The member for WARRINGTON also condemned the adop- tion of coercive measures; and the House adjourned about ten o'clock.
WEDNESDAY.—There was no sitting of the court. - . . . .

THUBSDAL—Before Captain Litton ad Mr. Armitage. AN AOGRAYATED Asseuvr.--Henry Evans, a respectably- dressed man, was brought up on a warrant charged with assaulting Elizabeth McGrail, a widow, residing at 15, Dixon-street, Warrington.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoner bad been lodging with the prosecutrix for some months, and she stated that on the morning of Tuesday the prisoner went into her bedroom, and put certain questions to her. She refused to comply with his requests, and he beat her in a most unmerciful manner. The parties had been keeping company for some time with the intention of being married, but the relationship had been broken off; and that had, no doubt, annoyed the prisoner.—The priso- ner, in defending himself, alleged that the prosecutrix had been guilty of familiar intercourse with a fellow-lodger.— In answer to Captain Litton' the prosecutrix said she wished to press the case, and further stated that what the prisoner had said was untrue. He had from the previous Saturday to the time when the assault was committed be- haved in a very violent manner. On Tuesday morning he went into her bedroom, where she was sleeping with her little girl, pulled her out of bed by the hair, and struck her three times on the side of the head and once in the eye. He used threatening language, and said "he would have his revenge." He then kicked her, and she fainted at the top of the stairs as she was about to descend. He had offered her marriage next March.—Captain Litton said the evidences of the assault, which was an aggravated one, were pretty well marked on the prosecutrix's face.—The prisoner was fined 40s. and costs or a month's imprisonment.—Mr. Howarth, the other lodger, made a statement refuting the charges made by the prisoner.—The prisoner was re-called, and. in- formed that if he used any harsh means towards the woman he would have to find heavy securities and be severely punished. ROBBING HIS FATHER.—Joseph Henshaw, a young man, who had been apprehended by Inspector Singleton, on the previous. evening, on a charge of stealing £2O from his father, John Henshaw, formerly of the Cemetery Inn. War- rington was remanded over to the Manchester police, on the application of Mr. Hunt.—The prisoner stated he had been robbed of £1.7 a the money by a girl in Liverpool. The drawer from which he stole the money contained £9O. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. J. White, Mr. Z. Armitage, and Councillor Monks.

"ALL DRlNK."—Catherine Noble was charged on remand with stealing a pair of boots from the shop of Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Booth, Buttermarket-street. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and said "it was all drink."—Mr. Hunt stated that the prisoner went to Mr.. Morton's on Saturday night, and offered the boots produced for pledge. Mr. Morton had some suspicions, and gave information to the police who found that the boots had been stolen from tb shop Of the prosecutrix. The prisoner had been previously committed for six months' imprisonment for a similar offence.—The prisoner was sentenced to two months' imprisonment. A DEFAULTING FUSTIAN CUTTER.—Ann Bannister was summoned by Mr. George Aspey, fustian cutter, who claimed 10s. compensation by reason of defendant having refused, on the 27th December, to fulfil her contract.—The defendant admitted the offence, and the Bench made an order for the amount claimed at is. od. per week.

div.head: WARRINGTON POPCE CASES.
div.p: WARRINGTON POPCE CASES.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Conn- cillor Fairclough, Major Cartwright, and Aid. Burgess. DISORDERLY PERSONS.—Charles Evans, a young man, was fined 55. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket street, on Saturday afternoon.—Ann Rigby was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Booth. street, early on Sunday morning, and was sent to prison for a month without the option of a fine.—For a similar offence, in Bewsey-street, Jane Maynes was sent to prison for 14 days.—A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted on John Garby for being drunk in Green-street, on the 15th inst. VAGRANCY.—EIIen Roberts and Martha Cord, characters well known to the police, were charged with being on the premises of James Monks, Arpley Rope Walk, at 7 o'clock on Sunday evening, with no visible means of existence.— The prisoners were sent to gaol for 14 days. Scwoot Arrummsca CASES.—The case of James Gorst, which was adjourned last week to allow the defendant to produce a medical certificate, again came up. The defendant had failed to obtain the certificate, and he was fined 2s. 6d. ' —William Clark was summoned by Mr. Riley for not send- ing his son, William Henry, regularly to school. The lad was ten years of age, and had only just learnt the alphabet. Defendant said he paid the school fees every week, but his wife must have kept the boy at home. Mr. Riley said the defendant's wife was a very loose character, and sent the boy to buy beer with the school pence. Major Cartwright: Is your wife the master? Defendant: She is in one sense. If I were to beat her she would bring me here. The case was adjourned for a week, the defendant promising to see that the boy went to school.—Joseph Worrell appeared in answer to a similar summons. His children Elizabeth, Ellen, and Frederick, had made respectively only 100, 248, and 258 attendances out of a possible 532. Defendant was fined 2s. 6d. in each case. William Worrall was fined ss. for a similar offence, his daughter Margaret having only made 102 attendances out of a possible 532.—Thomas Swar- brick, an old man was summoned for not sending his children Alexander, and Ida to school regularly. De- fendant said he was too poor to pay the school fees, and he had not applied for them to be paid because he was under the impression it would make him a pauper. The Mayor said it was quite a mistake; it would not do so. Defendant promised to send his children to school, and the case was adjourned for a month. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE.—Peter Manley was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart, at Latchford, on the 15th inst.—He stated he had only had three pints.—Major Cartwright: Three pints is a good start.—Fined 55., including costs. A DEFENDANT ORDERED INTO CUSTODY. Jonathan Finch, cab proprietor, was then called in answer to a charge of allowing a horse to be worked in an unfit state, and his son was charged with working the horse.—Defendant (very wildly) : I shall not go in the prisoners' box; I am not a prisoner. Am I a prisoner, Mr. Hunt ?—Mr. Hunt: You are a defendant ; go in the defendants' box.—Defendant's conduct in the box was so rough and noisy that the Bench ordered him to be kept in custody until Tuesday morning.— Major Cartwright said the defendant was not responsible for his actions, and he inquired of defendant's wife if he had the deliriunn tremens.—Mrs. Finch replied that her husband had had no liquor that she was awareof.—At the conclusion of the business of the court, the defendant was again put in the box having promised to be quiet.—P.C. Taylor, special constable, suid on the 13th inst. he was at the north gate at , Dallam Forge.—Defendant (excitedly) : Are you a sworn constable? Yes.—And does the Corporation allow you to , be sworn and work as a jockey ?—Mr. Hunt (to defendant): Be quiet—Defendant: I tell you I have to defend myself.— The witness, continuing, said the defendant's son had charge of a horse and cart. The horse walked with greatdifficulty, and appeared to be suffering from contracted sinews or a prick in the hoof.—Defendant (with much gesticulation) : Much you know about horses. Tha knows more about whiskey and old women, the does. Tha's bin a bad tha has. I'll have two months before I'll pay for that scoundrel.—The Bench remonstrated with the defendant as to his conduct,Ont without effect.—Defendant: How many sergeants is there as they can afford to look after horses instead of robberies—The Bench said they could not pro- ceed with the case, and ordered the defendant to be removed in custody.
TLTBSDAY.— Before Major Cartwright, Alderman Cbandley, and Conheillor Broadbent.

FINCH AGAIN BEFORE THE Bimmt.—Jonathan Finch, cab proprietor, was brought up charged with cruelty to a horse by allowing it to be worked in an unfit state; and further with being drunk and disorderly in the Police Court. Ths son of the prisoner was charged with working the horse, but Mr. Hunt subsequently withdrew that charge. The prisoner pleaded guilty to the charges of cruelty.—P.C. Taylor said he saw the prisoner's son in charge of a horse and cart at the north gate, Dallam Forge, on Thursday, the 13th inst. The cart was loaded with cinders. The horse appeared to be in much pain, and on the cart coming to a standstill, through some obstruction the horse stood on three legs. He spoke to the boy, who said the horse had been lawie ever since it was bought, and that its shoe had been taken off three times through some fault in the shoeing. In the con- stable's opinion it was suffering from contracted sinews from the difficulty which it experienced in putting its foot to the ground.—ln reply to Major Cartwright witness said the horse was in low condition, and in a perspiration through pain. 'He again saw the defendant working the horse on Saturday morning, and it was tken in a bad state. He had seen many cases of that kind, but ha had never in all his experience seen a worse case.—The prisoner said the horse had been taken to Manchester and would be killed by that time.—lnspeetor Singleton deposed to seeing the barge worked on the lath inst., and said it walked with difficulty.—John Dixon, assistant to Mr. Frederick Wall, veterinary surgeon, said be made an examination of the horse on the 15th inst. It was suffering from contracted sinews and inflammation of the fetlock and foot.—Aldertnan Chandley: Would it cause it great pain to work it? Yes.—The prisoner said he had to cart 16 loads of cinders to Dallam Forge a day.—Alder- man Chandley : Then this horse would have to make 16 journeys to Hallam Forge ?—Major Cartwright: A good horse could net stand that.—The Bench considered the case clearly proved, and the prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, in default 14 days' imprisonment.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoner's statement that the horse had been sent away and destreyed was not satisfactory. Some officer of the Humane Society might meet with the horse being worked, and some reflec- tions would be cast upon the Warrington police. It would be much more satisfactory if the prisoner would tell whet° he had sent.—The prisoner promised to do SO.—Major Cart- wright: With regard to the charge of drunkenness Mr. Hunt.—Mr. Hunt said he was responsible for the peace and order of the town, and a man coming into the court and stat- ing in the way Finch did on the previous day was very undignified and improper, and lie could not use language too strong in condemning it. He felt it to be his duty to press the case, not so much as punishment for Finch, but as a deterrent to othets.—After some discussion the Bench, con- sidering that the prisoner had been locked up 24 hours, dismissed him. THE DRUNKEN ENGINE DRIVER. Christopher Percy was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge- street, on the previous night.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoner wae a stranger to the town.—Prisoner said he was an engine driver, and was going to Manchester.—Majosgartwright Where did you work last? At a mill in Manchester.—Then you are not a locomotive engine driver? No, but I can do. —Councillor Broadbent: I would not like to ride on the locomotive you drove. (Laughter.)—The prisoner was dis- charged on promising to go to Manchester. Tunwr vuom A DWELLING-HOUSE. Elizabeth Pilling. ham, a respectable-looking married woman,was charged with stealing from the house of William Lane, plumber, 22, Charles-street, a white tablecloth, value 2s. 6d.—The pri- soner pleaded guilty.—lt appeared from a statement by Mr. Hunt that Mrs. Lane, wife of the prosecutrix, left the house during Monday afternoon, in charge of her daughter Mary, aged 8. Soon after the mother had gone the prisoner entered the house and took from a rail the table-cloth produced without saying anything. The woman then went to a house in Dallam-lane where she sold the table-cloth for sixpence, spending the money thus obtained in drink. The prosecutor when he came home from his work went to the prisoner's house and asked for the table-cloth, but he was told he could have it in the morning. The police were informed of the occurrence, and the property was recovered.—Prosecu- tor said he did not wish to press the case for the prisoner's husband's sake.—Mr. Hunt said this was the way in which the police were dealt with in these cases. When the police bad taken the trouble of tracing the thing out, and the pro- perty was in a fair way of being recovered, the parties with- drew. The police did not want to be dealt with so cheaply, and he must ask for a cenviction to be recorded.—The Bench discharged the prisoner, but informed her that a conviction would be recorded against her. -

"A COWARDLY Acr."—John Saulsby, a puddler, was brought up, under a warrant, charged with assaulting John Wood, landlord of the Old Ball public-house, on Saturday evening.—Prosecutor said the prisoner entered his house on the night in question and commenced to use very obscene language. He desired him to leave, but he refused to do so, and said he wanted a glass of hot rum. Witness refused to serve him and the prisoner picked up a tumbler which he sent with much force, the missile striking the landlord on the hand. He then sent another, but the landlord managed to escape it. The prisoner was not drunk.—Jawtes Thomas, who was in the house at the time of the occurrence, said the prisoner struck the landlord twice on the face with his fist, and sent the glasses as stated by the prosecutor.—P.C. Wil- kinson deposed to taking the prisoner into custody. He walked with the officer quietly until they arrived in Win- wick-street, when he tripped him up and before the officer could recover himself he was out of sight.—Prisoner denied striking or sending the glasses at the landlord, who, he said was drunk.—P.C. Wilkinson, re-called, said the landlord was sober.—Major Cartwright said it was a cowardly act to ' throw the glasses, and the Bench were dealing very leniently with him in fining him 20s. and costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: SEVERE FROST.
div.p: THE SEVERE FROST.

- A steamer from Barrow which arrived at Greenock on Wednesday reports that while four fishermen, named John and David M`Millan (brothers), Malcolm M`Lean, and Wil- liam M‘Kinnon, were crossing from Uist, Bara, in an open boat it was seen to capsize, and M`Kinnon was drowned. The other three appear to have managed to upwright the boat and got into it, but having neither oars nor sail they were found the next day drifting in the Sound, sitting on the seats dead. They had all perished from the fearful cold.

On Wednesday, at Connah's Quay, a port on the Dee, all the shipping was frozen up with ice measuring between 91t. and loft thick, and the owners of vessels in dock and in the river anticipate the high tides with great alarm, as it is feared that the ice floes when moved by the force of the tide will crush in the vessel's ribs. No vessel can now enter or leave the port. Twenty-two degrees of frost were regis- tered at Chester on Wednesday morning. At Hull the Humber is completely covered with drift ice, and in consequence of the fog and the immense masses of ice that have collected in different parts of to river traffic is almost entirely suspended. The docks are also covered with ice, and steam launches have to be employed for the , loading and unloading of the vessels. Telegraphic conmu- nication with all the principal centres was, on Wednesday, seriously interrupted by the hear frost which has collected round the wires and insulators. The distress in the town is beginning to assume a serious aspect. Several thousands of persons sre out of work. Steps are being taken by the trade societies to organise a system of relief. Mr. Steward's returns show the cold during Tuesday night round London to have been more intense than on the pre- vious night. At Brockley there were 24 degrees of frost; Stepney, 19; and Wimbledon, 18. At Berwick several fishermen have had their bands, ears, and noses frost-bitten. The men employed to clear the streets are also suffering very keenly. At Liverpool the river Mersey, on Wednesday, presented a very curious sight, large floes of ice drifting up and down with the tide; and at low water, when the tide was slack, there was a compact field of ice from one shore to the other. The numerous ferry steamers plying between Liverpool and the different depots on the opposite Cheshire shore expe- rienced great difficulty in cutting through such a rare obstruction. .

Accounts from various parts of the kingdom describe a sudden break-up of the frost. More especially was this the case on Wednesday night in the south and west of England, where enormous quantities of snow have fallen, but where rain is now reported in several places. At 8-30 p.m. the meteorological return anticipated southerly and westerly winds and gales, and much milder weather, with an intima- tion that sleet and rain are probable over our southern dis- tricts, With easterly and south-easterly winds and snow in the north. Temperature had already risen 50 deg. at Scilly, to 43 at Valentia, and to between 32 and M over the south- eastern counties. The air in London was much softer than of late.

On Wednesday a severe thunderstorm, which lasted more than an hour, passed over Caithness-shire and other parts of the North af Scotland. Sr. HELENS YOUNG MEN'S INSTITUTE—On Monday night the members of this Institute and friends assembled to hear an essay on "Combustion," by Mr. Drummond, teacher of the Chemistry class. There was a fair attendance. Mr. Gladstone's Secretary has informed the Midlothian Liberal Association that the report that the right hon.gentle- man was about to retire from the House of Commons owing to ill health is "perfectly groundless." There was a serious fire on Wednesday, at Bryn Hall, near Ruabon, the residence of Mr. W. C. Roscoe. The out- buildings and their contents were consumed, and five valuable hunters and a heifer perished in the flames. - - - - -

The Natal Mereury of December 11 reports a serious loss of life among the crew of the Ruby whilst that vessel was cruising off the coast of Madagascar. Two officers and twenty men were drowned b.y. the capsizing of their boats.

_ Mr. Gladstone has caused it to be made known that it is extremely doubtful, in consequence of the delay in the negotiations with foreign Governments, whether he will be Able to propose an alteration of the wine duties this year.

- At Stockport, on Wednesday, Mr. Moorhouse, e the Higher Brinksway Cotton Mill, was fined 1.3 for neglecting to properly fence a hoist in use at his mill. In December one of the mill hands who was looking down the shaft was struck on the bead by the descending cage and wao instantly killed, and this occurrence led to the prosecution being instituted by the Inspector of Factories. The annual meeting ef the National Federation of Liberal Associations was opened in Birmingham, on Wednesday. Mr. Jesse Collings, the President, attacked the Government on their Irish policy, and a resolution was proposed which seemed too strong for a large number of delegates, inasmuch as it implied a censure on the Government. Ultimately the , resolution was adopted in a modified form. At the Manchester Assizes, on Wednesday, Samuel Scott was indicted for baying on the 3rd instant, at Salford, at- tempted to murder his wife. The woman had previously suffered great abuse from her husband, and the attack which he made upon her on the day in question was of the mast ruffianly description. The jury found him guilty of wounding with. intent to do grievous bodily harm, and he was sentenced by Mr. Justice Field to fifteen years' penal servitude.

STAFFORDSHIRE IRON TRADE.— Wolverhampton, Jan. 26.—Business was seriously prejudiced on 'Change this afternoon by the frost. Numerous works are wholly stopped, wanting fuel, and the rest are on only half time, at an extra outlay of 2s. to 3s. per ton of coal. The pits having any accommodation are besieged with offers of new business at the advanced rates. Quotations of iron tended upwards all round, yet stocks of pigs are rapidly accumulating. Sheet firms who did not advance last week put up rates ss. per ton, but without booking sales. Hematite pigs remained at last prohibitory rates. THE "FENIAN SCARE" has travelled from Windsor Castle to the Tower of London. It does not yet appear to have reached the Mint and the Bank of England. A London contemporary announces that the armouries in the Tower are to be specially guarded. A report was printed in Lon- don on Wednesday to the effect that the Mayor of Liverpool, apprehending danger from the Fenians, had arranged with the captain of the guardship in the river to land men, if necessary, in aid of the local police force. The report isde- clared to be unfounded, but it is stated that the strength of the military force lying in Everton Barracks has been aug- mented.

THE HALF-YEARLY MEETING OF TH2 MANCHESTER, SHEFFIELD, AND LINCOLNSHIRE RAILWAY COMPANY was held on Wednesday. The Chairman, Sir Edward Watkin, M.P., in moving the adoption of the report referred to the Employers' Liability Act, and said that he felt bound to do all he could to prevent its passing, because be considered that a system of insurance against accidents of all kinds arising from industrial undertakings should be established. The Directors had not endeavoured to con- tract themselves out of the Act, believing that it would be better to wait and !tie what the larger companies intended doing, and to ascertain what were the wishes of a majority of their men. However unjust the law might be, there it was on the statute book, and they were bound to obey it. The balance available for dividend this half-year, the Chair- man said, was £111,605, against £98,296 in the correspond- ing period of 1879. The report was unanimously adopted, and a resolution authorising the payment of a dividend at the rate of 4 per cent. per annum upon the Company's or,' nary stock was passed.

div.head: SPIRITUAL PEERS.
div.p: THE SPIRITUAL PEERS.

The member for SOUTH DEVON, :in resuming the debate on the above question (the mover of the adjournment of the House being absent), said he unfortunately did not bear the arguments advanced by the Prime Minister, but from the perusal of the speech in the weekly papers he saw that the Prime Minister's arguments were unanswerable; but, in his opinion, he did not make out a case at all. ("Oh !") He did not propose to go into the question' of the disestablishment of the Church of England or of the House of Lords. (Hear, hear) He considered that one of the most striking and horrifying—(laughter)—signs of the times was the rapidity with which those extreme Radical doctrines seemed to be advancing. (Laughter.) At the time of the election nobody would have said anything about the House of Lords, but that ancient and illustrious assembly seemed all at onpe to have jumped into the arena of practical politics. He thought it required very strong proof to be brought to say that there was no necessity for the existence of the House of Lords, and the argument of the Prime Minister's that no clergymen were allowed to sit in the Lower House showed the more reason why they should have some representatives in the Upper House. The spiritual peers sat in the House of Lords as representatives of the Church of England, which was more influential than any church in the world. (Cries of " No, no.") It had interests at stake in the country as great, or perhaps greater than any other combined interests, and it was only right they should be represented in the British Parliament. One of the arguments of the Prime Minister was that the peers had voted spiritual against three great measures, but time had shown that the Irish Land Act of 1870, and the dis- establishment of the Irish Church, had not the effect it was proposed they would have when introduced, that was, to give peace to Ireland. That argument was perhaps the weakest and most disreputable advanced; it went to. show the absolute despotism which was at the bottom of all Radicalism. ("Oh.") The bishops had opposed the Radi- cals, who said," We are Sir Oracles, and when we speak let no dog bark." To show that the bishops had not been back- ward in promoting good reforms, he said that the Archbishop of Canterbury had initiated the commission on :intemper- ance. He did not know that there was any practical result from the commission, but a lot of valuable information had been obtained. In the ministerial statement they had a forecast of this resolution, and the carrying it into effect was alluded to as a reform in the constitution. He thought the British constitution was perhaps as perfect as ;human beings could make it—(" No no ") ; it was copied all over the world; it had stood the test Of ages and had made the country glorious and free, and it would be a long thins be- fore the nation would submit to its being tampered with, especially by those who had such a conscientious regard for B. adlaugh scrupks, and who spoke of religion as a bogie. (Applause). The second member for_CANTERBURY, in rising to support

the resolution which had .been so ably and eloquently moved by the Premier, said he was conscious to some ex- tent that he was performing an unnecessary task, for until they bad some arguments advanced by hon. gentlemen op- posite in refutation of the arguments brought forward by the Premier, those arguments must be treated as unanswer- able. When that question which was referred to in the ministerial statement was brought forward, they on the Government side imagined that the Opposition would pre- sent and answer the list in favour of the beloved bishops. An bon. gentleman opposite even broke into a prayer on the subject, and asked a blessing on his soul and body—(laugh- ter)—which he sincerely hoped he had received ; but it appeared that last week they left the bishops to the tender mercy of the Radicals. Although there were many good and valid objections to the bishops having votes in the House of Lords, the greatest of all which presented itself to the minds of all lovers of justice was the inequality that existed, and always would exist so long as the religious opinions of one part of the community Were represented to the total exclusion of all others • and he quoted from the remarks of the Bishop of Manchester, who said "it would cost him no great sacrifice if a certain newly formed society succeeded in relieving him of duties to which he could not find time to attend." .He thought it was only a sort of left- handed way of admitting that it was an injustice to others who happened to have different opinions to his lordship. The bishop appeared anxious to be relieved of his legisla- tive duties, as his diocesan duties left him no time to attend

..„ to affairs occupying the attention of the House of Lords. It would therefore be a kindness to prevent the admission of bishops to parliament; and they,' the Radicals, wished to save them from the wear and tear of political strife. (Hear, hear.) It appeared to him astonishing that a man who taught others the way to the other world should re- luire £15,000 a year to keep him going in this—(laughter) —and it was equally astonishing that a man, who above all others was considered to have a prepared mansion in Heaven, should'require a preliminary training here below by having a princely palace here. (Laughter.) It would be very much more in, conformity with the spirit of Christianity if the £338.000 per annum were shared amongst , those miserably poor curates and clergymen of the Church 1 of England who had to make such an awful struggle for an existence. _ . .

The member for LIVERPOOL : I rise to a point of order, as there is not the slightest connection between the resolu- tion and the pay of bishops. The SPEAKER : I don't see that there is anything out of order, as I think the hon. member, the second member for Canterbury, may refer in passing to the bishops quite easy. (Liberal cheers.) Second member for CANTERBURY : The hon. gentleman opposite who has just made an interruption has but a vague idea of the question itself. Bishop Ryle in acknowledging the receipt— Member for LIVERPOOL (sharply) : Bishop Ryle was never in the House of Lords at all. (Laughter). Second member for CANTERBURY : I hope you will credit
Member for LIVERPOOL: This has nothing whatever to do with the abolition of the spiritual peers, and I insist upon the hon. member resuming the debate on the resolution before the House.

The SPEAKER : The hon. member for Canterbury is per- fectly right in saying what he did, as he is travelling fairly towards the subject. (Cheers.) Second member for CANTERBURY: Mr. Speaker, Bishop 'Lyle, in acknowledging the receipt of £1,200 subscribed to- wards the furnishing of his residence in Liverpool— Member for LIVBRPOOL : I rise to a point of order—

_ Member for GREENWICH: Mr. SpQier, I rise to object to these frivolous objections by the hon. member for Liver- pool. The SPEAKER: Will the hon. member for Liverpool state his point of order? Member for LIVERPOOL: My point of order is that the furnishing of Bishop Ryle's house has nothing to do with the resolution before the House. _

The SPEAKER: I rule that the bon. member for Canter- bury is perfectly right, and I don't think the bon. member for Liverpool is justified in rising and interrupting the House in this manner..(Liberal cheers.) . . . . .

Second member for dANTERBIIRY : think if the hon. gentleman had listened to the preceding sentences of my speech he would haye seen clearly enough that the question to which I referred had some reference to the subject before the House. I was speaking of the enormous wealth, and the influence it had upon the spiritual peers. Bishop Ryle, in acknowledging the receipt of £1,200 subscribed tows.* the furnishing of his residence. makes use of the following sentences—.
Member for LIVERPOOL :I rise to order. It does not make the slightest difference what he said with respect to the furnishing of his house. .

The SPEAIIR : I shall have to appeal to the House to support me in this rnatter. It is really most refreshing, after the continual absence of the hon. member for Liver- pool, after the many exciting scenes we have had—l say it is really most refreshing to find that he is doing his best to keep up his ancient reputation. (Laughter.) It recalls to my mind the case of an old farmer who had habits similar to those of the hon. member for Livei pool—(laughter)—and who, in an agricultural meeting respecting a point of order— ,

The member for LIVERPOOL, who had been stamping the floor with his feet, again rose, and said, "Mr. Speaker," but was met with loud cries of" Chair," during which both the Speaker and the hon. member for Liverpool stood upon their feet, the member for Liverpool standing in a defiant atti- tude and attempting to address the House. Ultimately he was compelled to sit down, as the shouts of "Chair", did not seem to abate.
The SPEAKER then proceeded with the story about the farmer, who, he went on to say, so interrupted the business of the agrieultnral meeting, that

He was put into the ante-room, amidst a roar, And of the subsequent proceedings he heard no more. (Laughter.) Perhaps they would be compelled to deal with the hon. member for Liverpool in the same manner. (Loud laughter.) The member for LIVERPOOL rose and moved the adjourn- ment of the debate. • The member for SOUTH DEVON (Conservative) seconded the motion.

The member for CAMBRIDGE UNIVERSITY, from the Oppo- sition side of the House, said it would be consulting the dignity of the House to let the matter go on. (Hear, hear.) The second member for CA.NTERBIIRY said that he had stated almost everything he wished to say, and he would leave the question to the consideration of the House. The SPEAKER intimated that the debate on the resolution might proceed. The member for LIVERPOOL: I object to this House being treated with contempt. The SECRETARY for the COLONIES: Mr. Speaker-- The member for LIVERPOOL: I call attention to the motion before the House. The member for GREENWICH: I beg to call your attention to Rule 9—" The ruling of the Speaker shall be absolute and unquestioned for the time being.' (Cheers.) The member for LIVERPOOL then moved that the standing orders be suspended. The member for Sount DEVON seconded. The member for CAMBRIDGE UNIVERSITY moved that the debate be proceeded with. The member for MANCHESTER seconded the motion, whico was carried. The SEcErrasir for the COLONIES (Liberal) then ad- dressed the House in su Tort of the resolution that the [ritual peers be abolished from the House of Lords; and he
•rdi-

endeavoured to show from history that the spiritual peers had no right to sit in the House of Lords, as the bishops in the time of Henry HE. sat not as bishops but as barons, and were not spiritual but were territorial Lords. He addressed the House at some leneth. He said that the continual in- terruptions and objections of the member for Liverpool seemed to him to call upon the House to deal with them in a more effective manner. Ile had been connected ivith several debating societies, but he bad never experienced such conduct as sharacterised the hon. member* for Liver- pool.. . . - .

The msmber for Liverpool then rose, and said that had nothing to do with the spiritual peers. The SECRETARY for the COLONIES: I beg to assure him it is very bad form to get up and interrupt nervous speakers in the, way lie has done.

The member for LIVERPOOL: The observation of the hon. member opposite has nothing to do with the resolution, and whatever his opinion be I don't care. (Loud Liberal laug.h- ter and Conservative smiles.) The member for CARIIRIDGE UNIVERSITY continued the debate.
Ulthnately the debate amd the House was adjourned.
ACTION AGAINST A ST. HELENS SOLICITOR.

An action against a St. Helens solicitor, Mr. H. L. Riley, by a Mr. Proffitt, builder, of Widnes, has just been heard in London, when the plaintiff applied to continue the ex parte injunction issued against defendant on the sth inst. —Mr. Clare (instructed by Mr. Tomkies) appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendant appeared in person.—The plain- tiff had filed no further evidence, while the defendant sub- mitted affidavits of himself and his cashier, Mr. John G. Parker, auctioneer, Liverpool, and an assistant of his (George Sloan), Mr. Alleyne Browne, and Mr. Robt. Antwis and another. The hearing of the motion lasted upwards of three hours, and the defendant's case, shortly stated, was a denial of all the grounds on which the ex parte order had been obtained against him. Instead of owing the plaintiff money, the defendant and his cashier swore that upwards of £l,lOO was still owing from the plaintiff. Instead of the portable engine seized in December last having been on the plaintiff's premises, it had been disposal of to a third person in the manner referred to in the subjoined judg- ment of the Vice-Chancellor ; and, instead of the de- fendant's security having been for an estimated debt, the bill of sale was produced showing that both the debt and credit sides of the defendants- ledger had been concurrently signed by the plaintiff, and interest on both sides calculated up to that date. The defendant posi- tively deposed that he had never employed the accountant Ellis, or that he had threatened to seize the other effects comprised in the bill of sale. A question of adjournment was raised by the plaintiff's counsel ; but this also was dealt with by the Vice-Chancellor in his judgment. An affidavit of a clerk of the defendant's was put in on this point, showing that the plaintiff's notice of motion had been kept back seven days after the leave to serve it was obtained from the Court; and that the plaintiff's solicitor had wanted copies of the defendant's affidavits on an under- taking to pay for them instead of in exchange for cash, and had, therefore, been refused copies. The Vice-Chancellor delivered judgment as follows :—The position in which this case stands appears to me to be a very unfortunate one, especially as regards the condact of the plaintiff. The plaintiff obtained from me an ex parte injunction on the sth of January, aud the effect of the injunction was to re- strain the defendant from selling anything which was com- prised within the bill of sale which constitutes his security from the plaintiff. There was, contemporaneously, special leave given to the plaintiff to serve notice of motion for an injunction to be heard this day; the interim injunction which had been concurrently granted being to expire this day. I formerly used the word "unfortunate," but I think I ought to substitute a different term. Blatneably on the part of the plaintiff, the plaintiff permitted a very con- siderable time to elapse before the service of the experts in- junction and a considerable further time before the service of the notice of the motion for the injunction now applied for. Blameably, I say, and in my opinion this is a matter which ought to be seriously visited on the part of the court, for this reason: the court on these ex palt,opplications, is very much indeed at the mercy of those Wb make them. They come with an application for an order in the absence of the persons to be affected, very grievously abridging his rights if, in the result, it should turn out that the applica- tion cannot be sustained. That being done, it most fre- quently happens that the parties who are affected by such orders are most inconveniently pressed by the result of such applications; and I think good faith is not preserved with the court by plaintiffs who keep back the service of notices of motion of this description for such a period as that the motions cannot be effectively disposed of in the time which has been limited by the court for their being heard. The result of such conduct in this case has, however, been that the defendant with such time as has been allowed to him by the course pursued by the pl Aintiff, has fully answered the case which has been made by the plaintiff; and the defendant has done more than that. He offered to facilitate the preparations of the plaintiff for reply, but the plaintiff took no advantage of any such offers; and then the plaintiff's counsel comes into court to-day, when this motion ought to be opened, and says, "I have heard of a number of affidavits, which have been filed by the defendant too late to enable me to be instructed to answer them; let the motion stand ever." I declined to allow the motion to stand over, when I heard what had been going on in this matter since I was first applied to for the ex parte injunction ; and now it has been heard through. The case seems to me to be this: —The plaintiff is a person who borrowed money from the defendant, who is a solicitor, and for that he gave a bill of sale. The bill of sale is dated on the 19th July, 1879. It assigns various chattel properties, which are described in he deed, and creates powers over them to be exercised by the defendant for the purpose of securing that which is intended to be secured by the deed. The deed purports to secure an existing and ascertained balance of account of £2,079, to 'which was to be added a further sum of £3O immediately to be advanced, and then further sums which were afterwards to be advanced at the option of the defendant, when and as he choose, so as not to exceed in the whole the sum of .£3,500. That was the nature of the security, and the plaintiff's application in this action is in effect an application of this kind :—lt does not treat the bill of sale as having been ab initio invalid; it does not treat the bill of sale as being open to any flaw or any objection; It does not seem to treat the proceedings of the defendant, Which he was taking with a view to the realisation of his security, as open to any but one objection, but that was prima facie a fatal objection. If well founded, it was one which entitled the plaintiff to that relief which he was asking in this court. He said "the whole of the security has been paid off, and I am entitled to redeem, to take an account, and on its being found that defendant has been paid off, to have that reconveyance of my property to which I shall be so found entitled." That being the only matter which was challenged by the plaintiff in respect of the con- duct of the defendant of which he complained, this motion has been heard before me, and the bill of sale itself and a 'quantity of evidence which has been gone into have had to be considered. The effect of the bill of sale itself is some- what peculiar; and it is not framed so stringently as such securities are ordinarily framed now.. It commences with an absolute assignment of the subjects ,of security to the defendant, and that assignment is then -followed by various provisos regulating the mode in which the security is to be enforced. There is to be a demand made of payment. That demand may be oral, or it may be written. That demand, of caurse, is to proceed from the defendant to the plaintiff; and then, in another part of the deed, there is a provision for the defendaat proceeding to realise his security after such demand. "After such demand "means, of course, demand by the defendant for the payment by the plaintiff of the debt so demanded; and it appears to me on the frame of the deed that it is so conceived that the right to enforce the security by sale is one which does not arise till demand has been made. Now, en that part of the case these ques- tions and circumstances arise :—The plaintiff's application has been to restrain any sale by the defendant of any of the subjects of security. There are many subjects of security; but there was one particular article in the security the seizure of which by the defendant immediately led to the institution ef this action. On the 9th of November things had taken place with regard to that particular article' (I think it was a steam engine) which had removed it out of the custody of the plaintiff • and I think for the purpose of this motion I mast consider that it is proved before lone that he had been a party to a transaction by which he bad- set aside, or attempted to set aside, the title of the defen- dant, and had improperly dealt with that property, which belonged to the defendant, for the purpose of his security. Now, with regard to the rest of the subject matters of the security, nothing had been done by the defendant, nor had anything been threatened to be done; and it does appear to me that at that time there was no ground whatever on which the plaintiff could have come into this court, founded on the notion, which he set up, that as re- gards any of the other matters than the particular article seized without notice he was entitled in any way to put the defendant under an injunction, or anything which was equivalent to an injunction, founded on any impropriety of dealing on the part of the defendant. Of course, ha was entitled to commence an action on the ground which he had alleged in his writ that the defendant's security was paid off - but, as far as regards any complaint founded on what the'defendant had done, or threatened to do, with reference to the enforcement of his security, it appears to me that there was no ground whatever to fouad an action. Now, in that state of things I find myself compelled, as I think, by what's due to the administration ot justice in this case, bear- ing in mind bow largely contributory to the present condi- tion of things the plaintiff himself has been by the adoption of that course which I have indicated, to proceed to the im- mediate determination of this motion, what I have to ob- serve with regard to the particular article which was seized by the defendant is that I take judicial cognisarce of the undertaking which he has given not 'to proceed to an abso- lute sale of that article without the leave of the conrt ; but with regard to the rest of the security, I think I ought to make no order, except that in the event of this action not being prosecuted by the plaintiff, all the defendant's costs of this application must be !paid to him as costs in the cause.
Mr. Care. Will not your honour make all the coets'costs in the cause?

The Vice-Chancellor: No. Mr. Clare: There is one application I did not make, but you have so decided before—that was to save the motion. The Vice-Chancellor: You are always at liberty to re- new an interlocutory motion; but in this case, under the circumstances in which at has been brought before me, I think an immediate decision is due. It is, of course/ only a decision of the motion, and it is open to the plaintiff tog) on with his action if he chooses.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND,
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND,

On Monday night, a number of bands, playing Nationalist tunes, paraded the streets of Dublin. American flags were carried, together with a banner with the words, "Parnell and Victory. God save Ireland J" The second batch of men arrested in connection with the murder of Lord Mountmorres have, lite those seised imme- diately after the commission of the crime, been discharged from custody, the evidence not warranting their further de- tention. It is stated that the witnesses called showed great reluctance to give information. Miss Gardiner, a Mayo landlady of wide fame fer het determined attitude towards her tenantry, has been "Boy- cotted" for some weeks, and, has only been able to obtain food by the help of the police. On Monday morning a party of Orangemen from the North of Inelptd, said, to have been "fully equipped and armed with modern weapons," arrived at Ballina, and proceeding on cars to Miss Gardiner's estate, ten miles away, "effected her relief." 3

STATE TRIALS IN IRELAND: - Mr. Justice Fitzgerald on Monday delivered his charge to the jury in the State prosecutions. Mr. Parnell and others bf the traversers wee in court. The -.fridge declared that the law of conspiracy was clear, and not, as it bad been called, the invention et modern times. It was equally untrue that It was obsolete and set aside. There was no analogy what- ever between Trades Unionism and the Land League's system of agitation. He commented on the rules of the Land League furnished for the organisation and manage- ment of the local branches, and said he had no hesitation in stating that the organisation from which these proceeded was an illegal one. Mr. Biggar had stated in one of his speeches that the magistrates and judges is that country were partizan, and that the tenant who,sought for a remedy from these sources had no chance. It was also said to be useless for a tenant to expect redress from his landlord, for the Crown Council yulsapplied the truth and the juries were packed. Judge Fitzgerald stated that this was untrue and that the person who uttered it knew it to be so. His Lord- ship had not concluded when tke court rose. The Irish state trials were brought to a close on Tuesday evening shortly before eight o'clock. When the judges sat on Tuesday morning, the court was crowded in every part. Mr. Justice Fitzgerald continued his charge, pointing, out that the speeches of Messrs. Dillon, l3oyton. O'Sullivan, Sheridan Walsh, and Gordon clearly showed that the ob- ject of the conspiracy was to crush and starve out landlords, while some of the traversers expressed their intention to do away with British rule. He told the jury to discharge their duty without fear or favour, and to have respect for the suictity of the oaths they had taken to return a verdict according to the evidence. The jury retired at 12.30, and Mr. Parnell entering at the moment was loudly cheered. Mr. Macdonogh. Q C., took objection to the direction given to the jury as to the law of conspiracy, and the court ruled that if he applied for a new trial and the rule was refused, be could proceed by writ of error. At five o'clock the jury were sent for, and in reply to Judge Fitzgerald the foreman said that they were unanimously of opinion that they could not agree, a statement which caused laughter, Two jurors asked for further time to consider, and a third said they were ttn to two. This was received with cheers, which caused Judge Fitzgerald to toll the jury with warmth he could only receive a unanimous verdict. The jury again retired. The jury having returned into court twice and ,stated that they could not agree, Mr.' Macdonogh applied that they should not be discharged until they had had time to fully consider all the evidence. Judge Fitzgerald told the jury thill he should lock them up all Right, but ulti- mately consented to see them again at nine o clock. He said, when the jury had retired, he was afraid, after the scenes in court that day, they, were not likely to have a free and unanimous verdict. He directed the Sheriff to in- crease the force round the court, so as to prevent disorder or riot, and to see that no one was allowed to communicate with the jury. Great excitement prevailed in and near the Court. The foreman again entered the court shortly before eight, and said it was utterly impossible for the jury to agree, and they were discharged.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

CLYDE SUIPWRIGHTS.-The Clyde shipwrights in two yards have struck for an advance of 7e per ccnt. At a meeting held on Tuesday evening, it was resolved that the notices of the Bolton spinners for an advance of wages should be postponed to the end of March, at which time, it is stated, many of the employers are willing to con- cede the operatives' demand. RESTRAINT OF TRADE.-A meeting of the patent wrought nail trade has been held in Birmingham to consider the con- duct of a firm belonging to the Association which had broken the Association rules by underselling. Four distinct cases of underselling to the extent of about 10 per cent, having been established to the satisfaction of the meeting, it was resolved that legal proceedings should be taken to recover from the delinquent firm the stipulated penalty of £5OO in each case, or £2,000 in all. STAFFORDSHIRE IRONWORKERS AND THE WAGES QUES- TioN.-A largely-attended meeting of ironworkers in the Brierley-hill district was held on Monday. Mr. J. Capper attended, and pointed out how disastrously a strike would have resulted if entered upon three weeks ago. After dis- cussion, it was resolved that the operative members of the wages board should have instructions to give notice for an improvement of the sliding scale, and the district should be represented when the ironworkers' insurance scheme was considered. In the Ashton-under-Lyne district the representatives of the self-actor mule spineers had an interview on Wednesday with the President of the Master Cotton Spinners' Associa- tion, and they were,informed that an advance of wages to the amount of per cent. will be paid upon the work done after the making-up day next week. This determination is, it is said, the result of a previous direct understanding be- tween the committees of the employers and the operatives. On Wednesday, the operatives at Oldham decided to strike for a 5 per cent. advance, which the employers declined to give on Friday. THE LANCASHIRE fame TRADE.-There has' been only a very dull tone in the iron trade of this district during the past week. To a considerable extent business has no doubt been interfered with by the weather, which has put a stop to a good deal of work in which iron is largely used. Prices, if anything, have shown rather less firmess, but there is no actsal giving way on the part of makers, who still entertain a strong feeling of confidence with regard to the future, and are not at all anxious to commit themselves to long forward deliveries. Local makers of pig iron are kept going on old orders, but not many new sales are being made. Where business, however, is done it is at late prices, which remain firm at 47s 6d for No. 3 foundry and 413 s 6d for No. 4 forge, less 2-1- per cent, delivered into the Manchester district. For finished iron rather more enquiries are reported in some quarters, but prices are without material change, £6 per ton being about the average quotation for bars delivered into the Manchester district.
