DISTRICT NEWS.
[BIRD'S CUSTARD POWDER

(RArze ros Sr. HELENS.—On Monday at the Police Court, Mr. J. Kitchen, assistant overseer for Sutton, applied for and obtained the sanction of t'ne Bench to a poor rate to realise £7,379 at Is. 83. in the £, and a burial rate at Id. in, the £to realise £lBO. lie also received the sanction to the levying of a poor rate for Parr to realise £2,219 at Is. 93. in the £ and a burial rate for the same township at 2d. in the A to make £7B. There were £7 in arrears in the Sutton Rate, but none to carry forward to the New Parr poor rate. RAILWAY SESVANTS' ANNUAL DINNER AT Sr. HELENS. —On Thursday week, the employe' in the passengerdepart- mutat the railway station, held their annual dinner, towards which the principal tradesmen of the town subscribe, and, about 60 sat down to an excellent spread. Mr. Moss (station- master) occupied the chair. Amongst those present were Mr. Moss, Mr. Banks (mineral department), Mr. Newton (locomotive department), Mr. Dryburgh (chief clerk). Toasts were given from the chair and the proceedings were enlivened by several songs. A pleasanrevening was spent. AWFULLY SUDDEN DEATH Or A YOUNG MAN AT Sr. HELENS.—A very sadden death occurred in the street on Wednesday. James McMakin, Mosshouse Farm, Parr Flatt, a labourer, 17 years of age, the son of Alexander McMakin, farmer, left home at eight o'clock in the morning in his usual good health to attend a cattle sale at Haydock. He left Haydock about four o'clock in the afternoon with seine cattle for Liverpool, and got as far ,as Croppers-hill, Eccleston, when he fell with his face upon the ground in a St. Brandy was administered, but without effect, and he was takeq in a cart to Dr. Jameson, who pronounced life to be extinct.
FOR RICHEST CUSTARD. WITHOUT EGGS.

FIRE AT S. HELENS RAILWAY STATION.—OR Tues- day a--fire occurred at the London and- North-Western Rail- way Station, St. Helens. Some passengers in the waiting room noticing smoke issuing from the traffic inspector's room gave an alarm, and on opening the door the room was found to be in flames, and it was with considerable difficulty that an entrance was effected, but a plentiful supply of water being at hand the fire was extingufished before very great damage had been done. It appears that from some unexplained cause a quantity of fire had fallen from the grate on to the floor, which ignited, as the wooden flooring was found to have been• burnt to the depth of about a foot.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OP HOPE, KIRELAND- sravar, ST. HELENS.—The annual business meeting in connection with the above, was held in the school room on Friday last at 8 o'clock. The Rev. T. Wilshaw, presided. After some preliminary bumness had been disposed of, the election of officers for the chrrent year took place with the following result. President, Rev. T. Wilskaw ; vice-presi- dents, Mr. J. Lawless, Mr. J. Wilcock; Hon. Secretary, Mr. R. Melling Prescott; Hon. Treasurer, Mr: J. Wilcock; Reciting Masters, Mr. J. Brockbank, and Mr. R. M. Prescott; Singing Conductor. Mr. Petet Wright; Auditors, Mr. R. M. Prescott, and Mr. J. Brockbank. It was resolved that the celebrated Temperance dialogue, the trial of John Barleycorn, be rendered in the school on Monday the 6th of March next. Tan FROST AT PnEsoar.--Gtesat privation is being experienced by many families during the present severe season in Prescot. To add to the trouble, whole rows of houses in Derby-square and Warrington-road have been deprived of water, and the inhabitants have been forced to walk long distances for it. This week workmen from the water- works have daily opened the mains and afforded relief. A meeting was held in the Town Hall on Wednesday evening to take steps to relieve, as far as possible, thb existing dis- tress. Two years sgo subscriptions were collected and a soup kitchen opened, by which a great many poor people were assisted. From the fund then subscribed upwards of al still remain in the bank; and it was decided to obtain further subscriptions and aid the poor people in their present distress.

A GIRL BIJIINT TO DEATH AT ST. sad case of burning occurred at St. Helens the other day by which a little girl nearly four Years of age met with her death. Deceased was the daughter of a brickmaker named Wm. Pilkington, residing at 24, Park-road, and on the 18th- inst., was left in the house with her brother Thomas, 11 years of age, and two younger children. One of the children made a fire in the bedroom, and deceased's clothes caught fire, burning her terribly. Her cries attracting the attention of a neighbour named Ann Buttersbank, this woman ran into the house, and did what she could by throwing water upon the child, who, however, succumbed to the injuries in a few days after. An inquest was held at the Finger Post, Parr, and a verdict of "Accidental de...th "was re- turned.

INDECENT Asset:rig AT RAINFOED.—Mattbew Rogers, apparently abott 30 years of age, was charged with commit- ting an indecent assault upon Jane Farryman, a single womam, over 30 years of age, residing with her mother 4 Rainford, on Friday the 21st inst. It appeared that the prisoner overtook the complainant on Ormskirk-road, and after speaking to her, threw her down on the snow, and behaved indecently towards her, also threatening to kill her. Some men came up and remonstrated with him, and watched him for some distance on the road to see how he behaved himself. He again threw the woman down, and then they went to him and took the prisoner into a public house until a policemarb.P.C. Dutton, arrived.—He was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour.

DEATH ET EXPOSURE OF A WOMAN AT ST. HELENS. —On Wednesday morning, an inquest was held at the Finger Post Inn, Parr, before Mr. Barker, on the body of Mary Cox, 5, Baxter-street, Parr, who died under the follow- ing circumstances :—On Saturday night, a little after four o'clock, she went to Widnes with her son to see one of her children at Widnes. Having missed the last train from Widnes she determined to go home to her hus- band and children by some means, and she started with her son to walk the distance from Widnes to St. Helens. Before she arrived at Appleton she fell, and the son finding her unable to walk, carried her as best he could to Peasley Cross, where he arrived at half-past five in the morning, and then laid her down by the side of the street whilst he went as fast as he could to inform his father. On returning they found deceased apparently sleeping, and they carried her home, where she died soon after their arrival. Deceased has suf- fered from heart disease, and the jury returned a verdict of died from "Natural causes" (heart disease), her death being accelerated by exposure to the cold. GREAT SEATING MATCH, NEAR ST. HELENS.—On Tuesday, a skating match which caused a great deal of ex- citement, took place at Carr Mill dam, and was witnessed by about 12,000 persons. The match was between John Hill, of Billinge, collier, who is supposed to be the "crack " in the district, and Thomas Gee, a wheelwright, residing in Park-road, Parr. The distance was 300 yards, and the match was for £l5 a side. Before the race a number of Gee's friends possessed of a triangle, a kettledrum, a flute, a tin whistle and a tambourine, paraded their man about the ice, and at intervals shouted Success to Gee." The friends of Hill were armed with brushes and sticks' and they paraded their man singing "See the conquering hero comes." At half-past three a start was made, Gee keeping the lead for the first 100 yards, when Hill passed his opponent, and gradually increasing in speed reached the goal about six yards in advance of Gee. Hill is a big, sturdy fellow, and not an over graceful skater, whilst Gee, who is Small of build but well set, is a beautiful easy skater. Betting was carried on pretty freely, and one or two fights were engaged in. Several pigeons were sent in the air with white tape attached, to Billinge, announcing the victory, the Billinge men having previously arranged to "send word whoam." LOCAL GOVERNNENI BOARD INQUIET AT ST. HELENS. —The Town Council of the borough of St. Helens having applied to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow £5,000 for works of water supply, £2,511 for works of street improvement, £2,750 for a survey of the borough, and £2,450 for an infectious diseases hospital, an enquiry was held yesterday, at the Town Hall, by Captain Robert C. T. Hildyard, late Royal Engineers, who had with him Dr. Parsons, medical officer to the Local Government Board. There were also present the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Harrison), Mr. Alderman Gamble, J.P., Councillors Twyford, J.P. (chairman of the Health Committee), Belabor, Allen, and Hanson ; Mr. J. P. 51•Kinlev, Mr. Brewis (town-clerk), Mr. Craik (deputy town-clerk, Mr. Johnson (borough treasurer), Mr. Hart (borough engineer), and Mr. Gaskin (water en- gineer). The Commissioner, having made some formal in- quiries, remarked that it was obligatory that money borrowed under the Public Health Act must be invested in Exchequer bills or other Government securities. He then proceeded to make enquiries regarding the proposed Infectious Diseases Hospital, and was informed by Mr. Brewis that the Cor- poration had entered into a provisional contract with the owners of the house called Peasley Vale, Sutton. The pur- chase money was £2,300, and the cost of furnishing would be £l5O. There were also two cottages, and the total area was 3 acres 3 roods 35 poles. It was further stated by the surveyor that the house was twenty-five yards fiom the turnpike road, and the:.e was a small natural stream twenty-two yards from the house, which lay six or eight feet from the nearest level to the sewer. The sewage from the house, therefore, could not run into it. He (the surveyor) had not formed any plan or estimate as to what to do with the sewage —The Inspector took that as a serious question.—The Surveyor said he did not think the nature of the soil was suitable to treat sewage on, it was a loamy top soil of fifty or sixty inches over tolerably stiff clay. The geological formation was coal, and the clay was a surface deposit two feet six inches or three feet thick.—Mr. Councillor Allen, who has lived in the house for ten years, said the cellars were sometimes flooded, and the drains found their way into the brook.—Mr. P. M.Kinley asked if the level of the cellar was not under the level of the present brook, and was answered by the inspector that the evidence showed the cellars were generally dry,— The Inspector and most gentlemen present then proceeded to view the premises. On their return at two o'clock, the application of £2,511 for the purchase of property and im- provement of Arthur-street, was inquired into. Property amounting to £1,160 had been purchased at a sale by auc- tion, but LOGO was expected to ba realised by sale of laid, &c,, whilevthe remainder of the money was for making the toad. After hearing Mr. Gaskin's statement that his esti- mate of £5,000 for works of water supply was up to Feb- ruary, 1883, and that the price of water was cheaper in St. Helens than in any other town in the kingdom, the Inspector said he should be able to report favourably on all the appli- cations, and the inquiry then terminated.

He charged two- man: The case is adjourned until next Monday, when the pence per hour for the use of the dominoes, and if, on their question of costs will no considered. being brought back he found the numbers complete and all [Mr. Henry Reynolds here left the Bench.] went on properly during the game, he returned the person THE MANAGER OF THE COCOA ROOMS IN or persons who took them, one penny. He never saw any ' COURT. money pass between people playing since he had charge of the place. If he had any suspicion that gambling was going on, he immediately called the dominoes in. Cross-examined by the Superintendent: He admitted having had to stop a person named Hayes, who used to fre- quent the place; and another named Marshall. He reckoned it his special duty to look after these games. Superintendent Williamson : I do not think if you had you would have been brought here. Witness (sarcastically) : I do not think it is my duty to go to the window and listen to what my customers are talk- ing about. In further cross-examination, witness said he had never had complaints from private individuals about gambling at the house. He had had them from mothers, who had requested him not to serve their children, but they were not young men, as those were who were in the room on the night referred to. Mr. Linaker then addressed the Bench at some length. He contended that the defendant was justified in keeping the house open to the time at which the excise officer en- tered. The refreshment license held by him justified him in keeping open when the licensed houses were closed. In support of this contention, he referred to a case which was decided on appeal, in January, 1876, after the Amendment Act of 1874 had been passed. He next quoted the judgment of Justice Field on the point. The Chairman : Then you contend that this license permits you to keep open till five o'clock in the morning? The Magistrates' Clerk ruled that Mr. Linaker's version of the Act was not a sound one. Mr. Linaker then expressed a wish to make some obser- vations upon a case that he alleged was somewhat similar, and which had been heard before the Recorder of Liverpool a few days ago. A search was made for a Liverpool paper containing the report, but it could not be found. The Magistrates Clerk said that even if the journal were r found, Mr. Linaker knew it could not be received as evidence I in a court of justice. Mr. Linaker considered that after the observations of Superintendent Williamson at the opening of the case, he was bound to address the Bench in answer to them. The Chairman : The Superintendent did not proceed with his remarks upon you objecting to ,them ; and do you think, under the circumstances, it is necessary for you to allude to them further ? Mr. Linaker felt called upon to do so, after the strong ob- servations of the Superintendent. In the first place, he said that the company in question was started by Canon Bar- clay, Mr. John Simpson, the late Mr. Charles Hazlehurst, and several other leading gentlemen in Runcorn. The names of the gentlemen upon the directorate must, he thought, be a sufficient guarantee that they would not for a moment tolerate any such proceedings as the Superintendent of the police had stated had come to his knowledge. He must say he considered it was the bounden duty of Super- intendent Williamson to have brought these matters under the notice of the directors, and not have come to that court and made such sweeping charges for the first time. There had been no communication with the directors at all. Superintendent Williamson protested against the remarks of Mr. Linaker, who, he considered, was rather going out of his way. He was not supposed to know who the directors were; they did not send him a prospectus of the company. He quite agreed with Mr. Linaker that the gentlemen con- nected with the directorate were of the highest respectability, and would not have tolerated such conduct had they been acquainted with it. If he had known the gentlemen upon the directorate, he should certainly have communicated with them. But there was one gentleman sitting next to Mr. Linaker (pointing to Mr. J. O. Jackson, who preserved an imperturbable coolness as the attention of all present WU fastened upon him) to whom he had complained; and Mr. Jackson was the only one he knew personally. Mr. Linaker submitted that in the second case there was not sufficient evidence to warrant the Bench in inflicting a fine. There had been no evidence brought forward to prove that the alleged offence had been committed with the know- ledge of Moore. The defendant had charge of two other rooms, and the police said that when they wen, into build- ing Moore was talking with certain people. The defendant wholly denied that he had seen any gambling going on. To warrant a conviction it must be proved that the offence had been committed "knowingly." The magistrates then retired to consider their verdict,and on their return into court, after some eight minutes' ab- sence, they said they had decided to convict in both cases. As to the first charge, they felt that it involved a question of law, and that it was just possible the defendant might have considered he was acting rightly in keeping the house open. They should, therefore, only inflict a nominal fine of Is., and costs 12s. 6d. In the second case defendant would have to pay a fine of 205., and costs 12s. 6d. Mr. Linaker gave notice of appeal in both cases.

CONVICTIONS FOR GAMBLING AND BEING OPEN AT IMPROPER HOURS. Mr. William Moore, who has been manager of the building belonging to the Runcorn Coffee and Cocoa House Co. since its commencement, was sum- moned for having, on the 17th instant, whilst licensed to keep a refreshment house, under the 23 Vic., c. 27, unlaw- fully kept it open during the time it ought to have been closed, viz., 11-20 p.m.; and also with having suffered gaming in the house, by certain persons whose names were unknown. Mr. W. H. Linaker' solicitor, and secretary to the company, represented the defendant, who pleaded not guilty to both summonses. Mr. John Simpson and Mr. J. 0. Jackson, directors of the company, occupied seats near Mr. Linaker. The court was crowded. Superintendent Williamson said he was sorry he had found it necessary to have had to summons the defendant there on the charges of keeping open at improper hours on the night in question. He did not know what Mr. Linaker would plead in answer to the summonses, but the defendant certainly could not plead ignorance on the matter, as he (Mr. Williamson) had told him on 'several occasions, that he was doing wrong in following such a course. It was in consequence of various and numerous complaints in reference to boys and young men going to the rooms, that he found it necessary that some steps should be taken to put a stop to the bad conduct all eged to be taking place. On the night of the 17th inst., he instructed two officers to visit the building, and they would tell the Bench what they saw. Now, as far as he was concerned, as the representative of the police force in the town, he had no wish whatever to press the case unduly against the defendant; but he wished to make it clear to him that he could not do these things with impunity. No doubt it was quite against the wish of the promoters of the rooms that this sort of conduct had been permitted. The defsndant had, however, now to answer for it, and, perhaps, he would be able to say something for himself. As to the gambling, he was informed that the charge he had to bring against the defendant, as to the matter, was very grave indeed. Moore might, possibly, try to escape the legal liability involved in the case, but never- theless, there was a certain moral liability attaching to him on the ground of having permitted what it was his duty to have prevented. Young men, he was told, had gone there, and at first commenced gambling for small sums— Mr. Linaker wished to know if the Superintendent in- tended to prove what he had been saying by witnesses to be called that day, but he had no right to state what he had been told unless he was going to substantiate it by calling witnesses? The Superintendent said he should not call witnesses as to everything he had stated. The Chairman advised Mr. Williamson not to go into anything in relation to which he was not going to call wit- .. , news. The Superintendent said the police would prove to the Bench that they were at a window at the back of the premises of which the defendant was manager, that they could see into a certain room; that they saw money pass from one player to another, and could hear through the window very gross conversation indeed. This went on for a long time, and then the Inspector called the attention of the manager to the affair, and he said, "Well, I have no knowledge of it; I do not allow gaming." Ile could, how- ever, tell their worships that the defendant, along with other gentlemen' came to see him, and told him that on various occasions he had caught some of the visitors playing for money, and had endeavoured to prevent it. As to the swearing and bad conduct in the house, Mr. Moore added that he had cautioned some of the visitors about it, and they had replied that "if he did not let them be," they would leave the place and go there no more; and he was afraid of injuring the custom. Now, he thought the Bench would consider that a very idle excuse to be made by the manager of an establishment which they must all admit was insti- tuted for the welfare of the public at large. When, how- ever, the privileges granted to such a place were abused, it became one of the greatest evils they had in the town. This was owing to the fact that, when the public-houses were Closed at eleven o'clock at night, all the roughs in the town made a practice of going to these rooms, and thus kept the town in a state of commotion long after it ought to be quiet. The result of these gatherings had been that the police had often found the greatest difficulty in preventing breaches of the peace amongst the visitors on leaving the building. Inspector Hollingsworth said that on the night of the 17th inst. he visited the cocoa rooms at ten minutes to twelve. and found three men in one "bar," two in another, mid the house open. He observed two men enter by the front door, and they were supplied with a cup of cocoa and some pies. He spoke to the defendant (who was in the bar where the three men were, which was on the left hand on entering), and asked him if he had an excise license, and he replied that he had. He asked him if he would let him see it, and he showed it to him, on which he saw that it was a refresh- ment house license, granted to Mr. Moere He told defen- dant he should be obliged to report . him for keeping the house open after eleven o'clock, on which he said, "Why don't you go and look after other houses." (witness) He said, di That is a question for us, andnotfor you." Defen- dant was rather indignant, apparently thinking the police were exceeding their duty, and he (witness) told him that it was a question between him (defendant) and the magis- trates as to whether he ' was allowed to keep open or not. That completed his own evidence as to the first case. As to the second case, witness proceeded to state that he was directed by the Superintendent to go to the cocoa- rooms on the night mentioned; and he left the office, at about half-past seven, in company with Sergeant Walley. They went to a window at the rear of the house, and heard the company playing at dominoes. They listened for some time, and heard several games won and lost. At the end of each contest one would say to the other, "Give us that halfpenny," or "Give me that halfpenny that I have put down." He could not see into the room at his ' corner of the window, because of the blind. Sergeant Wal- ity.was at the other corner. After remaining at the window about twenty minutes, they went to the front of the build- ing, and entered. They walked into the room where the dominoes were being played, and found about five people engaged in the game. One of these was a boy from 14 to 15 years of age • another about 16, and the others were young men from 18' to 20. There was only one set of dominoes.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 29, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 29, 1881.
WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday afternoon. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis presided. and there were also present the Revs. George Holloway and Father Clarke, Messrs. J. Brock, R. Shaw, H. W. Deacon, Martin Taylor, Dr. O'Keeffe, and G. H. Danby (clerk). DISTRIC T EDUCATION COMMITTEE. _ _ _

The report of this committee was read by Mr. Deacon and passed. ft stated that during the month of December the number of cases summoned had been 176, of which 78 were applications for payment of fees, and 98 for contra- vention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 48 cases. There had been 13 prosecutions before the magistrates, and convictions had been obtained in each case.

;SAD CASE OF SUICIDE AT WIDNES. On Tuesday an inquest was held at the Main Top Hotel, Mersey-road, Widnes, by Mr. Barker, deputy county coroner, on the body of Henry Digby Mann, of 22, James- street, labourer, who was found hanging dead in his kitchen late on Saturday night. Mr. Davies acted as foreman of the jury, and considerable interest was taken in the case by the general public, owing to a rumour that deceased had committed suicide owing to a quarrel between him and his wife. In opening the proceedings, Mr. Barker said it appeared that deceased had had some words with his wife on the morning of the day when he was found dead, and a letter had been found near the body, written by the unfortunate man, which it would be his duty to read to them, as it might affect their verdict, or the decision at which they would arrive as to his state of mind. Elizabeth Mann, who is about 28 Years of age, said she was the wife of deceased, and. the last work at which he was employed was as a bricksetter at the Widnes Mete Works. She would have been married to him four years if he had lived until the 22nd February. She and her husband lived very comfortably together. Deceased was eat of work one week, owing to the frost. They had no means of living but those arising from her own work when he was not doing anything. A certain man told her, the day before her hus- band's death, that when he was engaged on a job he would not work. On the Saturday morning she told him what the man had said to her, and when be came down stairs he began cursing about it She replied that she be- lived the statement made by certain people that he would not work when he had the chance was correct. In reply to this, he asked her to look at his hands, as a proof that he was a worker. Something very strange then seemed to come over deceased, and he danced up and down the room, cursing swearing, and otherwise " carrying on." She had never seen him do so before; and she understood that at the works he was known as one whom no one (would vex. He had always behaved very kindly to her. It was twenty minutes past ten when they had the disturbance' and she left him by the fireside and went off to her work. When she left he did not speak to her and appeared very quiet. Before dinner she went into the house again, at about twelve o'clock, but she did not see hini at the time. Between one and two in the afternoon, she again entered the house, and he asked her if she was going to sweep up. She said "No " ; and that was all that passed. She then went to work and. left him reading the paper by the fireside. She did not co home till about eleven o'clock at night, and found her husband hanging against the wall—between the window and the scullery— behind the kitchen door. He was hanging by a piece of rope. She called out to him, but he did not answer. She turned his face to the wall, seeing that he was quite dead, and then ran into the street, screamed, and called the neighbours, who came in and cut him down. He had never threatened "to do for himself," and was a very steady man. She did not kbow that he was in any trouble. At this part of the enquiry, the Coroner showed the wit- ness the letter which had been found near her husband. She remarked that she could not identify it herself, but those who had seen it said it was like deceased's hand- ' writing. 1-re generally wrote a clear, bold hand; and she thought his hand must have trembled very much when he wrote the letter. By the Foreman: The child went to the door several times during the afternoon, and said his father woeld not open it. By the Inspector of Police: Was he a sober man? He never had dtink but twice since we were married, and that was given to him. By a Juryman : Durinethe morning she fancied she saw her husband hanging a clock against the wall, and a very queer feeling came over her.—When you went in at twelve o'clock, what gave you the shock? I don't know: a feeling came over me that I had better not go to the front door, "or my husband would stop me." She had a very great dread upon her. By the Inspector: Has he been short of work lately? He had been at work a short time; but I have had to keep him many times since our marriage, when he has been out of work.—Was he ever low spirited? Yes, he was low spirited throughout the week, and said he did not know how they were going to live. She replied that there were many other people in the same positson, and they must try to do as well as they could. Witness, continuing, said her husband had plenty to eat on the Friday night, when they had some milk for supper. By the Inspector: Had you sufficient that morning? Yes; there was bread and bacon lb the house, and tea and sugar. Of course the food had rather run down, owing to it being Saturday. He had frequently had his tea at her mother's during the week.—Did he ever threaten to commit suicide? Ii; never. By the Foreman: Did he ever try to prevent you going to your mother's? No; never.—Then, why did you feel frightened? Because this feeling came over me. Henry Smith deposed that he lived near to the deceased, and had known for three years. He was a steady man, and did not knew that anything had happened to put him out of the way. He last saw &ceased alive a fortnight be- fore, when he was in work and in his usual health and spirits. Between ten and eleven on Saturday night he was called into the house, and found him hanging by a rope which was attached to a nail in the wall. Thera was a chair beside him. Another man cut. the body down. He (wit- ness) felt at his hand, and, findimikthat it was quite cold, he said to the man who was witlFlFlra, "Cue him down." He believed deceased had been dead three or four hours. He had worked with Mann, but he had never complained to him. By the Foreman: Deceased was a very open-minded man, and always seemed to be in good spirits. By a Juryman: He had never known any unpleasantness between deceased and his wife, with the exception of a word now and then "the same as man and wife." He worked with him for a long time at Messrs. Hutchinson's. By the Inspector: Deceased always appeared to do his portion of the work. The Coroner said there could be no doubt in the case that the unfortunate man committed suicide by hanging himself; his to aba t any yv e the evidence time. vd comfortably and the only matter for the jury to consider was the state of ePf insanity.ersonal lyto, tith he could not see that geeera,nwdithhiLweiefxe Caer- p hiesearr mindee d w o s Lon of a little quarrel on the day of his death. The letter which deceased wrote was as follows : My Dear Wife,—! hope God will Forgive me, for the act I am about to do I hope those that told you about me will look after you when jam gone. lam almost broken-hearted. May God bless you and my Little son.' Kiss him for me. Good by for ever.—Your unhappy husband, H. D. MANN. This letter seemed to have been written whilst deceased was thinking. of committing this act. Perhaps the better course for the Jury would be to return a verdict of "Committed suicide; ' they might even return one of fele de se. It was, however, the custom to avoid doing so, and to obviate that unhappy necessity, it would be well if tbey could return one to the effect that deceased committed suicide, but there was not sufficient evidence to show his state of mind at the time. If deceased had not written the letter, he (the speaker) could not have seen that there was anything to trouble him. The jury adopted the -recommendation of Mr. Barker, and returned a verdict as suggested.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Fletcher (chairman) hod Mr. George Pilkington. Twit TOPERS' LlST.—Thomas Doyle and William Reid, labourers, were each fined ss. and ss. 6d. costs, for having been drunk and disorderly in Widnes-road, on the 22nd inst. The cases were proved by Sergeant Eastham.—John 'nosey was convicted of drunkenness and causing a distur- bance in Catherine-street, on the 10th inst. Evidence was given in the case by P.C. Palmer. This was the ninth ap- pearance of the prisoner at court, and he Was fined 10s. and costs.—Thomas Burns and William Berns were charged with having been found drunk in the Star Inn, Elizabeth-street. P.C. Pitt stated that on the Bth inst, he was called to the inn, and found the two defendants there drunk, and they declined to leave. He had seen them in the street previously to find- ing them in the public-house, where they had not been ' supplied with any drunk. Each defendant was fined ss. and Mts. CHARGE AGAINST A PIIBLICAN.—Harrison Turton, pub- lican, who did not put in an appearance, was summoned for assaulting his wife.—Mr. Moore, of Warrington, appeared for the wife, and asked the Bench to adjourn the case for three months, as his client wished to give him another chance. —The magistrates consented to do so. A CARELESS CARTER.—Wm. Gandy, a carter, of 50, Crom- well-street, was charged with having been at too great a dis- tance from his cart, on the 14th inst.—P.C. Laing stated that at ten o'clock at night he saw the horse and cart coming down Widnes-road, with no one in charge of them. In a few minutes the defendant, who had been in the Grapes Inn, followed them.—Gandy made a very neat apology to the Bench for his negligence, and he was let off on paying 4s. 6d. costs. MISCELLANEOTIS.—DanieI Brannon, a working man, was convicted o. using filthy language to Mrs. Ann Tobin, and was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace three months, himself in £lO and one surety in £5, or be imprisoned seven days. Defendant: Mrs. Tobin carries the key of Market- street, and will continue to do so as long as she has money, and Mr. Swift to back her. (Laughter.)—Mary Duffy was summoned for wing defamatory language to Annie Glancey, on Saturday night. Several witnesses were called in the case, on both sides, but of no public interest. The Bench thought there were six of one and half-a-dozen of the other, as far as complainant and defendant were concerned, and dismissed the snmmons.

MOVEMENT OF TnooPs.—On Wednesday morning a detachment of the 18th Hussars passed through Prescot on their way from Warrington to Liverpool. DEFRAUDING THE ALTILINCHAM RAILWAY COMPANY. —Elisha Lockett, formerly a sergeant in the Cheshire Con- stabulary, and now a bailiff of the Manchester County Court, was charged at the Sale Petty Sessions on Monday with defrauding the Manchester South Junction and Altrincham Railway Company on the 13th, 14th, and nth instant. The defendant lives at Altrincham. It was alleged that his practice was to take a return ticket, Manchester to Stretford, and to return to Manchester the next day with the return half of the ticket issued to Stietford. By this means the defendant saved 2s. 9d. a week. The Chairman of the Bench strongly commented on the case and the position of the defendant, which he said would cause him to be the last person to be suspected of sach a fraud. The defendant, who admitted the offence, was fined 40s. and costs in the first case, and Ls. and costs in the other two, in all £5 as.

div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE.

The recommendations of the Simm's Cross managers were :—That the salary of Miss Alice L. Hunter, assistant mistress in the junior girls' department, be increased from £4O to .£45 per annum ; that of Clara Pommy, assistant mistress in the junior boys' department, increased a similar amount; and that W. J. Handley, Sarah Stout, and Mary Smith be engaged as monitors. West Bank managers re- commended i hat the resignation of Miss A. A. Barnes, as- sistant mistress in the junior girls' department be accepted. The Management Committee reported that Mr. Thomas Balmer had been appointed chairman, and Mr. Wm. Crab- tree, correspondent of the West Bank managers, for the pre- sent year. They recommended that the resignation of Mr. A. McClellan, as the manager of the Warrington-road. school, be accepted, and a letter forwarded to him thank lug him for his services. The Committee's report and recommendations were passed, on the motion of Mi. MARTIN 'Axton, seconded by the CHAIRMAN.

div.head: VACANCY ON THE -BOARD
div.p: THE VACANCY ON THE -BOARD

On the motion of the 6tanntesr, seconded by Dr. O'KEEFE' the following resolution, which had been given notice of by Mr. Timmins, was passed :—" That the resigna- tion of Mr. W. H. Price, as a member of the Widnes School Board, be accepted from the 27th inst., in accordance with his wish, expressed by letter dated Nov. 27th, 1880." The CHAIRMAN remarked that Mr. Danby would notify the arrangement to the Department; and the next ordinary meeting might be called, as a special one, for filling up the vacancy, on quater of an hour earlier.

THE LOCAL BOARD DECLINING TO FULFIL A CONTRACT. Mr. MARTIN TAYLOR said a matter had come to his notice which he thought ought to be brought before that meeting and go to ale general public. It was in relation to a con- tract whin had been entered into with the Local Board to supply schools belonging to the School Board with coke for the current year. The Local Board had, he believed, declined to supply the coke in abcerdance with their con- tract. Owing to this decision, the School Board were pre- vented from using slack and coke mixed,as required by their stoves, the flues of which were very small, and easily be- came closed. It certainly appeared to him that the Local Board had been guilty of a breach of contract, and the de- livery of the coke could be claimed, as there was no strike at the works, or anything which would prove a valid excuse for not:supplying it. The Citatuntarr: I feel sure tkat they are bound to sup- ply it. Mr. TAYLOR: How many times has the cart been sent to the works hr coke? The CLERK: I think twice. Mr. TAYLOR: I think that a letter should be sent to them peremptorily demanding a supply in accordance with the contract. The Clerk ought to go to the office with the carters, and take nothing but a denial from an official in authority. If they then persist in not acceding to the re- quest, we ought to purchase coke at some other place, and charge them with the cost. The CHAIRMAN: As individual traders, we should cer- tainly claim delivery of the coke. It was then resolved, without any formal motion :—"That the Chairman of the School Management Committee, having reported that the Widnes Local' Board have declined to execute orders for coke, the Clerk be instructed to write to the Local Board, calling their attention to the -contract, and in- timating that the School Board held them liable for any loss sustained in consequence." The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: ST. HI.LENS POLICE INITELLIGENCE.
div.p: ST. HI.LENS POLICE INITELLIGENCE.
FRIDAY.

STEALING COAL.—Edmund Knowles, of Sutton, was charged with stealing coal of the value of 2d. from Thomas Samuels, and he was fined 10s. and cost. STEALING A GLASS LESTUE.—Henry Mullen, of Windle, was charged with stealing a glass lustre from the public- house of William Butler, St. Helens, on Wednesday. The prisoner went to the house and was served with some liquor, and some time after he left the house the lustre was missed. Information was given to the 'police, and the prisoner was apprehended, and the lustre found,in his pessession.—He was fined £2 and costs.

MISCELLANEOUS.—MichaeI Callaghan, Eceleston, was fined 7s. 6d. and costs on a charge of being drunk and dis- orderly; Margaret Curren, Mary Johnson, and Elizabeth Lawrenson, the last named having been up several times previously, and spent during the last two years a great deal of her time in gaol, were sentenced to 14 days' imprison- ment for using obscene language in the street. MONDAY—Before Dr. Twyford and Mr. H. A. Bright. COLLIERS' WIVES BEGOlNG.—Susannah Prile and Ann Morris, colliers' wives, from Wigan, were charged with begging in Liverpool-road, on Sunday night, but they were discharged on promising to leave the town. DRUNKENNESS AND BREACHES OF THE PEACE—John Kelly, for being drunk at Windle was fined ss. and costs ; Richard Baines, of Sutton, was Charged with being drunk on Sunday night, and having been before the magistrates six times previously, he was fined 10s. ' and costs ; George Grimes was charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting with another.man on the canal bank, east, and , was bound over in £lO and one surety of £5 to keep the peace for three months; James Fryer, for allowing his dwelling-house chimney to be on fire, was fined Is. and costs. , A CAUTION TO GATE-KEEPERS.—John Hampton, of Rainford, was charged with wilfully obstructing the free passage of the railway station, at Rainford, by closing the road a long and unreasonable time.—P.C. Dutton said the gates were closed at twenty-five minutes past two on the morning of the 15th inst. A carter drove up to the gates and was unable to pass until twenty minutes to three, when the train came back from Rainford Junction —Defendant said he accompanied the train from Rainford ta the Junc- tion, that being part of his duty, and the passage was obstructed because he was unable to get back and open them, the luggage train being delayed by the fog.-In answer to the Bench, defendant admitted that it was his duty to open the gates before he went with the train.—Tbe case was dis- missed, and the defendant cautioned. SELLING WHISKEY ON THE ICE.— Thomas Tunstall, collier, Merton Bank-lane, was charged with selling intoxi- cating liquors without having a license authorising him to do so.—P.C. Cottam stated that on Friday, the 14th inst., be went to Carr Mill dam, which was frozen, and a great many persons were skating upon it. He saw defendant supply twopennyworth of whiskey to a man named Smith, and also to a man named Roberts.—P.C. Smith said he was in plain clothes, and asked defendant for twopennyworth of whiskey, which was supplied to him.—Tunstall, was fined 108. and costs. GAME CASES.—Charles Lawrenson was charged with using iancs te r,t aa ni dogalso for wtthh e p usingur pao si ue r cohf e rtadkoi gn gtoga l le goanmtehoe nlBt hthe 9th inst., being Sunday—Defendant pleaded guilty to the first charge, and not guilty to the latter.—Mr. Marsh ap- peared to prosecute on behalf of the Earl of Derby, and, after addressing the Bench, called Richard Hankinson, night watchman for the Earl of Derby.—Witness said he lived at Windle, and near Mr. Thomas Swift's farm. On the 18th inst. he was at home, when a neighbour came in and gave him some information. Ho went out and saw defendant with a dog. The defendant showed the dog a hare which was in a grass field, and the dog ran after it, killed it, and then returned and was put into the slip by the defendant, who sent some little boys to fetch the hare, but they were prevented by witness.—John Cropper was charged with using a dog for the purpose of taking game. A little boy named Halsall, residing with John Thompson, gamekeeper for Lord Derby, said that on the 18th inst., at half-past two, he was going on an errand to Mr. Ranson, Windle, when he saw two men, the defendants, with a dog in a slip, near the pl , Witness ran,cita nr tre se i tt do oladgb oh ranui st m3oa afters yt ear r what tsh, aaat nn he a killedao d seen ie te inta: Griffin Inn, Eccleston. He knew their names, and had defendants , known Cropper about 18 months, He saw Cropper take the hare. The utTohfetlhmarseli Cropper ran after the dog, took the hare from it, and placed whewn going to see a police- ith two more men, and his master told the defendants that they would be summoned. Superintendent Johnston said there were no similar offences andmi ti nn ,ohnt stehy7menkeet tt. followinghe w o morning, against the defendants. Lawrenson was fined 10s. and costs for the offence on the 9th, and both defendants were fined 10s. and costs on the charge of the 18th.—John Golding and William Hill, young men, were each charged with having, at Bold, unlawfully entered a certain close of land with a gamekeeper last Monday night was watching, when be gun for the purpose of taking game. Mr. Swift said that the saw three men coming along the road. One of them, how- ever parted company with the others, and there was no ,charge against him. Mr. Swift, having stated the case to the Bench, called Harry Davies, gamekeeper for William Charles Jones, the owner of land in Bold, where he also preserves game. On the night in question, he saw three men walking along the road. Two of the men turned up Sandy-lane, and the other, John Critchley, went straight along the road and passed witness. Witness, with another man named Whalley, followed the two men at a distance, and they found one standing at the hedge of a cabbage garden, and the other five or six yards off. Witness and his mate concealed themselves, and by so doing lost sight of the defendants for about 20 minutes. Ulti- mately witness saw a man standing near the garden in a field about 100 yards from the road, and close to the hedge of the cabbage garden. The man had a gun with him. Witness went towards him, and the man seeing some one approaching him, "took to his heels," witness shouting out to him that he knew him. He then went to Goulding's house, and in a short time Hill arrived, Goulding entering about three minutes later.—Cross-examined by Mr. Riley,

who appeared for the defence, witness said he did not hear any report of a gun during the 20 minutes they were con- cealed.—John Critchley, bricklayer, residing at Bold, said he was in company with the two defendants. After parting company with the defendants he came into contact with a farmer named Whalley, to whom he gave some information about the defendants.—Cross-examined by Mr. Riley, wit- ness said he was in the company of the defendants about two hours, and during all that time he never saw a gun in their possession, and he did not see they had a gun when they parted.—Samuel Whalley corroborated the keeper's statement, and said he saw the keeper chase both the defen- dants. The men passed close by him when pursued by the gamekeeper. Goulding had a gun in his possession at the time.—Mr. Riley said some of the evidence had come upon him as a great surprise. There was, however, a very strong circumstance that would cause a doubt to rise in the minds of their worships in the fact of the man Critchley saying that hesaw no gun in the possession of the defendants when he parted from them.—Goulding, who had been fined 6d. and costs for taking fish from a pond about two years ago, was fined .£2 and costs. Hill, a ship's carpenter, son of the late Mr. Hill, builder, St. Helens, was fined II and costs. A HUSBAND'S TROUBLES —Jonathan Tunstall was charged with assaulting Elizabeth Tunstall, his wife, on the 15th January.—Complainant said her husband, on Saturday night, kicked her out of doors, and threatened to knock her head off.—Defewlant, who appeared to be very deaf, said he went home and asked for his supper, which was not ready. They got to words, and defendant told his wife that he was "not going to walk about the streets ashamed of himself, over head and ears in debt," and if there was not an altera- tion made before long she had better leave the house, as her room was better than her company. Bills were continually coming in to him of his wife's transactions, and he had been obliged to pawn his watch in order to pay off part of his debts.—The case was dismissed, and the defendant asked that he might have the children and live away from his wife.—The Bench said they could do nothing in the matter, and P.C. Wellwood caused some amusement by ordering the couple off with the injunction, Go home, and make it up." A PAINFUL CASE.—Peter Fredsham, about 18 years of age, residing in Windle, was charged with stealing a rail- wapeleeper from a siding of the London and North-Western Railway Company, at St. Helens.—A policeman charged him with the offence, and in reply the prisoner said he had taken it home to make a fire, as his little brothers and sisters were starving.—As prisoner had been in the cells two or three days, he was discharged on the payment of Sc. by his father.

STEALING COAL—Martin Mullen was charged with steal- ing a quantity of coal from some wagons, the property of Messrs. Lockwood and Leith, on Friday evening.—A boy deposed to seeing prisoner filling a bag with coals out of a wagon, and prisoner, who had several previous convictions recorded against him, was sent to prison for 14 days. A VERY CURIOUS MISTAKE.—WiIIiam Dixon was charged with stealing a glass from the Globe Vaults, Ormakirk-street, on Saturday.—Charles Henry Taylor, manager of the vaults, said the prisoner and his wife called at his house for a "glass of rum hot," which he ordered to be served.—A ser- vant deposed to serving the rum to prisoner, who, on being afterwards charged with stealing the glass, said he "put the glass in his pocket in a mistake."—Prisoner was sent to prison for 21 days. THE SCUFFLE AT THE CHARITY BALL —John Kelly, a young man, a book-keepef for a firm of builders in the town, was charged with assaulting Joseph Tideswell, keeper of the Town Hall. Mr. Swift appeared to prosecute, and Mr. I Riley represented the defendant. From the complainant's' evidence it appeared that on the occasion of the Catholic ball, and shortly after four o'clock in the morning, defendant I caused some disturbance in the arrangement of the coats drc., which were in the charge of the complainant and his assis- tants, defendant having los, his coat ticket. He was told to wait until the company had dispersed. Kelly ultimately got his coat, and on the Town Hall keeper going to turn out the I lights and lock the doors, he, to his surprise, saw Kelly with some bandmen in the refreshment department. He told 'them that it was time to go home, and as Kelly was ad- vanced in drink, he led him down the Town Hall steps, leaving him safe in the street. Afterwards he went to finish his duties. He again found the defendant in the hall, and again conducted him to the bottom of the steps, using no II more violence than was necessary, and advising him to go home. Kelly used foul language, and said that he would do as he liked. Tideswell said he would have to be cross with him if he did not go away, and on Tideswell turning round to go up the steps he felt a knock upon the eye, the force of which knocked him to the ground, and a slight scuffle ensued. He pursued his duties and on going home he found his eye was considerably damaged and be applied a leach. He had been attended by a surgeon, and was under his care at the time. In consequence of the injury inflicted be was confined to his bed six days.—Cross-examined by Mr. Riley: (Tideswell) did not know that he was a man of considerablearritability, and he did not threaten to throw somebody down stairs after the previous charity ball; but he had a row with Kirkham, the auctioneer. It was not a fact he fell out with the corporate officials awhile ago, though he had been summoned by one for having threatened his life, and was bound over.—Mr. Riley contended that justice had been fully met on the night of the ball. Good temper and civility were esential qualifications for a hall keeper, and no doubt Tideswell had taken that action, as he would be aware that the using of any unnecessary violence would jeopardise his position. He had, therefore, a substantial interest in proving that he was the aggrieved and not the aggressor; and it was important to remember that there were no witnesses to the assault. Tideswell had said Kelly was drunk, and he thought that the Bench could not conceive that Kelly aimed a deliberate blow at Tideswell. No doubt both of them were excited, one of them from his natural irritability of temper, and the other through , having taken drink. Tideswell could not parade himself as a paragon of good temper, and he asked their worships not to stigmatise Kelly as a violent and even wicked man who had no regard for the feelings of others.—Mr. James Bennett, Raven Hotel, deposed to seeing Tideswell drag Kelly down the steps like a piece of timber • John Leonard, polisher at the Union plate glass works, said he saw two men scuffling in the street, and to the best of his opinion the stouter man (meaning Tides- well) was on the top of the other.—Defendant was fined 40s. and costs.—Mr. Swift made an application for the solicitor's fee, but the Bench declined to grant it. IST. HELENS CALEDONIAN ASSOCIA- TION ANNUAL DINNER.

- - The first dinner of this society, which is to be made an annual affair, was given on Tuesday evening, in the Fleece Hotel. The society has been in existence a year, and was formed for the purpose of eutabliehing and fostering a social feeling between the Scotehmen og the town, and for reliev- ing those of their countrymen who stood in need of help. The dinner was appropriately decided to be held on Tuesday night—the evening of the 25th January being what is known in Scotch parlance as "Burns' Nicht." About forty persons sat down to dinner, which was prepared in Mrs. Taylor's usual style, and was heartily enjoyed by those who partook of it. Two splendid haggises, or Scotch puddings, graced the table, and they were said to be the finest ever served in the town. They were supplied by Mr. Morton. Mr. Sutherland occupied the chair, and Dr. Ogden the vice-chair. After the usual loyal and patriotic toasts had been given, The SECRETARY (Mr. Muir) said the first meeting of the Caledonian Association was held in December, 1879, when the society was formed, and it had gone on ever since. The total receipts amounted to £7 Ss. 6d, and there was a little balance left over. The expenses were rather heavy, seeing that the society was newly formed, but they had relieved over 50 persons and sent them to where they desired to go. The subscription was 10s., but they were now going to re- duce it to 2s. 6d., because, finding Abet 15 persons had carried the society on at 10s., they thought they might get 50 at the lower rate. He hoped they would be able to enrol a great many more members, and while they did not admit Englishmen—as a member af the society must be a native of Scotland, be of Scotch parentage, or have property in Scotland—they would not, however, refuse the English- man's mite. (Applause.) Dr. OGDEN then proposed the toast of the "Caledonian Association," and spoke of the good the society had been able to accomplish. There were a great many Scotchrnen in St. Helens, and he thought that by a little effort the society might be considerably increased in numbers.

The toateit having been drunk, Mr. WILLIAMSON responded on behalf of the association, and said that as St. Helens was midway between two large towns, Liverpool and Manchester, a good many people necessarily passed through from one town to the other, and of course mmy were Scotchmen, 50 of whom they had heard had been relieved. Not only had the secretary re- lieved them, but he had accompanied them to the station and, as a proof that the money had not been ill-spent, NW. Muir had obtained the ticket at the railway station. (Cheers.) The CHAIRMAN then proposed "the Memory of Burns' remarking that wherever a Scotchman was found there was an admirer of Robert Burns. (Hear, hear.) In England the great poet was Shakespeare, in Ireland they had Moore, and in Scotland Burns. They commenced that evening's dinner by saying Burns' "Grace before dinner," and though some people said that Burns was not an authority in sacred matters, still in this respect he showed a master's hand, as he did in sentimental matters. He would ask them to drink to the "Memory of the immortal Burns." The toast having been drunk, "Our Native Land" was afterwards given and other toasts followed. Dluing the evening Mr. A. Muir sang "Hearts of Oak," Mr. James Russell "Scotch Eminence," Mr. Dunlop (draper) a humorous Scotch song, Mr. McEwing, song. Mr. Roderick McKenzie, of Liverpool, was engaged specially for the oc- casion, and, in the historical dress of a Scotch Highlander, he performed at intervals specimens of bag-pipe music.

INQUEST AT STOCKTON —HBATIL—On Monday Mr. James E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the London Bridge Inn, Stockton Heath, touching the death of John Jones, 84 years of age, who resided at Apple- ton. On Friday, the 21st inst., a widow named Hannah Holtewho has been in the habit of visiting the deceased, went to his house and found him laid on the floor behind the door. She called in a neighbour and his wife, and then went for a police constable. P.C. Fryer on his arrival raised the man up, but he was dead and quite cold. There were no marks of violence on the body, and the goods in the house had not been in any way disturbed. Under these circumstances the jury returned a verdict of " mnd dead." At the Coroner's inquest at Accrington, on Thursday, as to the death of Henrietta Leaver, aged six years, a verdict of wilful murder was returned against the fatlaer, James Leaver.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The weekly meeting of this Board was held on Wednes- day, at the Workhouse, under the presidency of Mr. W. Darbyshire. There were also present—Messrs. Wallington, Blackhurst, Harrison, Woolfall, Brown, Longshaw, Marsh, Hall, Gibson, Houghton, Kilshall, Pennington, Fairhurst, and J. C. Sutton (clerk). THE STATE OF THE HOUSE. The MASTER (Mr. G. Mackey), in his weekly report, stated that the number of inmates in the preceding week , was 513; admitted, 51; discharged, 9; dead, 3; total, 552; as compared with 490 in the corresponding week in last year. I During the week 94 vagrants had been relieved, of whom 75 were men, 14 women, and five children. MAJOR CARTWRIGHT OBJECTS. During the administration of relief, MajorCaRTWItIOHT complained that the Chairinan and the Clerk virtually decided the amount of relief to be given in certain cases without having put it to the Board, a course to which he took strong objection. Addressing the Clerk, , he remarked: You are not the governor of the Board in the distrioution of relief. I object to it very strongly. Let us have no whispering, please. What you have to say, speak up. Mr. BROWN said in deference to the Chairman, Major Cartwright's remarks were uncalled for. The fact was the Major sat there with two or three others in private conver- sation, the cases were heard and deliberated upon, and he said nothing, but at the end he found fault. This was not a solitary case. It was unfortunately the common rule at this Board. If the gentlemen wou'd only listen to the cases, and let them get on with the work, the Hoard would get done in half the time. LONGSHAW : I do think Major Cartwright is very hard this morning upon the chairman. The chairman comes punctually to take the chair and. give relief to the poor people, and we are determined the poor people shall have relief. Here are three of us who came to give relief, and ' then the others come at eleven o'clock for special business, and everything must be knocked aside for them. Then these questions are raised; but if these gentlemen would attend with the chairman the business would be got through and the poor people sent away. I do think it is out of place. Major Cartwright wants to be chairman, and the whole of the Board! (Applause.) Major CARTWRIGHT: I never heard anything like it. Mr. WONALFALL : I object to the statement made by Mr. Longshaw. He says there were only the chairman and two or three other Guardians present at ten o'clock. I and Mr. Harrison were here before half-past ten ' • but we were not in this room. We were attending to the business in the other room. Therefore I object to the remarks of Mr. Longshaw. Mr. WALLINGTON : Mr. Chairman, let us go on with the business. The CHAIRMAN: I should like to make some remarks. Major CARTWRIGHT: I pat it very fairly. I say this, let us hear. The CHAIRMAN: You have spoken. I should like to make one or two remarks. It was a case that did not want much consideration. It was a woman who had been able to keep her children for the last five years, and the officer said she was not in a poorer position than she had been during the last five years. She was an able-bodied woman, and the law expec ed an able-bodied woman to keep herself and one child. She had two children, and it was the custom of the Board to give Is. 6d. per week to one child. She had only two, and he did not think it was necessary to put the ques- tion to the Board, because it was not deviating from the practise of giving Is. 6d. for one child. Major CARTWRIGHT: Do I understand you that it was an additional is. 6d. The CHAIRMAN: No, it is the first application. Major CARTWRIGHT: Aye, for three of them. She had no work. The CHAIRMAN: She has work. Major CARTWRIGHT: But she said here to-day that she had no work to go to. Mr. BROWN: The fact is that the Major has not heard the case; and why should our time be taken up by having it repeated? It is a piece of liberty taken by Major Cart- wright. The CLERK: She is a fustian cutter, working for Mr. Platt. The CHAIRMAN: And she has 7s. a week coming in. Major CARTWRIGHT: But she said trade was bad. The CLERK: I should like to know if I am to answer the chairman when he puts a question to me. I should not be taken to task by a single member of the Board. I should like to get the decision of the whole Board on the question. One member should not school and rate me in that way. Major CARTWRIGHT: I did not school and rate you at all. Let us hear what you say to the chairman, and then we shall be satisfied. Mr. Bnowle : You are there, and why don't you pay atten- tion. Major CARTWRIGHT: I do pay attention. Mr. Bt./km{l3lm : Well, I don't see much in it to make all this noise about it. The allowance of is. 6d. a week was ultimately granted. OUT-DOOR RELIEF. Major CARTWRIGHT asked what the increase of out-door relief was. Had the clerk any idea? The CLERK: No; I have not at this moment. I will give you a list next week: Mr. Wanmorctrow remarked that Mr. Harbourne's relief had increased from £3O to .£35. THE NEW OFFICERS. The CLERK read communications from the Lai Govern- ment Board approving of the appointments of Miss Harriet Pugh as nurse' and Mr. Basil Shearer as enquiry officer, and also stating that the plans of the fever hospital would be taken into consideration as soon as circumstances in that department would permit. THE CALLS. The CLERK stated that Warrington was the only township which had paid the call for the current half-year. Burton- wood owed 2, Cuerdley 1, Grappenhall 2, Haydock 1, Houghton 2, Latchford 2, Newton nearly 3, Penketh 2, Rix- ton 3, Sankey 1, Southworth 3, Thelwall 2, Winwick 1, and Rixton 1. He asked that those townships who were two calls in arrear should be summoned. The Board instructed the Clerk to take out summonses against the defaulting overseers. A SEAMSTRESS WANTED. The visitors' book contained the following entry :—Mrs. Mackey made an application for a temporary seamstress during the present pressure of inmates in the House. The Committee recommended one to to obtained at a salary not exceeding £25 a year and rations. Major CARTWRIGHT stated the number of inmates admitted last week was 51. Up to that morning he was very glad to find there were only 10 admitted, making an increase of 61. They bad now within four, half as many children as there were at the Barracks. There were only Mrs. Mackey and Ellen Langley to do the work and the committee recom- mended some assistance. Ellen Langley was engaged in the cooking department. The CHAIRMAN : Is the pauper labour all utilised? Major CARTWRIGHT: There is very little of it, lam sorry to say. Mr. WALLINGTON thought there were not sufficient members present to pass such a recommendation as that proposed.

The Cweinmest said if it was a temporary appointment they could make it that day, but if they were going to appoint a person permanently at a yearly salary of £25 and ratio's, they would have to give notice. Major CARTWRIGHT : Precisely, that is what we object to. The CHAIRMAN: By the next Board day, a fortnight hence, the pressure may be over. I think Mrs. Mackey ought to get a person to assist at once. Mr. WALLINGTON : Will that person be dismissed as soon as the pressure is over ? Major CARTWRIGHT said it would be competent for any member to move that she be dismissed. The recommendation was approved, although Mr. Wallington thought a seamstress could be got for Tess money.

SCHOOL SUPERINTENDENT'S REPOILT. The superintendent of the school (Mr. H. M. Mines) re- ported that the number of children attending school was 105 boys and 75 girls—total 181. Of this number 40 boys and 40 girls were receiving industrial training. Admitted during the week 19, discharged 0, sent to hospital 5, returned 3. According to article 91 of the new regulations, he had written to the Clerk informing him that the schools were now full, the number of children having reached the maximum. He had also asked for orders for admission to the schools in future to be granted on a set day of the week, and also that requisitions for food might be made out on the same day in order to facilitate their work. The additional help granted by the Board on Wednesday last had not yet been furnished. Considering the extreme severity of the weather he was pleased to report that the children continued in a remark- ably healthy condition. Mr. Bnowm : I wish something could be done whereby boys and girls could be sent out to service or apprenticed, and lodge in the house. Major CAR TwltionT : Oh, no, that would never do. You must not make this house into a lodging house. 11 V. rli■ --.1" R. • •••',Nit.7...• -• MISTABLISIIMENT, DOG and WINE LICENCES.— . .112,1 The Commissioners of Inland Revenue remind those who keep Carriages, or Male Servants, or who use Armorial Bearings, that their Licences must be renewed in the month of January. Dog Licences must be renewed at the same time, and when- ever any additional Dog is kept a Licence must be immediately obtained. Farmers and shepherds may obtain exemptions for Dogs kept and used solely for tending sheep or cattle on a farm, but a declaration that the dogs are so used must be made to the Supervisor of Excise for the district. Licences or exemptions are not transferable from one person to another. The penalty for keeping a dog without licence or exemption is £5, TAKIIiG ORDERS FOR Wrms, Stn.—The Commissioners also give notice that no person may solicit, take, or receive any order for wine or spirits unless he holds a licence for that pur- pose or is the bona fide traveller for a firm duly lioenoed in the United Kingdom. The penalty for so acting without licence is £lOO. When the residence of the offender is not known, orls out of the United Kingdom, the summons will be left at the house or place where the offence was committed. London, lst January, 1881.
